questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation is brought to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and colicky suprapubic pain radiating to the back. Her temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), blood pressure is 110/76 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination reveals a dilated cervix with visible products of conception. Suction curettage is performed, and all products of conception are evacuated. Maternal serum laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit: 32% Leukocyte count: 8,000/µL Blood type: AB negative Anti-Rh antibody titer: Negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Administer anti-D immune globulin to the woman.
No further workup or therapy for the woman or fetus
Order materal blood and endometrial cultures
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Administer anti-D immune globulin to the woman.

Rh-negative pregnant women exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood can develop Rh alloimmunization, leading to hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn in future pregnancies.

Indication in This Case:

•

Rh-negative mother (AB negative)

•

Abortion with evacuation of products of conception

•

Negative anti-Rh antibody titer → not yet sensitized

Management:

Administer anti-D immunoglobulin (RhIg) to prevent maternal formation of anti-D antibodies.
questions.learning: Administer anti-D immune globulin to the woman. Rh-negative pregnant women exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood can develop Rh alloimmunization, leading to hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn in future pregnancies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ritodrine is a medication primarily used to prevent premature labor. Which of the following is NOT a typical maternal complication associated with its use?
questions.explanation: Ritodrine is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist used as a tocolytic to suppress uterine contractions in preterm labor. Due to its systemic beta-adrenergic effects, it is associated with several well-known maternal complications. These include fine skeletal muscle tremors (Option A), significant tachycardia and palpitations (Option B), and potentially life-threatening pulmonary edema (Option D), especially when used with corticosteroids or excessive IV fluids. Notably, the metabolic effect of ritodrine is to increase blood sugar levels through glycogenolysis; therefore, it causes hyperglycemia, NOT hypoglycemia (Option C). Hypoglycemia is the correct "NOT" choice as it is the opposite of the expected physiological response to beta-agonists. Clinicians must carefully monitor maternal pulse, lung sounds, and glucose levels during ritodrine administration to ensure patient safety. Thus, hyperglycemia is the standard metabolic side effect of this medication
questions.learning: Ritodrine is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist used as a tocolytic to suppress uterine contractions in preterm labor. Due to its systemic beta-adrenergic effects, it is associated with several well-known maternal complications.

questions.text: Which of the following is true for decorticate rigidity?
options: It is produced by the removal of cerebral cortex and basal ganglia
Flexion of lower limbs and extension of upper limbs occurs
It is characterized by flexion of upper limbs and extension of lower limbs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is characterized by flexion of upper limbs and extension of lower limbs

• Removal of the cerebral cortex (decortication) produces decorticate rigidity.
• Characterized by flexion of the upper extremities at the elbow and extensor hyperactivity in the lower extremities.
• The flexion can be explained by active rubrospinal excitation of flexor muscles in the upper extremities; the hyperextension of lower extremities is due to the same changes that occur after midcollicular decerebration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are examples of primary active transport except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SGLT

Primary active transport directly utilizes energy from ATP hydrolysis to move substances against their electrochemical gradient. In contrast, secondary active transport uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (usually Na⁺) that was generated by primary active transport.

• SGLT (Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter) does not directly use ATP.
• It transports glucose against its concentration gradient by utilizing the Na⁺ gradient created by the Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase.
• Therefore, SGLT is a secondary active transporter, not a primary active transporter.

| Primary Active Transport | Secondary Active Transport

| ------------------------ | --------------------------

| Direct ATP use | Indirect ATP use

| Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase | SGLT

| H⁺-K⁺-ATPase | Na⁺-amino acid cotransporter

| Ca²⁺-ATPase | Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28 year old male admitted with history of altered sensorium and hydrophobia. A suspicion of rabies was made and you want to diagnose the condition. You have taken corneal scrapings from the patient and which of the following tests will you do to confirm your diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Viral culture

Viral culture from corneal scrapings is used to confirm diagnosis.

Multiple tests in succession/simultaneously are the best. Usually Direct Fluorescent Antibody test followed by virus isolation/culture is useful.

Virus isolation through culture: Best specimens are brain and saliva. CSF, corneal smears and centrifuged urine can also be used.

Option A: Serological tests like indirect immunofluorescence are insensitive.

Option B: Negri bodies can only be demonstrated in brain (pyramidal cells of Ammon’s horn, and the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum are the most common site).

Option D: Real time-PCR Amplification Detection of rabies virus RNA is highly sensitive and specific. This technique can detect virus in freshsaliva samples, skin, CSF, and brain tissues. However it is not confirmatory test.
questions.learning: Viral culture Viral culture from corneal scrapings is used to confirm diagnosis. Multiple tests in succession/simultaneously are the best.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden-onset right leg pain. An investigation was done, and the obtained image is shown below. What is the investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ultrasound Doppler

The image shows a triphasic pattern of the arterial waveform, which is seen in the ultrasound doppler.

Doppler ultrasound is used in diagnosing peripheral arterial disease. It uses a handheld doppler ultrasound probe placed at an arterial site. This transmits a continuous wave. A receiver inside the probe picks up the reflected beam. The change in frequency between the reflected beam and the transmitted beam gets converted to a pulsatile audio signal.

A normal arterial wave has a triphasic signal. A triphasic wave has three waveforms consisting of a sharp systolic wave with a forward uprise and fall, a second wave with reverse flow occurring in diastole, and the last wave with a forward flow taking place during diastole.

Doppler ultrasound can detect moving blood. However, it does not provide information on whether the blood flow is sufficient for the maintenance of limb viability.

Other options:

Option A: Digital subtraction percutaneous angiography (DSA) is a procedure wherein a radiopaque dye is usually injected percutaneously into the femoral artery. Images obtained are digitalized and the background may be removed for a clear image. It provides information on dynamic arterial flow and can be combined with endovascular intervention if needed.

Option C: Plethysmography is a semi-quantitative method to measure segmental blood flow and velocity in the carotid and peripheral vascular systems.

Option D: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or MR angiography, is an imaging modality that can be used when duplex ultrasonography cannot be done or if it cannot produce a clear image. MRA avoids ionizing radiation.
questions.learning: Ultrasound Doppler — The image shows a triphasic pattern of the arterial waveform, which is seen in the ultrasound doppler. Doppler ultrasound is used in diagnosing peripheral arterial disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best investigation for aneuploidy? A.In Situ Hybridization B.Conventional cytogenetics C.PCR D.Sanger sequencing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A & B

Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy). The most appropriate investigations are karyotyping (conventional cytogenetics) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) because they directly evaluate chromosome number and structure.

• Conventional cytogenetics (karyotyping) visualizes the entire chromosome set and is the gold standard for detecting numerical abnormalities such as trisomy 21, trisomy 18, and monosomy X.
• In situ hybridization (FISH) uses fluorescent probes targeting specific chromosomes and provides rapid detection of aneuploidy, commonly used in prenatal and interphase cells.

PCR and Sanger sequencing are primarily used to detect gene-level mutations or small sequence variations, not whole-chromosome number abnormalities. Therefore, they are not ideal for detecting aneuploidy.
questions.learning: A & B Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy). The most appropriate investigations are karyotyping (conventional cytogenetics) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) because they directly evaluate…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During an autopsy of a 65-year-old man who died from myocardial infarction, which staining methods are commonly employed to demonstrate infarcted areas of the heart muscle?
questions.explanation: During a forensic or clinical autopsy, detecting an early myocardial infarction (typically 2-12 hours old) can be challenging through gross examination alone. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) is the macroscopic staining technique used to highlight areas of infarction. TTC reacts with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in viable myocardium to produce a deep red color. In infarcted tissue, where enzymes have leaked out, the area remains pale or unstained, allowing for clear visualization of the damaged region. Oil red O (Option A) and Sudan black B (Option C) are used to stain lipids and are not specific for myocardial ischemia. Masson trichrome (Option D) is a histological stain used to highlight collagen (fibrosis) in old, healed infarctions, rather than the acute phase. Using TTC allows pathologists to accurately locate and measure the extent of the ischemic injury shortly after death. This is essential for confirming the cause of death in cases of sudden cardiac arrest where traditional histological changes might not have had sufficient time to develop
questions.learning: During a forensic or clinical autopsy, detecting an early myocardial infarction (typically 2-12 hours old) can be challenging through gross examination alone.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, excessive nasal discharge, and a solid, purplish mass in the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a teenage male with recurrent, spontaneous, profuse epistaxis (nosebleeds) and a visible, purplish, vascular mass in the nasopharynx is pathognomonic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option A) is more common in adults and is associated with Ebstein-Barr virus and neck nodes. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B) is a malignant tumor seen in younger children and is usually more destructive. Pyogenic granuloma (Option C) is typically a small, friable lesion on the nasal septum (Little’s area) rather than a large nasopharyngeal growth. Because the demographic and the site of the vascular growth are so specific, JNA is the definitive diagnosis. Biopsy is generally avoided due to the extreme risk of hemorrhage; diagnosis is confirmed via imaging like CT or MRI showing Holman-Miller sign
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a teenage male with recurrent, spontaneous, profuse epistaxis (nosebleeds) and a visible, purplish, vascular mass in the nasopharynx is pathognomonic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme?
questions.explanation: Tolcapone is a medication used as adjunct therapy in Parkinson’s disease. Its specific mechanism of action is the inhibition of the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) enzyme. This enzyme is responsible for the metabolic breakdown of catecholamines, including levodopa and dopamine; inhibiting it prolongs the duration of action of these catechols in the CNS and peripheral tissues. Amantadine (Option A) works by increasing dopamine release and inhibiting its reuptake. Rotigotine (Option B) is a dopamine receptor agonist. Selegiline (Option D) is a selective monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitor that prevents the breakdown of dopamine within the brain. Because only tolcapone targets the COMT pathway, it is the correct answer for this biochemical mechanism. Note that tolcapone requires regular monitoring due to the risk of hepatotoxicity
questions.learning: Tolcapone is a medication used as adjunct therapy in Parkinson’s disease. Its specific mechanism of action is the inhibition of the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with a defect in collagen maturity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scurvy

Scurvy is associated with a defect in collagen maturity.

Scurvy results from ascorbic acid or vitamin C deficiency. Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for the enzyme prolyl hydroxylase, required for the hydroxylation of prolyl residues in collagen. This enables each collagen fibril to form a uniform and flexible triple helix configuration in the body’s connective tissues.

Its deficiency results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, thereby resulting in the impaired formation of mature connective tissue; the clinical manifestations of this deficiency include petechiae, ecchymosis, coiled hairs, inflamed and bleeding gums, joint effusion, tooth loss, bone fracture,  poor wound healing, and fatigue which can be attributed to impaired collagen synthesis all of which are typical of scurvy.

Risk factors include chronic alcoholism, diseases such as celiac disease and Crohn’s disease, associated with malabsorption and poor nutrition.

It is treated with vitamin C supplementation.

Other options:

Option B- Rickets is caused due to deficiency of vitamin D in children which is characterized by the continued formation of the collagen matrix of bone but its incomplete mineralization or demineralization. Children have soft, pliable bones.

Option C- Beriberi is caused due to deficiency of thiamine. It can either be dry beriberi characterized by peripheral neuropathy or wet beriberi characterized by edema due to dilated cardiomyopathy.

Option D- Night blindness is caused by a deficiency of vitamin A. Deficiency can also lead to pancreatic insufficiency, repeated gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and urinary infections, and xeropthalmia.
questions.learning: Scurvy Scurvy is associated with a defect in collagen maturity. Scurvy results from ascorbic acid or vitamin C deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought with progressive pallor, recurrent infections, and failure to thrive. On examination, the child has hypopigmented skin and sparse, light-colored hair. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia and neutropenia. Which of the following micronutrient deficiencies best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copper

The combination of anemia + neutropenia + hypopigmentation of skin and hair is characteristic of copper deficiency. Copper is a cofactor for several important enzymes:

• Ceruloplasmin → involved in iron metabolism (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺)
• Cytochrome c oxidase → energy production
• Tyrosinase → melanin synthesis

Pathophysiology:

• ↓ Ceruloplasmin → impaired iron mobilization → anemia
• Impaired immune function → neutropenia
• ↓ Tyrosinase activity → ↓ melanin → hypopigmentation

Clinical associations:

• Malnutrition
• Excess zinc intake (interferes with copper absorption)
• Menkes disease (genetic copper deficiency)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Zinc: Causes dermatitis, delayed wound healing
• Selenium: Cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease)
• Iron: Causes anemia only (no neutropenia or hypopigmentation)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient receiving antitubercular therapy (ATT) develops visual disturbances. Which ATT drug is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the high-yield pharmacological principle detailed in Question 75. Among the first-line antitubercular drugs, Ethambutol is well-known for causing optic neuritis, leading to visual problems such as decreased acuity and red-green color blindness. Rifampicin (Option A) affects the liver and causes red fluid discoloration. Streptomycin (Option B) targets the eighth cranial nerve, causing hearing loss and balance issues. Pyrazinamide (Option D) is most associated with liver toxicity and joint pain due to high uric acid. The ocular toxicity of Ethambutol is often related to the total cumulative dose. It is vital for clinicians to perform regular visual screening for any patient on a long-term course of this medication. If a patient reports "blurred vision" or difficulty seeing traffic lights (red/green), the drug must be discontinued immediately to prevent permanent blindness. This specific side effect is a favorite topic on medical board exams due to its serious clinical implications

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a direct cause of maternal death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eclampsia

Eclampsia is a direct cause of maternal death, whereas the other options given are indirect causes of maternal death.

The ICD(International Classification of Diseases) has recommended dividing maternal deaths into two groups :

* Direct obstetric deaths are maternal deaths resulting from obstetric complications of the pregnant state like pregnancy, labor and puerperium or from interventions like incorrect treatment or a chain of events resulting from any of the above.

* Indirect obstetric deaths are maternal deaths resulting from previous existing diseases or diseases that developed during pregnancy and which were not due to direct obstetric causes, but which were aggravated by physiological effects of pregnancy.

The main global causes of maternal deaths are:

* Severe bleeding

* Indirect causes (anemia, malaria, heart diseases)

* Direct causes (infections, unsafe abortions, eclampsia, obstructed labor, ectopic pregnancy, anesthesia-related complications, etc.).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following induction agents is most appropriate for a patient with cardiac disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate is considered to be the most appropriate induction agent for cardiac patients.

Etomidate has minimal effect on cardiovascular function due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptors. They act on alpha 2 adrenoreceptors and increase blood pressure which helps to maintain cardiovascular stability after the induction.

Etomidate is the induction agent of choice in patients with cardiovascular disease, reactive airway disease, and intracranial hypertension,

Due to its unique hemodynamic stability, it is used as a short-term sedative in hemodynamically unstable patients like patients requiring cardioversion or in patients with unstable angina for minor operative procedures.

Long-term use of etomidate in trauma or terminally ill patients will cause a reversible inhibition on 11 beta-hydroxylase which decreases cortisol production and increase 11 deoxycorticosterone. This results in adrenocortical suppression.

Other options:

Option A- Ketamine has a stimulatory effect on the sympathetic nervous system and results in increased blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This leads to an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption and so it is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease.

Option C- Propofol is a myocardial depressant agent. It reduces sympathetic activity, leading to vasodilatation that results in a reduction of blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

Option D- Thiopentone is also a myocardial depressant agent. It causes peripheral vasodilatation, reduction in the ventricular filling, negative inotropic effect, and reduction in a sympathetic outflow from CNS. this results in a reduction in blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.
questions.learning: Etomidate Etomidate is considered to be the most appropriate induction agent for cardiac patients. Etomidate has minimal effect on cardiovascular function due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptors.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaints of poor vision in one eye. On examination, there is no obvious squint. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction reveals +1.00 D in the right eye and +5.50 D in the left eye. Fundus examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anisometropic amblyopia

Anisometropia is defined as a difference in refractive error between the two eyes, leading to unequal image clarity.

Difference in myopia, hypermetropia, or astigmatism between eyes.

Clinical significance:

• Can cause anisometropic amblyopia (lazy eye) in children
• Due to unequal image size/clarity (aniseikonia) → brain suppresses one eye
• Important cause of unilateral amblyopia

Types of Amblyopia (Lazy Eye)

A. Isoametropic Amblyopia

Occurs when both eyes have high but equal refractive error.

• Brain receives blurred images from both eyes.
• Usually due to high:

• hypermetropia,
• myopia,
• or astigmatism in both eyes equally.

Example:

Both eyes have +7D hypermetropia → bilateral blurred vision → amblyopia develops in both eyes.

B. Strabismic Amblyopia

Occurs due to squint (strabismus).

• Brain suppresses image from deviated eye to avoid diplopia.
• Suppressed eye becomes amblyopic.

Example:

Child with esotropia suppresses input from one eye → reduced vision in that eye.

C. Anisometropic Amblyopia

Occurs when there is unequal refractive error between the two eyes.

• Brain prefers clearer image from better eye.
• Blurred eye gets suppressed and becomes amblyopic.

Example:

One eye +1D, other eye +6D hypermetropia → poorer eye develops amblyopia.

D. Deprivation Amblyopia

Occurs when visual stimulus is blocked during visual development.

• Most severe form.
• Due to obstruction of visual axis.

Causes:

• Congenital cataract
• Ptosis
• Corneal opacity

Example:

Unilateral congenital cataract prevents image formation → amblyopia.
questions.learning: Anisometropic amblyopia Anisometropia is defined as a difference in refractive error between the two eyes, leading to unequal image clarity. Difference in myopia, hypermetropia, or astigmatism between eyes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The laboratory results show serum triglyceride levels > 2000 mg/dl. Which deficiency could be contributing to the patient's condition?

VLDL- very low density lipoprotein
LDL- low density lipoprotein
HDL- high density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Apolipoprotein C II

The elevated triglyceride levels and symptoms of acute pancreatitis are likely related to a deficiency in apolipoprotein C II.

Apolipoprotein C2 is a lipoprotein lipase cofactor that catalyzes cleavage of chylomicrons. Defective apo C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Lipoprotein lipase is an extracellular enzyme that is present in the capillary walls of most tissues. It is chiefly synthesized by the adipose tissue, and cardiac and skeletal muscles. A deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II leads to type 1 hyperlipoproteinemia or familial chylomicronemia which leads to an increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

Option B: Apo B48 is involved in the assembly of chylomicrons. Defects in this protein are not associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.

Option C: Apo B100 binds low-density lipoprotein receptors. For the uptake of LDL, apo B100 acts as a ligand for the low-density lipoprotein receptor.

Option D: Apo A1 activates lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). LCAT is the enzyme present in HDL, which is activated by apo A1. LCAT converts free cholesterol (amphipathic) in HDL to cholesterol ester(hydrophobic). The initial discoidal shape now becomes spherical. This facilitates reverse cholesterol transport.
questions.learning: Apolipoprotein C II — The elevated triglyceride levels and symptoms of acute pancreatitis are likely related to a deficiency in apolipoprotein C II. Apolipoprotein C2 is a lipoprotein lipase cofactor that catalyzes cleavage of chylomicrons.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs used in the treatment of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) has a direct spasmolytic action on gastrointestinal (GI) smooth muscle?

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A scientist is studying the invasion of malignant colon cancer cells into surrounding tissues in an experimental model. Over time, the cancer cells are observed to detach from each other and degrade the extracellular matrix, allowing the tumor cells to invade the basement membrane and access nearby blood vessels. Which of the following substances is most likely upregulated to facilitate basement membrane invasion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metalloproteinases

Tumor invasion and metastasis require cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) and basement membrane to spread into surrounding tissues and blood vessels. A key mechanism is the upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which are enzymes that break down components of the ECM, including:

• Type IV collagen (major component of basement membrane)
• Laminin
• Proteoglycans

This degradation allows tumor cells to penetrate the basement membrane and invade adjacent tissues, facilitating metastasis.

Why not the other options:

A. Acid hydrolases: Lysosomal enzymes involved in intracellular digestion, not the main enzymes degrading the basement membrane during tumor invasion.

B. E-cadherin: A cell adhesion molecule. In cancer invasion it is typically downregulated, allowing tumor cells to detach from each other.

C. Hyaluronic acid: A component of extracellular matrix that helps tissue hydration and cell migration but does not degrade the basement membrane.
questions.learning: Metalloproteinases Tumor invasion and metastasis require cancer cells to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) and basement membrane to spread into surrounding tissues and blood vessels.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Examine the given clinical image. Which of the following surgeries is being performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total maxillectomy

The image depicts a Weber–Ferguson incision, which is classically used for total maxillectomy to provide wide exposure of the maxilla, orbit, and nasal cavity.

• Total maxillectomy involves removal of the entire maxilla, often including:

• Maxillary sinus
• Hard palate
• Part of orbital floor (depending on extent)

• Indicated for malignancies of maxilla/maxillary sinus

• Weber–Ferguson incision:

• Extends from upper lip → along nose → infraorbital region
• Provides excellent access to midface structures

Why not other options:

• Partial maxillectomy: Limited resection, less extensive incision
• Ethmoidectomy (partial/total): Done endoscopically or via medial orbital approach, not this incision

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A molecular biologist is investigating whether a specific transcription factor binds to the promoter region of a target gene in living cells. The researcher uses a technique that cross-links proteins to DNA, immunoprecipitates the protein of interest with a specific antibody, and then identifies the associated DNA sequences. This technique is primarily used to study which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Protein–DNA interactions

Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) is a molecular biology technique used to determine whether a specific protein is bound to a particular region of DNA inside living cells.

It is widely used to study:

• Transcription factor binding
• Histone modifications
• Chromatin remodeling proteins
• Epigenetic regulation of gene expression

| Technique | Studies

| --------- | -------

| ChIP | Protein–DNA interactions ✅

| ChIP-seq | Genome-wide protein-binding sites

| RIP | RNA–protein interactions

| CLIP | RNA–protein interactions with nucleotide-level resolution

| DRIP | DNA–RNA hybrids (R-loops)

| 3C / Hi-C | DNA–DNA interactions (chromatin architecture)
questions.learning: Protein–DNA interactions Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) is a molecular biology technique used to determine whether a specific protein is bound to a particular region of DNA inside living cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old pregnant G3P2L2 woman presents to you at 36+6 weeks. Ultrasound is done and shows the fetus is in a transverse lie. The liquor is adequate, the placenta is normal, and she has no risk factors. Both her previous deliveries were normal vaginal deliveries. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. External cephalic version

A pregnant woman G3P2L2 presenting at 36+6 weeks with a transverse lie without being in labor is managed with an external cephalic version (ECV), followed by vaginal delivery.

In a transverse lie, the fetus' long axis is perpendicular to the mother's. The shoulder is typically placed above the pelvic inlet when lying transversely. The head occupies one iliac fossa, and the other by the breech. This results in a shoulder presentation.

Management of transverse lie:

1. Before labor/early in labor - If the membranes are intact (like in this case), it is recommended that ECV should be offered and attempted whenever possible.

Prerequisites for ECV - Women who have reached 370/7 weeks of gestation. Multiparity, unengaged presenting part, nonanterior placenta, nonobese patient, and abundant amnionic fluid improves the chances of ECV.

Absolute contraindications - When vaginal delivery is contraindicated, e.g. placenta previa

Relative contraindications - Early labor, oligohydramnios or ruptured membranes, known nuchal cord, structural uterine abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, multifetal gestation, and prior abruption of the placenta

2. Active labor - A cesarean delivery is frequently necessary for such a scenario (Option A). The lower uterine segment is not occupied by the fetal feet or head in a dorsoanterior or back down position. A vertical hysterotomy incision is usually necessary for such a position. In a dorsoposterior or backup position, one or both feet can be gripped through a small transverse incision and delivered by breech extraction.

Expectant management refers to allowing vaginal delivery to happen. It is chosen when the version fails or is contraindicated. Vaginal delivery may be considered in the case of small fetuses with congenital malformations or dead fetuses (Option C).

Transverse lie (malpresentation) is a contraindication to induction of labor (Option D).
questions.learning: External cephalic version — A pregnant woman G3P2L2 presenting at 36+6 weeks with a transverse lie without being in labor is managed with an external cephalic version (ECV), followed by vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids.

When the tissue sample goes through rapid freezing, it becomes firmer. The ice acts as an embedding media allowing the tissue to be sectioned.

The temperature range in the cryostat machine usually ranges from 0⁰C to -35⁰C. The majority of the tissue can be appropriately sectioned between -15⁰C to -25⁰C. Tissue samples that contain water can be sectioned at a higher temperature. The tissues that contain more fat will need to be cut at a lower temperature.

The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues. It is used in the following conditions:

• Fat emboli in lung tissue
• Renal cell carcinoma
• Sebaceous gland tumors of the skin
• Lipid-rich carcinomas

Fixatives containing alcohols, or routine processing with clearing, will remove lipids. Fixation can be achieved by the following methods:

• Physical methods - heating, microwaving, cryopreservation
• Chemical methods - immersion of specimen in fixative, perfusing vascular system with a fixative

Given below are a few fixatives with their uses:

Technique/Tissue
Fixative

Electron microscopy
Glutaraldehyde

Trephine biopsy-bone marrow
Zenker's fluid (AZF fixative)

GI biopsies
Bouin's fixative

Brain
Formalin ammonium chloride

Adrenal biopsy
Orth's fluid

Pap smear
Ethanol

The most commonly used fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin.
questions.learning: Frozen section — A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An adult patient presents with a pulsatile swelling in the neck just below the angle of the jaw, exhibiting an outward expansile impulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A pulsatile neck swelling located at the carotid bifurcation (below the angle of the jaw) that exhibits an expansile impulse is classic for a Carotid Body Tumor (Option D). This is a highly vascular paraganglioma. A hallmark sign is that the swelling can be moved side-to-side but not up and down (Fontaine's sign), as it is fixed to the carotid artery. The provided angiography (Option DSA) demonstrates the pathognomonic "Lyre sign", where the tumor physically splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart. Grave's disease (Option A) involves generalized thyroid enlargement. Branchial cysts (Option B) and thymic cysts (Option C) are soft, non-pulsatile masses . Because the tumor is intensely vascular and intimately associated with the major neck arteries, it pulsates with the arterial pressure. Surgical excision is the treatment but carries a high risk of vascular or nerve injury
questions.learning: A pulsatile neck swelling located at the carotid bifurcation (below the angle of the jaw) that exhibits an expansile impulse is classic for a Carotid Body Tumor (Option D).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which nerve is implicated in causing the syncopal episode observed during earwax syringing in a patient?
questions.explanation: Syncopal episodes (fainting) during ear syringing or canal manipulation are caused by the vagal reflex. The Arnold's nerve, which is the auricular branch of the Vagus nerve (CN X), provides sensory innervation to the posterior and inferior parts of the external auditory canal. Physical stimulation of this nerve by cold water or mechanical pressure during syringing can trigger a parasympathetic response, leading to bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope. The Auriculotemporal nerve (Option A, a branch of CN V3) innervates the anterior and superior canal wall but is not linked to the vagal reflex. The Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C, CN IX) and its branch, the Jacobson’s nerve (Option D, providing sensation to the middle ear), are not involved in the innervation of the external canal. To prevent this "Arnold's reflex," syringing should ideally be performed using water at body temperature. Therefore, the auricular branch of the vagus is the definitive anatomical structure responsible for this specific procedural complication

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with severe hyperglycemia is started on insulin therapy. Which of the following effect is expected?
options: Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT2
Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4
Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT4
Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4

Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting GLUT4 translocation from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, thereby increasing glucose uptake. In contrast, GLUT2 in the liver and pancreatic β-cells is insulin-independent.

Why is B correct?

• Skeletal muscle expresses GLUT4, which is activated by insulin, leading to increased glucose uptake.

Why not the other options?

• A. Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT2: Skeletal muscle does not express GLUT2.
• C. Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT4: The liver expresses GLUT2, not GLUT4.
• D. Increased glucose uptake by liver via GLUT2: Although the liver uses GLUT2, its glucose uptake is not increased by insulin through GLUT2 translocation; insulin instead promotes glycogen synthesis and glycolysis after glucose enters hepatocytes.
questions.learning: Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle via GLUT4 Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting GLUT4 translocation from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, thereby increasing glucose uptake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a 100-m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP is derived from _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphocreatine

In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy.
The ATP concentration in a muscle is low enough (4 millimolar) to sustain contractions for 1-2 seconds after which ATP is dephosphorylated into ADP. The ADP is re-phosphorylated by phosphocreatine for the next 5 to 8 seconds.

ADP is re-phosphorylated by 3 sources.

• Phosphocreatine after 2 seconds upto 10 seconds.
• Glycolysis (anaerobic) after 10 seconds upto a minute
• Oxidative metabolism - after a minute upto 2-4 hours.
questions.learning: Phosphocreatine — In a 100-m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine, which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a markedly swollen foot associated with multiple discharging sinuses, as shown in the provided image. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the classic clinical triad for Mycetoma (Madura foot): localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of purulent fluid containing granules. Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection typically contracted by farmers who work barefoot and sustain minor trauma from thorns or soil. It can be caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma). Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) presents as a non-healing ulcer but not with multiple sinuses and granules. Nocardia (Option C) is a cause of actinomycetoma but the overall "condition" is termed Mycetoma. Sporotrichosis (Option D) usually follows a "lymphocutaneous" pattern with nodules along the lymphatic channels rather than a massive localized foot swelling. Therefore, the characteristic physical appearance of the sinuses and swelling in a rural worker confirms Mycetoma as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The image depicts the classic clinical triad for Mycetoma (Madura foot): localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of purulent fluid containing granules.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the staging system used for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)?
questions.explanation: The Radkowski classification is the most widely utilized staging system for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor found almost exclusively in adolescent males. The system stages the tumor based on its extension from the nasopharynx into the sinuses, pterygopalatine fossa, and intracranial compartments. TNM Staging (Option B) is the universal system for malignant cancers and is not applied to JNA. The Ann Arbor system (Option C) is used for lymphomas. Dukes criteria (Option D) is used for staging colorectal cancer. Staging JNA correctly using the Radkowski system is crucial for surgical planning, as these tumors are prone to massive hemorrhage. Management typically involves preoperative embolization to reduce blood flow, followed by either an endoscopic or open surgical approach depending on the stage of extension
questions.learning: The Radkowski classification is the most widely utilized staging system for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor found almost exclusively in adolescent males.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A middle-aged man with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse presents with complaints of painful urination and itching. On examination, Gram-negative intracellular cocci are observed. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The above clinical scenario along with the Gram stain showing gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes is suggestive of infection by Neisseria gonorrhea.

Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by Neisseria gonorrhea. It uses pilli in adhesion to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. The cocci penetrate the intracellular spaces to reach the subepithelial tissue by the third day of infection. The incubation period is 2-8 days.

The major symptoms include vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria, usually without urinary frequency or urgency. The specific symptoms seen in males and females are as follows:

In female patients:

About half the female patients remain asymptomatic. But, patients typically present with urethritis, cervical discharge, pruritus, dysuria, and intermenstrual bleeding.

The ectocervix and vagina are not usually affected in adults as the stratified squamous epithelium is resistant to infection by the cocci. The acidic pH of vaginal secretions is also protective. The principal sites of invasion for gonococcal infection are the columnar and transitional epithelium.

Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Other complications are tubo-ovarian abscesses and ectopic pregnancies. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz Hugh Curtis syndrome). The patient presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness with abnormal liver function tests.

In male patients :

• Acute urethritis
• Genital discharge: It is mucopurulent that can be described as that resembling the flow of seed (semen).
• Strictures
• Water-can perineum: The infection may spread to the periurethral tissues causing abscesses and multiple discharging sinuses.

Lab diagnosis:

The discharge is collected and subjected to Gram's stain which reveals gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. It is non-sporulating, non-motile and aerobic but may grow anaerobically also. It acidifies glucose but not maltose in serum sugars. Stuart's transport medium is used. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar. Specifically, Thayer-Martin agar is used to isolate Neisseria gonorrheae.

Treatment:

According to CDC guidelines (2021), treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal infections is as follows:

• Weight <150 kg – Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (IM) in a single dose
• Weight ≥150 kg – Ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscular (IM) in a single dose

Concurrent chlamydial infection must also be treated unless it has been excluded by molecular testing. First-line drugs used are as follows:

• Oral azithromycin 1g single dose
• Oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (non-pregnant patients only)

The sexual partners of the patient must be treated to reduce the risk of recurrence. Expedited partner therapy refers to the index patient delivering therapy to one's own partners. However, this type of empirical therapy ignores the importance of direct counseling.

Other options:

Option A: Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive bacterium that can cause various infections, but it is not typically associated with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or intracellular gram-negative cocci.

Option C: Proteus vulgaris is a gram-negative bacillus and is not typically associated with sexually transmitted infections. It is more often linked to urinary tract infections but would not appear as gram-negative intracellular cocci.

Option D: Chlamydia trachomatis is another common cause of sexually transmitted infections. It is an obligate intracellular bacterium that is difficult to visualize using standard Gram staining.
questions.learning: Neisseria gonorrhoeae — The above clinical scenario along with the Gram stain showing gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes is suggestive of infection by Neisseria gonorrhea.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is measured without any straining while examination under POP-Q system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TVL

The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized and internationally accepted method for assessing and staging pelvic organ prolapse (POP). It uses nine specific anatomical measurements relative to the hymenal ring.

Among these measurements, Total Vaginal Length (TVL) is the only parameter measured without the patient straining (Valsalva maneuver). It is measured with the prolapse completely reduced.

Why not the other options?

• B. Pb (Perineal Body): Measured during maximum Valsalva/straining.
• C. GH (Genital Hiatus): Measured during maximum strain, from the external urethral meatus to the posterior hymen.
• D. Point D: Represents the posterior fornix (only present if the uterus is present) and is measured during maximal Valsalva.
questions.learning: TVL — The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized and internationally accepted method for assessing and staging pelvic organ prolapse (POP).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a unilateral throbbing headache that worsens with exposure to bright light. She occasionally skips breakfast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms are classic for migraine: a unilateral, throbbing headache associated with photophobia (light sensitivity). Migraines are significantly more common in women and are often triggered by factors such as skipping meals (fasting) or stress. While hunger can trigger a headache (Option A), the specific throbbing nature and photophobia point toward migraine. Tension headaches (Option C) are typically "band-like," bilateral, and not associated with severe photophobia. Cluster headaches (Option D) are excruciating, unilateral, and located around the eye, but they occur in "clusters" of multiple short attacks per day and are much more common in men. Migraine management involves avoiding known triggers, acute treatment with triptans or NSAIDs, and potentially prophylactic medications if attacks are frequent. This 30-year-old woman is the "typical" patient profile for this neurological disorder
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms are classic for migraine: a unilateral, throbbing headache associated with photophobia (light sensitivity). Migraines are significantly more common in women and are often triggered by factors such as skipping meals (fasting) or stress.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The given graph shows the effect of PTH on blood calcium and phosphate levels in an experimental animal. How does PTH increase plasma calcium levels?
options: By decreasing renal excretion of calcium
By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium

The parathyroid hormone increases the plasma calcium levels by increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium.

By regulating intestinal reabsorption, renal excretion, and the exchange of these ions between the extracellular fluid and bone, PTH offers a potent mechanism for controlling the concentrations of calcium and phosphate in extracellular fluid.

The parathormone (PTH) increases Ca+2 concentration by:

• Increased reabsorption of Ca+2 by renal tubules, decreasing the urinary Ca+2 excretion
• Increasing bone resorption, leading to Ca+2 release into the ECF
• Decreased phosphate reabsorption by the renal tubules, increasing the urinary excretion of phosphate
• Conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol which increases intestinal Ca2+ absorption

Activation of the osteoclasts occurs due to activated osteoblasts and osteocytes that send secondary signals to the osteoclasts. Preosteoclast cells become mature osteoclasts when their receptors are activated by RANKL, a significant secondary signal. Activation of the osteoclastic system occurs in two stages: (1) immediate activation of the osteoclasts that are already formed and (2) formation of new osteoclasts.

PTH administration decreases proximal tubular reabsorption of phosphate ions, which results in a rapid loss of phosphate in the urine. At the same time that PTH reduces phosphate reabsorption, it also increases calcium reabsorption through renal tubules. This ultimately leads to a decrease in the renal excretion of calcium.

Furthermore, it increases the reabsorption of hydrogen and magnesium ions while decreasing the reabsorption of ions from amino acids, potassium, and sodium in a manner similar to how it affects phosphate. Distal tubules and the thick ascending loop of the Henle are the primary sites of the increased calcium reabsorption.
questions.learning: By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium The parathyroid hormone increases the plasma calcium levels by increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The infant is suffering from which of the following abnormalities?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation in the infant, characterized by a specific lenticular opacity, is an "oil drop" cataract. This finding is pathognomonic for galactosemia, a metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase. The accumulation of galactitol within the lens leads to osmotic swelling and the characteristic "oil drop" appearance on retroillumination. In contrast, "snowflake" cataracts are typically associated with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (Option A). Options C and D refer to glycogen storage diseases: Hers disease involves liver phosphorylase deficiency, and Von Gierke's involves glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; neither is primarily associated with this specific ocular finding. Early diagnosis of galactosemia is critical, as switching to a lactose-free diet can often lead to the regression of these early-stage cataracts and prevent systemic complications like liver failure and intellectual disability

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pituitary gland

Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the options given above except the pituitary gland.

Sodium iodide symporter is expressed mainly in the thyroid gland and is responsible for iodine uptake in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland.

Sodium iodide symporter (NIS)

The NIS is mainly present in the basolateral membranes of the thyrocytes. The NIS transports two Na+ ions and one I- ion into the cell against the concentration gradient. The energy for this transport is derived from the Na+-K+ ATPase pump. Na+-K+ ATPase pumps sodium outside the cell and causes low intracellular sodium concentration. This causes sodium to enter the cell by facilitated diffusion. Along with sodium, iodide ions also enter the cell. Since the energy to transport sodium and iodide ions in NIS is derived from Na+-K+ ATPase pump, this is called secondary active transport.

The NIS is also expressed in:

• Salivary glands
• Gastric mucosa
• Placenta
• Ciliary body of the eye
• Choroid plexus
• Mammary glands
• Certain cancers are derived from these tissues.

The significance of these extrathyroidal NIS is not known.
questions.learning: Pituitary gland Sodium iodide symporter is present in all of the options given above except the pituitary gland. Sodium iodide symporter is expressed mainly in the thyroid gland and is responsible for iodine uptake in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland.

questions.text: Identify the hormone from the picture

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A pregnant female at 37 weeks of gestation with a history of prosthetic heart valves is currently taking warfarin. She comes for a routine antenatal check-up. What is the appropriate management advice?
options: Switch to low molecular weight heparin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Switch to low molecular weight heparin

Warfarin is contraindicated near term due to risk of fetal intracranial hemorrhage and maternal bleeding during delivery. Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause: Warfarin embryopathy

Major complications include:

• Nasal hypoplasia
• Stippled epiphyses
• CNS abnormalities
• Fetal bleeding

Because of these risks, warfarin is avoided near delivery.

In pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves, anticoagulation should be switched to low molecular weight heparin in the last weeks.

LMWH does not cross the placenta and provides effective anticoagulation.

Immediate delivery is not indicated solely for anticoagulation management.

| Period | Drug

| ------ | ----

| First trimester | Heparin

| Second trimester | Warfarin may be used in some cases

| Near delivery (after 36 weeks) | Heparin / LMWH
questions.learning: Switch to low molecular weight heparin Warfarin is contraindicated near term due to risk of fetal intracranial hemorrhage and maternal bleeding during delivery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can make a tower of 3 blocks, runs, copies his mother while sweeping and has a vocabulary of 8–10 words. His developmental age is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 18 months

Developmental milestones are assessed across four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and social/adaptive skills. The combination of milestones in this child corresponds most closely to a developmental age of 18 months.

Why is C correct?

The child demonstrates several classic 18-month milestones:

• Tower of 3 blocks ✔ (Fine motor)
• Runs ✔ (Gross motor)
• Copies mother while sweeping (imitative play) ✔ (Social/adaptive)
• Vocabulary of 8–10 words ✔ (Language)

These milestones are characteristic of an 18-month-old child.

Why not the other options?

• A. 12 months ✘

• Walks with support or independently
• Says 1–2 meaningful words
• Tower of 2 blocks

• B. 15 months ✘

• Walks well
• Scribbles
• Tower of 2 blocks
• Vocabulary around 3–5 words

• D. 24 months ✘

• Tower of 6 blocks
• Runs well and climbs stairs
• Vocabulary >50 words
• Uses 2-word sentences
• Copies a vertical line
questions.learning: 18 months Developmental milestones are assessed across four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and social/adaptive skills. The combination of milestones in this child corresponds most closely to a developmental age of 18 months.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What proportion of a country’s Gross National Product (GNP) is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) to be allocated toward healthcare expenditure?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) has historically and globally recommended that a nation should allocate at least 5% of its Gross National Product (GNP) for expenditure on the healthcare sector to ensure adequate provision of essential services. This target is considered the minimum investment required to achieve significant improvements in public health indicators and progress toward Universal Health Coverage. Options A (2.0%), B (2.5%), and C (3.5%) represent lower expenditure levels often seen in many developing nations, including India, which has set an intermediate national goal of reaching 2.5% of GDP by 2025. Adequate healthcare financing is critical for strengthening primary health infrastructure, ensuring the availability of essential medicines, and reducing the catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure that often pushes families into poverty. National health accounts track this spending to monitor the government's commitment to the health and well-being of its citizens. Achieving the 5% GNP target is a key barometer of a country's health system performance
questions.learning: The World Health Organization (WHO) has historically and globally recommended that a nation should allocate at least 5% of its Gross National Product (GNP) for expenditure on the healthcare sector to ensure adequate provision of essential services.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with endophthalmitis 5 days after cataract surgery. All of the following treatments can be used, except _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous steroids

Intravenous steroids are not used for the treatment of endophthalmitis.

Endophthalmitis is defined as an intraocular inflammation that predominantly affects the inner spaces of the eye and their contents, i.e. the vitreous and/or the anterior chamber. The cardinal features of endophthalmitis are pain, swelling of the lid and diminished vision. Once the endophthalmitis sets in it is important to treat all the cases empirically with a combination of antibiotics and steroids from the beginning.

Steroids are given in endophthalmitis to reduce the inflammation of the tissues. The preferred route of administration is either by intravitreal injections, topical concentrations or oral route. Intravenous route of administration of steroids is not used in endophthalmitis.

Acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis occurs within 1-7 days after cataract surgery and the most important factor to prevent it is preoperative administration of 5% povidone iodine.

The various drugs,routes and surgical management used to treat endophthalmitis are as follows:

• The mainstay of treatment is intravitreal injections of antibiotics.
First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus ceftazidime 2.25mg in 0.1ml.
Second choice: Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus amikacin 0.4mg in 0.1ml.
If there is no improvement, a repeat intravitreal injection should be given after 48 hours
• Topical Solutions of antibiotics are started immediately and used frequently
Vancomycin (50mg/ml) or cefazolin (50mg/ml)
Amikacin (20mg/ml) or tobramycin
• Systemic antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice.
• Steroid therapy includes
Intravitreal injection of Dexamethasone(0.4mg in 0.1ml) which is started along with antibiotics.
Topical Dexamethasone (0.1%)
Oral steroids such as prednisolone are started after 24 hours of intensive antibiotic therapy.
• Supportive therapy are
Cycloplegics such as Atropine 1%
Anti-Glaucoma drugs such as oral acetazolamide or timolol in patients with raised intraocular pressure
• Vitrectomy- Pars Plana Vitrectomy is done if the patient does not improve with the above therapy in 48-72 hours or when the visual acuity is reduced to hand movements near the eye.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A child presents with acute exacerbation of asthma. Which of the following would you do?

1. Chest X-ray
2. Oxygen administration
3. Salbutamol nebulization three times in 60 minutes
4. Administration of oral corticosteroids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2,3,4

A child coming with acute exacerbation of asthma will be administered oxygen, salbutamol nebulization three times in 60 minutes, and oral corticosteroids.

Exacerbation of asthma is known as an increase in symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and/or breathlessness. If the child has cyanosis, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, altered sensorium, and oxygen saturation of <90%, the exacerbation is considered life-threatening.

Based on the severity, acute asthma is classified as mild, moderate, and severe.

Home treatment for acute exacerbation involves parents administering short-acting, beta-2-agonists by metered-dose inhaler with/without a spacer and facemask. One puff for every 30–60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs with monitoring. If symptoms are relieved after inhalation, the child can continue salbutamol inhalation every 4–6 hours. If there is no improvement or partial improvement, the child should be transferred to a hospital.

In a child presenting to the hospital with severe symptoms, start inhalation of oxygen, short-acting beta-2-agonists such as salbutamol or albuterol that can be used every 15–20 minutes for the first hour and administer oral prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg). Oxygen inhalation is stopped if an oxygen saturation of >95% cannot be maintained.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following best describes craniosynostosis?
options: It is delayed fusion of one or more cranial sutures preventing growth perpendicular to the suture.
It is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, preventing growth perpendicular to the suture.
It is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, facilitating growth perpendicular to the suture.
It is delayed fusion of one or more cranial sutures facilitating growth perpendicular to the suture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, preventing growth perpendicular to the suture.

Craniosynostosis is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, resulting in restricted skull growth perpendicular to the fused suture. To compensate, the skull grows parallel to the affected suture, producing characteristic cranial deformities.

The severity depends on:

• Which suture is involved
• Number of sutures involved
• Age at fusion

Why not the other options?

• A. It is delayed fusion of one or more cranial sutures preventing growth perpendicular to the suture: Incorrect. Craniosynostosis is caused by premature, not delayed, fusion.
• C. It is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, facilitating growth perpendicular to the suture: Incorrect. Growth is restricted, not facilitated, perpendicular to the fused suture.
• D. It is delayed fusion of one or more cranial sutures facilitating growth perpendicular to the suture: Incorrect because both the timing and mechanism are wrong.
questions.learning: It is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, preventing growth perpendicular to the suture. Craniosynostosis is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, resulting in restricted skull growth perpendicular to the fused suture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painless lump in her left breast. She describes it as freely mobile with a rubbery consistency. On examination, the mass is confirmed to be approximately the stated size. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a painless, rubbery, and highly mobile breast mass in a young woman is the classic description of a Fibroadenoma. Due to its extreme mobility within the breast tissue, it is colloquially known as the "breast mouse." A breast abscess (Option A) would be intensely painful, red, and warm, often associated with fever. A Phyllodes tumor (Option B) is a differential but typically grows very rapidly to a much larger size and occurs in older women. Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option D) usually presents as a firm, fixed, hard mass with irregular borders in an older age group. Given the specific age of the patient and the "rubbery" texture and "highly movable" nature of the mass, fibroadenoma is the definitive and most common benign diagnosis. Management typically involves ultrasound confirmation and sometimes a fine-needle aspiration for cytology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the image shown, which diuretic acts at the site labeled “A” and was prescribed to a 50-year-old woman for the management of hypertension?
questions.explanation: The diagram identifies the Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) as location 'A'. The class of diuretics that specifically targets this segment is the Thiazides, such as Hydrochlorothiazide. Thiazides work by inhibiting the symporter on the luminal membrane, thereby increasing the excretion of sodium and water. They are considered first-line pharmacological agents for the management of primary hypertension. Mannitol (Option A) is an osmotic diuretic acting primarily on the proximal tubule and descending limb. Acetazolamide (Option C) inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Furosemide (Option D) is a loop diuretic that targets the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop. While loop diuretics are more potent, Thiazides are preferred for chronic hypertension because they have a longer duration of action and a favorable cardiovascular profile. Clinicians must monitor for side effects like hypokalemia and hypercalcemia. Correctly localizing the site of action of these drugs is essential for understanding their clinical utility and adverse effect profiles in renal medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Of the following, which gene mutation is most frequently linked to medullary thyroid carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RET

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is most commonly associated with MEN2A and MEN2B, which occur due to mutation in the RET gene.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a tumour of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies. Most of the MTCs occur sporadically. However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.

Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age, whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age. Features of MTC include:

* Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy

* Dysphagia, dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded

* Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin

* Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production

* Metastasis is blood-borne

* Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma

It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib.

Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5 years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1 year of age in MEN2B mutation.

Surgical management of MTC is as follows:

Extent of cancer
Surgery done

MTC without LN involvement

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + level VI LN involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection (therapeutic) + Modified radical neck dissection (prophylactic)

MTC + other LNs involved

Total thyroidectomy + Central neck dissection + Modified radical neck dissection (therapeutic)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient with suspected gastrointestinal infection, which culture medium is commonly used in the laboratory to differentiate lactose- fermenting bacteria from non-lactose fermenters?
questions.explanation: MacConkey agar is a specialized differential and selective culture medium widely used in microbiology. It contains bile salts and crystal violet, which inhibit the growth of gram-positive bacteria, making it selective for gram-negative organisms (like Enterobacteriaceae). Crucially, it contains the sugar lactose and a neutral red pH indicator. Bacteria that are lactose fermenters (e.g., E. coli) produce acid, which turns the colonies pink. Non-lactose fermenters (e.g., Salmonella or Shigella) do not produce acid and appear as pale or colorless colonies. Bile salt agar (Option A) is used for isolating Vibrio cholerae. Thayer-Martin agar (Option B) is selective for Neisseria species. Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (Option D) is used for the growth of fungi. Identifying the lactose fermentation pattern on MacConkey agar is the foundational first step in the laboratory identification of aerobic gram-negative bacilli, helping clinicians narrow down the etiological agent of a gastrointestinal or urinary tract infection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: _______ excreted in the urine are used as a screening test for pheochromocytoma.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urinary metanephrines and VMA

Urinary metanephrines and VMA excreted in the urine are screening tests for pheochromocytoma.

Vanillyl Mandelic Acid is the end product of the catabolism of catecholamines, whereas metanephrines are the byproducts in the catabolism of catecholamines and are excreted in the urine in patients with pheochromocytoma.

* VMA is the urinary product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine.

* In pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, there is an excessive synthesis of catecholamines which causes the enhanced synthesis of VMA and its excretion in the urine.

* It is a good screening test for pheochromocytoma and is also used to diagnose and follow up neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma.

Option B: Albumin is excreted in Nephrotic syndrome.

Option C: 5-HIAA (5-hydroxy indole acetic acid) is excreted in Carcinoid syndrome.

Option D: Glucose is excreted in Diabetes Mellitus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman gave birth to a child 8 months after the death of her husband. The in-laws claim that the child is not their son, however, the DNA testing confirms the paternity. The child is known as ____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posthumous child

The child delivered after the death of the biological father, or a child delivered after the death of the biological mother, usually when delivered by a cesarean section is a posthumous child.

Legal issues involved with a posthumous child are legitimacy, inheritance of property, and the case of compensation for slander against the mother.

Other options :

Option A: Illegitimate child is a child born out of wedlock i.e. when the parents are unmarried.

Option C: A surrogate child is born out of a pregnancy in which a woman gives birth to a baby for a person who is not able to have children.

Option D: Supposititious child or fictitious child is when a woman pretends to go through pregnancy and delivery. Later, she produces a living child on her own to obtain money or claim the property.
questions.learning: Posthumous child — The child delivered after the death of the biological father, or a child delivered after the death of the biological mother, usually when delivered by a cesarean section is a posthumous child.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of feed forward control mechanism?
options: Exercise resulting in heart rate increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exercise resulting in heart rate increase

Exercise resulting in heart rate increase is not an example of feedforward control mechanism. However, thinking about exercise and it resulting in a heart rate increase would be an example of feedforward control mechanism.

Feedforward control is that which makes an anticipatory or adaptive response without a specific stimulus.

Temperature control - Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by the hypothalamus before the changes in environmental temperature changes the core body temperature. Thus, shivering in response to cold environment would be an example of feedforward control.

In the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, the thought of food itself and not food per se produces a gastric secretion.

The cerebellum has a feed-forward inhibition that limits the duration of the excitation produced by any given afferent volley.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct about oral rotavirus vaccines? I. The storage should be at 2–8°C II. The vaccine should be used within 2 hours of reconstitution or opening III. Past history of intussusception is a contraindication IV. The vaccine can be given if the baby has ongoing diarrhoea Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I and III

Rotavirus vaccine is a live attenuated oral vaccine included in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) to prevent severe rotavirus gastroenteritis, one of the leading causes of severe diarrhea in infants and young children.

The vaccine should be stored at 2–8°C, and a previous history of intussusception is a contraindication to its administration.

Why is C correct?

• I. The storage should be at 2–8°C. ✔

• Correct.
• Rotavirus vaccine must be maintained in the cold chain (2–8°C) to preserve its potency.

• II. The vaccine should be used within 2 hours of reconstitution or opening. ✘

• Incorrect.
• This recommendation applies to certain reconstituted injectable vaccines (e.g., BCG, measles-containing vaccines), not oral rotavirus vaccines.

• III. Past history of intussusception is a contraindication. ✔

• Correct.
• Rotavirus vaccines are contraindicated in infants with:

• Previous intussusception
• Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
• Severe allergic reaction to a previous dose

• IV. The vaccine can be given if the baby has ongoing diarrhoea. ✘

• Incorrect.
• In infants with moderate or severe acute gastroenteritis/diarrhea, vaccination should generally be deferred until recovery.
• Mild illness is not a contraindication.
questions.learning: I and III Rotavirus vaccine is a live attenuated oral vaccine included in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) to prevent severe rotavirus gastroenteritis, one of the leading causes of severe diarrhea in infants and young children.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Chimeric DNA is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Organ transplantation

Chimeric DNA is associated with organ transplantation, especially bone-marrow transplantation.

In organ transplantation, chimeric DNA refers to the mixture of donor and recipient genetic material that occurs when donor cells begin functioning within the recipient's body. It is used for long-term monitoring of bone marrow transplant recipients. Detecting changes in the levels of donor-derived cells can provide early warning signs of graft failure, rejection, or relapse of underlying disease.

Note: The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
• Producing proteins such as:

• Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
• Insulin, growth hormone
• Hepatitis B vaccine

• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
• Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation
