questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complains of significant eye discomfort while reading printed text or using digital screens, despite having normal visual acuity and an otherwise unremarkable eye examination. The only abnormal finding is a Schirmer’s test result of 5 mm. What is the most appropriate and effective treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of discomfort during visually intensive tasks (like reading or screen use) and a Schirmer's test result of 5mm (normal is mm) are diagnostic of Dry Eye Disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). A result of 5mm indicates significant aqueous tear deficiency. The most effective and standard first-line treatment for managing symptoms and protecting the ocular surface is the frequent use of lubricants (Option C), such as artificial tears or gels. Steroids (Option A) are only used for short-term control of severe inflammation and carry risks of glaucoma or cataracts. Antihistamines (Option B) are used for allergic conjunctivitis and can actually worsen dry eyes by reducing tear production. Since the patient has normal visual acuity, prescribed spectacles (Option D) would not address the underlying tear deficiency. Therefore, tear film replacement with lubricants is the most appropriate management
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of discomfort during visually intensive tasks (like reading or screen use) and a Schirmer's test result of 5mm (normal is mm) are diagnostic of Dry Eye Disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: From which of the following amino acids is melanin primarily derived?
questions.explanation: Melanin, the primary pigment responsible for skin, hair, and eye color, is biosynthetically derived from the amino acid Tyrosine. In melanocytes, the enzyme tyrosinase catalyzes the oxidation of tyrosine into DOPA and then dopaquinone, which eventually polymerizes into melanin. A congenital deficiency of tyrosinase results in albinism. Phenylalanine (Option C) is the precursor to tyrosine, but the direct substrate for the melanin pathway is tyrosine itself. Tryptophan (Option B) is the precursor for serotonin, melatonin (the hormone, not the pigment), and niacin. Alanine (Option D) is involved in glucose metabolism but not pigment synthesis. Melanin provides critical protection against ultraviolet radiation damage. Understanding this biochemical pathway is essential for grasping various dermatological conditions and inborn errors of metabolism. Therefore, while phenylalanine is part of the broader metabolic chain, tyrosine is the immediate and primary amino acid precursor for melanin production

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman with a family history of Marfan syndrome presents with unilateral tonsillar swelling, and visible pulsations are noted on oral examination. What is the most likely cause of this tonsillar enlargement?
questions.explanation: Patients with Marfan’s syndrome have a genetic predisposition to connective tissue weakness, making them highly susceptible to arterial aneurysms. A unilateral tonsillar or pharyngeal swelling that exhibits "visible pulsation" is a red-flag sign for an aneurysm of the adjacent carotid artery . The internal carotid artery (ICA) passes immediately lateral to the tonsillar fossa in the parapharyngeal space. An extracranial (Option A) aneurysm in this segment can protrude medially, mimicking a tonsillar mass. Intracranial aneurysms (Options B and D) would present with neurological deficits rather than a visible oropharyngeal mass. The external carotid artery (Option C) is further removed and less likely to present as a tonsillar swelling. Biopsy or incision of such a "pulsatile mass" is strictly contraindicated due to the risk of catastrophic hemorrhage. Diagnosis must be confirmed with CT or MR angiography. Therefore, the anatomical location and Marfan association indicate an extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false about Rubella infection?
options: It is a type of droplet infection
Infection in early pregnancy causes a milder form of disease in the fetus
Fetus affected in late pregnancy may have only deafness
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infection in early pregnancy causes a milder form of disease in the fetus

Earlier the rubella infection occurs in pregnancy, greater is the damage to the foetus.

The major determinant of the extent of fetal infection in congenital rubella syndrome is the gestational age at which fetal transmission occurs.

Rubella infection in 1st trimester can cause:

• Abortions
• Still birth
• Skin lesions - blueberry muffin rash
• Congenital rubella syndrome

questions.text: A cook prepares sandwiches for 10 people going for picnic. Eight out of them develop severe gastroenteritis within 4-6 hrs of consumption of the sandwiches. It is likely that on investigations the cook is found to be the carrier of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus aureus

The cook is most likely to be carrier of Staph. aureus.

The onset of food poisioning with in 4-6 hrs of food is mainly due to:

• Staphylococcus aureus

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Marshall's triad (punctate lacerations, bruises, and abrasions) is seen in which type of blast injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary blast injury

Marshall's triad in a bomb explosion is seen due to secondary blast injuries.

Marshall described the characteristic injuries associated with bomb explosions. It includes:

• Abrasions
• Bruises/ contusions
• Puncture lacerations

Blast injuries are classified as:

• Primary injuries- effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterized by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this.
• Secondary injuries- injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries.
• Tertiary injuries- are caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects.
• Quaternary injuries- all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. eg, flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.
questions.learning: Secondary blast injury Marshall's triad in a bomb explosion is seen due to secondary blast injuries. Marshall described the characteristic injuries associated with bomb explosions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and serum calcium levels are elevated. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42% and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Multiple myeloma

In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. The incidence of multiple myeloma increases with age, and it is more commonly seen in males than in females.

Signs and symptoms

* Bone pain is the most common symptom

* Pathologic fractures

* Recurrent bacterial infections

* Renal failure

* Normocytic normochromic anemia elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%) and presence of Dutcher bodies, Russel bodies, and Mott cells.

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation)

Option A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen. Peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

Option B: Acute lymphocytic leukemia presents with a hypercellular marrow that is packed with lymphoblasts. These lymphoblasts, when compared to myeloblasts, have more condensed chromatin with less prominent nucleoli.

Option C: In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), patients typically present with a dragging sensation in the abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. The peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described as having a garden party or a college girl appearance.

Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

Description

Russell bodies

They are globular intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins (Ig).

Plasma cells filled with multiple Russell bodies are called Mott cells.

Dutcher bodies

PAS-positive intranuclear inclusions containing Ig seen in some of the plasma cells are called Dutcher bodies.

Flame cells

Plasma cells with fiery red cytoplasm are called flame cells.

PAS: Periodic acid Schiff
questions.learning: Multiple myeloma — In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with a yellow- green, foul-smelling vaginal discharge associated with dysuria and dyspareunia, without itching. On speculum examination, the vulva and vaginal walls are inflamed. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The presence of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling, often frothy discharge accompanied by inflammation of the vaginal walls and dyspareunia (painful intercourse) is highly characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis. A specific sign often seen on speculum examination is the "strawberry cervix". Candida albicans (Option B) typically presents with a white, curdy (cottage cheese-like) discharge and intense itching, which is absent here. Gardnerella vaginalis (Option C) causes bacterial vaginosis, characterized by a thin, gray-white discharge with a "fishy" odor, but generally lacks significant vaginal inflammation or dyspareunia. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Option D) primarily causes cervicitis but can overlap; however, the classic description of the discharge favors Trichomoniasis. Treatment involves metronidazole for both the patient and their partner to prevent recurrence. Thus, Trichomonas is the most likely causative agent
questions.learning: The presence of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling, often frothy discharge accompanied by inflammation of the vaginal walls and dyspareunia (painful intercourse) is highly characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior interosseous nerve injury causes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of extension at finger

The correct answer is loss of extension at fingers.

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) supplies the finger and thumb extensors.

Wrist extension is largely preserved due to extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, so wrist drop does not occur.

Supination is mainly by biceps brachii and supinator, which are not significantly affected.
questions.learning: Loss of extension at finger — The correct answer is loss of extension at fingers. The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) supplies the finger and thumb extensors.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the odor produced by the change seen in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Odorless

The image shows a mummified body and it is odorless.

Mummification is a modification of putrefaction. Dehydration or drying and shrivelling of the cadaver occurs from water's evaporation, but the body's natural appearance and general facial features are preserved.. The mummified body is odourless. It is a late sign of death.

It begins in the exposed parts of the body like the face, hands, and feet. Then it extends to the entire body including the internal organs which may later disappear due to putrefaction and maggot activity. During the process of mummification, the whole body loses weight up to 60 to 70% and all the internal organs become a single mass.

Factors necessary for the production of mummification are the absence of moisture in the air and the continuous action of dry or warm air. It occurs in bodies buried in shallow graves in dry sandy soils, where evaporation of body fluids is very rapid due to the hot dry winds in summer. Chronic arsenic or antimony poisoning favours the process. Differential decomposition is a condition in which some parts of the body show mummification and other parts show adipocere formation.
questions.learning: Odorless — The image shows a mummified body and it is odorless. Mummification is a modification of putrefaction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: You are evaluating a patient in the burns unit in your ward. The patient is suffering from 3rd degree circumferential burns along the thorax and abdominal area. The patient received 8L of Ringer lactate at the primary facility before being referred to your hospital. His BP is 82/54 mmHg, HR is 130 BPM. His urine output for the last 3 hours is less than 20 mL. What is the next step in this case?
options: Measure urine output after 1 hour and continue fluids.
Give a diuretic to help with the possible urinary retention
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure bladder pressure.

Severe burn patients with circumferential full-thickness (3rd degree) thoracoabdominal burns who receive large-volume fluid resuscitation are at high risk of developing abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) due to massive capillary leak, visceral edema, and third spacing. ACS leads to intra-abdominal hypertension, causing impaired venous return and organ hypoperfusion.

Key clinical clues suggesting ACS in this patient:

• Circumferential trunk burns (restrictive “burn eschar” + raised compartment pressures)
• Received massive fluids (8 L RL)
• Persistent hypotension (82/54) and tachycardia
• Oliguria (<20 mL over 3 hours) despite aggressive resuscitation

→ suggests renal hypoperfusion, not urinary retention

The next best step is to measure intra-abdominal pressure, most commonly via bladder pressure measurement, which is the standard bedside method for diagnosing intra-abdominal hypertension/ACS.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In routine microbiology laboratory work, which culture medium is most commonly used for the isolation and identification of Salmonella species?
questions.explanation: Wilson and Blair (Bismuth Sulfite Agar) is a highly selective and characteristic medium used for the isolation of Salmonella typhi and other Salmonella species. It contains bismuth sulfite and brilliant green, which inhibit the growth of most other intestinal bacteria (like E. coli). Salmonella species reduce the sulfite to sulfide, which reacts with iron to produce colonies with a distinct jet-black, metallic sheen. PLET medium (Option A) is selective for Bacillus anthracis. BCYE (Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract) medium (Option B) is the specific requirement for Legionella pneumophila. Stuart's medium (Option D) is a non-nutrient transport medium used to maintain the viability of samples during transit to the lab. Using specialized media like Wilson and Blair is essential in public health and clinical settings for the definitive identification of the causative agents of enteric fever and food poisoning. The unique black-colony morphology provides a rapid and clear visual confirmation of Salmonella presence in clinical or environmental samples
questions.learning: Wilson and Blair (Bismuth Sulfite Agar) is a highly selective and characteristic medium used for the isolation of Salmonella typhi and other Salmonella species.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient was infected by Bacillus anthracis. Under which of the following bioterrorism categories does this organism fall into:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Category A

Bacillus anthracis which causes anthrax is categorized under category A bioterrorism agent.

Bioterrorism is the deliberate release of an agent by attackers that causes one or more of a variety of different diseases. The agents of bioterrorism are classified into 3 categories.

* Category A

* Category B

* Category C

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with an acute exacerbation of COPD required mechanical ventilation and experienced a consistent drop in oxygen saturation. Auscultation revealed vesicular breath sounds on the right side. Based on the chest radiography findings, what would you expect to hear on auscultation of the left side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent breath sounds

Absent breath sounds on the left side are expected in this case of left pneumothorax.

A pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, causing lung collapse and preventing normal lung expansion, which leads to absent or diminished breath sounds over the affected area. In patients with COPD, particularly during an acute exacerbation, the already weakened and hyperinflated lung tissue can rupture, leading to a pneumothorax. This is a serious complication, especially when mechanical ventilation is required, as the pressure from the ventilator can exacerbate the pneumothorax.

Other options:

Option B: Bronchial breath sounds: Typically heard in conditions like pneumonia, where there is lung consolidation, not in a pneumothorax.

Option C: Increased vesicular breath sounds: These indicate hyperinflation or normal lung function, which is not possible in a collapsed lung.

Option D: Increased vocal fremitus: Fremitus is usually decreased or absent in pneumothorax due to the insulating effect of air in the pleural space.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Many GPCR receptors act via an increase in cAMP. The steps involved in this mechanism are given below. Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in the cAMP signal transduction pathway? 1. Activation of adenylate cyclase 2. Activation of PKA 3. Conversion of ATP to cAMP 4. Phosphorylation of target proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 2 and 4

Correct answer is B because GPCR activation first stimulates adenylate cyclase (1), which converts ATP to cAMP (3).

cAMP then activates protein kinase A (PKA) (2).

Activated PKA phosphorylates downstream target proteins (4), producing the cellular response.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 2 and 4 Correct answer is B because GPCR activation first stimulates adenylate cyclase (1), which converts ATP to cAMP (3). cAMP then activates protein kinase A (PKA) (2).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following parameters are assessed during preoperative airway assessment for a surgical patient? 1. Mouth opening 2. Ability to protrude the jaw 3. Thyromental distance 4. Cervicomental distance Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The important parameters in preoperative airway assessment include:

1. Mouth opening — Correct

• Adequate mouth opening is essential for laryngoscope insertion and airway manipulation.
• An inter-incisor distance >3 cm is generally considered favorable.

2. Ability to protrude the jaw — Correct

• Assesses mandibular mobility and predicts difficulty in aligning the airway axes.
• Inability to protrude the lower incisors beyond the upper incisors suggests a potentially difficult airway.

3. Thyromental distance — Correct

• Measured from the thyroid notch to the mentum with the neck extended.
• A distance <6–6.5 cm suggests a potentially difficult intubation.

4. Cervicomental distance — Incorrect

• It is not a standard parameter used in routine preoperative airway assessment.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The important parameters in preoperative airway assessment include: 1. Mouth opening — Correct • Adequate mouth opening is essential for laryngoscope insertion and airway manipulation. • An inter-incisor distance >3 cm is generally considered…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with left knee pain, which he notes is often worse at night. He has been using aspirin for pain relief. An X-ray of the knee is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmark of Osteoid osteoma is bone pain that is worse at night and is dramatically relieved by Aspirin or other NSAIDs. This is due to the high concentration of prostaglandins within the tumor. The radiograph confirms the diagnosis by showing a radiolucent nidus (less than 2 cm) surrounded by an area of reactive sclerotic (dense) bone. Chondroblastoma (Option A) is an epiphyseal lesion with a different radiological appearance. Skeletal TB (Option C) causes "cold abscesses" and joint destruction rather than a discrete cortical nidus. Osteosarcoma (Option D) is a highly aggressive malignant tumor showing a "sunburst" periosteal reaction and large-scale bone destruction. Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor, most common in the femur and tibia of young adults. While some may resolve spontaneously over several years, the preferred treatment is percutaneous radiofrequency ablation, which provides immediate and permanent pain relief. The specific response to Aspirin is the key diagnostic "trigger" in medical examinations
questions.learning: The clinical hallmark of Osteoid osteoma is bone pain that is worse at night and is dramatically relieved by Aspirin or other NSAIDs. This is due to the high concentration of prostaglandins within the tumor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is in labour, and during delivery, the baby's head is delivered, but the shoulders get stuck. The baby's head is at the introitus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Shoulder dystocia

This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.

Shoulder dystocia, defined as a head-to-body delivery time >60 seconds, occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or the sacral promontory respectively.  A positive turtle sign may be seen which refers to a definite recoil of the head back against the perineum.

Risk factors for the development of shoulder dystocia include maternal diabetes mellitus, obesity, post-dated pregnancy, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, etc.  Wood's corkscrew maneuver is used to deliver the impacted shoulder in this condition.

Woods corkscrew maneuver: Progressive rotation of the posterior shoulder 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion releases the impacted anterior shoulder.

Other options:

Option A: Face Presentation - In a face presentation, the baby presents with the face as the presenting part instead of the vertex. The baby’s head is typically fully extended, leading to complications during delivery. However, once the head is delivered, the body usually follows without significant issues. The scenario described involves difficulty after the head is delivered, specifically with the shoulders, which is not characteristic of face presentation.

Option B: Occipito-sacral arrest- This refers to the baby being in a persistent occiput posterior position (with the baby facing up towards the mother’s abdomen rather than down). Labor may progress more slowly or stop when the baby’s head fails to rotate and descend properly. However, like with CPD, occipito-sacral arrest typically results in difficulty before the head is delivered, not after. If the head has been delivered but the shoulders are stuck, it indicates a different issue.

Option C: Cephalopelvic disproportion(CPD) - CPD occurs when the baby's head or body is too large to fit through the mother's pelvis. This can lead to labor not progressing or being arrested before the baby’s head is fully delivered. In CPD, labor arrest or failure to descend is seen, and the baby’s head may not pass through the pelvis at all. Since in the scenario described above, the head is already delivered and the shoulders are the issue, CPD is less likely to be the cause.
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia — This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A mother of a 5 day old baby presents with the complaint that her baby is "unable to latch on " for breastfeeding. She also says there is some leakage of milk at times and on examination, there is bilateral tenderness and swelling. What is the most likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breast engorgement

The most likely cause for this is due to breast engorgement.

Breast Engorgement :

* Common in women who do not breastfeed often, leakage of milk and breast pain is seen.

* Presents 24 to 72 hours post-partum, peaks 3 to 5 days after delivery and resolves spontaneously

* Characterized by bilateral breast tenderness and swelling typically

* Treatment is by cold compresses and analgesics.

* Breasts can be supported with a sports bra or binder.

* Antibiotics are not indicated.

* Pharmacological or hormonal agents are in general not recommended to suppress lactation.

Other options:

Lactational mastitis:

* Pathogenesis: Bacteria enters ducts through nipple and multiplies in stagnant milk.

* A firm, red, tender, swollen quadrant of unilateral breast, +/- myalgias, chills, malaise

* Treatment:analgesia,frequent breast feeding or pumping,antibiotic of choice: Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin

Bacterial mastitis

* Localized inflammationdue to ascending infection or infection due to milk stasis

* Dull pain

* Tenderness, erythema

* Antibiotics, analgesics

Breast abscess

* Occurs as a complication of mastitis, pus formation

* Throbbing pain

* Point tenderness, erythema

* Induration of skin(if chronic), lymphadenopathy

* Fluctuation test +ve

* Aspiration of Pus, antibiotics, analgesics
questions.learning: Breast engorgement — The most likely cause for this is due to breast engorgement. Breast Engorgement : * Common in women who do not breastfeed often, leakage of milk and breast pain is seen. * Presents 24 to 72 hours post-partum, peaks 3 to 5 days after…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient of hemophilia received multiple blood transfusions. Which of the following metabolic abnormalities can be seen in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metabolic alkalosis

Among the given options, the metabolic abnormality seen in a patient who has received multiple blood transfusions is metabolic alkalosis.

This is because the excess sodium citrate (anticoagulant) in the transfused blood gets converted to bicarbonate leading to metabolic alkalosis. Each mmol of citrate generates 3 mEq of bicarbonate (a total of 23 mEq of bicarbonate due to each unit of blood).

Metabolic acidosis can also be seen in multiple blood transfusions as citrate is acidic, but metabolic alkalosis is more common.
questions.learning: Metabolic alkalosis Among the given options, the metabolic abnormality seen in a patient who has received multiple blood transfusions is metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the condition?
options: May be caused due to pin prick injury
Most common causative organism is Klebsiella
May be treated initially by antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common causative organism is Klebsiella

The condition depicted above is known as a felon and the false statement is "most common causative organism is Klebsiella" as the most common organism causing felon is Staphylococcus aureus.

* A felon  (a.k.a whitlow) is an abscess in the subcutaneous tissues of the distal pulp of a finger or thumb (thumb is more common).

* Infection can be caused by a penetrating injury from a foreign body or from “finger sticks” for medical reasons (e.g., hematocrit and blood glucose determinations).

* S. aureus is the organism most commonly isolated from fingertip infections.

* Abscesses beginning deep, especially if untreated, penetrate the periosteum and cause osteomyelitis; the more superficial ones cause skin necrosis.

* Treatment consists of antibiotics and an incision for drainage. The vertical incision is preferred and all septa are to be broken during drainage.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Slow waves are generated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interstitial cells of Cajal

The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electrical rhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features.

In the stomach and the small intestine, these cells are located in the circular smooth muscle layer near the myenteric plexus. In the colon, they are at the submucosal border of the circular muscle layer.

The slow waves usually do not by themselves cause muscle contraction in most parts of the gastrointestinal tract, except perhaps in the stomach. Instead, they mainly excite the appearance of intermittent spike potentials, and the spike potentials in turn actually excite the muscle contraction.

Note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.
questions.learning: Interstitial cells of Cajal — The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with fever, ear pain, difficulty swallowing, and swollen testicles. Based on the clinical features and the provided image of his jaw, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of fever, ear pain (referred from the parotid), and the visual finding of significant parotid gland swelling (parotitis) that obliterates the mandibular angle is characteristic of Mumps . A critical diagnostic hallmark in this adolescent male is the presence of swollen testicles (orchitis), which is a classic extra-salivary complication of the mumps virus in post-pubertal males. Croup (Option A) presents with a barking cough and stridor, not jaw swelling. Infectious mononucleosis (Option C) causes massive lymphadenopathy (bull-neck) and tonsillar membranes, rather than primary parotid involvement. Herpangina (Option D) is caused by Coxsackievirus and features blisters in the back of the mouth. Because the clinical triad of parotitis, fever, and orchitis is pathognomonic for this viral infection, Mumps is the definitive diagnosis. Management is primarily supportive, as the disease is typically self-limiting but requires monitoring for complications like meningitis or pancreatitis
questions.learning: The combination of fever, ear pain (referred from the parotid), and the visual finding of significant parotid gland swelling (parotitis) that obliterates the mandibular angle is characteristic of Mumps .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Paris green dust is commonly used to kill which of the following?
questions.explanation: Paris green (copper acetoarsenite) is a specialized stomach poison used in public health for mosquito control. It is primarily applied as a dust to the surface of stagnant water bodies to target Anopheles larvae, which are the vectors of malaria. Unlike Culex larvae, which feed at the bottom, Anopheles larvae feed at the water's surface, where they ingest the toxic Paris green particles. Houseflies (Option B) are typically managed with residual sprays or baits like malathion. Bedbugs (Option C) and cockroaches (Option D) require different classes of insecticides, such as pyrethroids or organophosphates, applied to cracks and crevices where they reside. While Paris green was a historical cornerstone of malaria eradication programs, it has largely been superseded by more modern larvicides (like Temephos) and biological control agents (like Bti) due to the environmental risks associated with its arsenic content. However, it remains a classic topic in exams regarding historical vector control strategies
questions.learning: Paris green (copper acetoarsenite) is a specialized stomach poison used in public health for mosquito control. It is primarily applied as a dust to the surface of stagnant water bodies to target Anopheles larvae, which are the vectors of malaria.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for arthritis in acute rheumatic fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspirin

Aspirin is the preferred drug of choice in the treatment of arthritis in Acute rheumatic fever.

Aspirin is a noncompetitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase(COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. It can be effective in treating carditis and arthritis which are seen commonly in acute rheumatic fever.

Uses of aspirin:

* Analgesic and antipyretic uses.

* Acute rheumatic fever

* Rheumatoid arthritis

* Post myocardial infarction and stroke due to its antiplatelet action.

* Prevention of preeclampsia

The treatment of Acute rheumatic fever is symptomatic.

* Antibiotics:
All people diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever (ARF) should be administered antibiotics effective against the precipitating group A streptococcal infection. Penicillin is typically the preferred antibiotic.

* Salicylates and NSAIDs:
These can be used to alleviate symptoms such as arthritis, arthralgia, and fever once the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is confirmed. Aspirin is the first choice. It is typically prescribed at a dosage of 50–60 mg/kg per day, with a maximum dose of 80–100 mg/kg per day (4–8 g/day in adults), divided into 4–5 doses throughout the day.
questions.learning: Aspirin Aspirin is the preferred drug of choice in the treatment of arthritis in Acute rheumatic fever. Aspirin is a noncompetitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase(COX) enzyme.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the plane between the highest points of the iliac crests?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L4-L5

The plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest is called the supracristal plane.

Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman attends a routine gynecological visit and expresses concern about her family history of cancer. During counseling, the gynecologist explains that oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) have a protective effect against certain malignancies. Which type of cancer is not reduced in risk by the use of OCPs?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are known to provide a protective effect against endometrial cancer. Their use lowers the risk of developing this cancer, and the protection becomes stronger with longer duration of use, persisting even after discontinuation. This benefit is due to the hormonal action of OCPs, which helps regulate the menstrual cycle and reduces prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen, a key factor in endometrial carcinogenesis. In contrast, OCPs do not significantly influence the risk of cervical cancer, although preventive measures like Pap smear screening and HPV vaccination are effective. The association with breast cancer is variable, with some studies showing a slight temporary increase in risk that declines after stopping OCPs. Similarly, bladder cancer risk is unrelated to OCP use and is more strongly associated with factors such as smoking, chemical exposure, and chronic irritation
questions.learning: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are known to provide a protective effect against endometrial cancer. Their use lowers the risk of developing this cancer, and the protection becomes stronger with longer duration of use, persisting even after discontinuation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with a recent onset of 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Refractive correction

The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction.

Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses

Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

Algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

* R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics

* O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia

* O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component

* P: Prism correction: for remaining error
questions.learning: Refractive correction — The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction. Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A newborn baby brought by the mother with complaints of the left upper eyelid moving up and down during breastfeeding or thumb sucking which disappears when the baby is not being fed. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marcus–Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon.

Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking syndrome:

* About 5% of all cases of congenital ptosis are associated with the Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon.

* The vast majority are unilateral.

* Etiology: a branch of the mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected to the levator muscle.

* Signs

* Retraction of the ptotic lid with stimulation of the ipsilateral pterygoid muscles by chewing, sucking, opening the mouth, or contralateral jaw movement.

* Less common stimuli to winking include jaw protrusion, smiling, swallowing, and clenching of teeth.

* Jaw-winking does not improve with age although patients may learn to mask it.

The following image shows a woman with Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon. See how her right eyelid ptosis retracts with the opening of the mouth.

Other options:

Option A: In 3rd nerve palsy (oculomotor nerve) - Due to the involvement of the superior rectus and medial rectus, elevation and adduction will also be impaired, which is not the case here.

Option B: Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder associated with a decrease in postsynaptic depolarization due to the blocking of acetylcholine receptors by autoantibodies. It is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles.

Option C: In lagophthalmos, there is incomplete closure of the palpable aperture when the patient attempts to close the eyes due to congenital deformity, paralysis of the orbicularis muscle, ectropion or contraction of the lid.  It may be due to a malfunction of the facial nerve. Treatment includes the management of exposure keratopathy with frequent instillation of lubricants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A skin graft was performed on an immuno compromised patient using tissue obtained from another immuno compromised donor. Several weeks later, the recipient developed contractures along with systemic symptoms. What is the most likely underlying cause of this complication?
options: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells
questions.explanation: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and mount an immune attack. This typically occurs when an immunocompromised host is unable to reject the donor cells. In the context of a graft from another immunocompromised individual, donor lymphocytes may still be present. GVHD presents with systemic features such as fever, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction, along with local changes like contractures. Graft failure (Option B) is a local event resulting from poor blood supply leading to early necrosis, not systemic symptoms weeks later. Host-versus-graft rejection (Option C) requires a functioning recipient immune system, which is absent here. Delayed wound healing (Option D) is common in immunocompromised states but does not account for the systemic multi-organ involvement. Therefore, GVHD is the most probable cause
questions.learning: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and mount an immune attack.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis based on the finding given in the CT image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumatised superior turbinate

The given CT image reveals a pneumatised superior turbinate.

The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized. It forms an important landmark to identify the ostium of the sphenoid sinus which lies medial to it. This pneumatization is common in the lateral nasal wall, although it is less frequently seen in the superior turbinate compared to the middle turbinate.

In most cases, pneumatized superior turbinate is an incidental finding during radiological examinations. It can lead to nasal obstruction, headache, epistaxis, anosmia, and postnasal drainage.

Asymptomatic cases of superior turbinate pneumatization generally do not require treatment. However, when symptoms are present, various surgical techniques can be considered, including outfracture, crushing, radio-frequency ablation, turbinoplasty, and microdebrider surgery.

Turbinoplasty is contraindicated if inferior turbinate pneumatization is associated with the maxillary sinus because it may result in the formation of a second ostium. In addition, total turbinectomy is not performed because it may cause atrophic rhinitis.

Other options:

Option A: Pneumatization of the middle turbinate leads to an enlarged middle turbinate that is ballooned out, this is called concha bullosa. The CT image shown below depicts concha bullosa.

Option C: Onodi cell is a posterior ethmoidal cell that may grow posteriorly, either by the side of the sphenoid sinus or superior to it. Onodi cell is surgically important as the optic nerve may be related to its lateral wall.  A CT image of an onodi cell is shown below.

Option D: Haller cells are air cells situated in the roof of the maxillary sinus. They are pneumatized from anterior or posterior ethmoid cells. Enlargement of Haller cells may lead to maxillary sinusitis as it may encroach the ethmoid infundibulum, impeding draining of the maxillary sinus. A CT image of Haller cell is shown below.
questions.learning: Pneumatised superior turbinate — The given CT image reveals a pneumatised superior turbinate. The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient undergoing ECT for his severe depression was given thiopentone and succinylcholine. The purpose of these medications was to?
options: To induce anesthesia and relax muscles
To prevent memory loss after the ECT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To induce anesthesia and relax muscles

Thiopentone and succinylcholine are given for anesthesia induction and muscle relaxation respectively.

Thiopentone sodium is a barbiturate and acts by opening chloride channels, whilst succinylcholine is a depolarising muscle relaxant.

ECT can be of 2 types:

• Direct - without anesthesia and muscle relaxant
• Modified - with anesthesia and muscle relaxant

Currently modified ECT is preferred and is given with adequate spacing i.e., no more than 3 ECT sessions per week.

After adequate preparation, a current of 200-1600mA (110V for 0.1-1 seconds) is given, resulting in an adequate seizure. Electroconvulsive therapy treatments are associated with retrograde amnesia for a period of several minutes before the treatment and anterograde amnesia after the treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During laparoscopic surgery, where shouldn't the trocar be inserted?
questions.explanation: Trocar insertion sites must be carefully selected to avoid major vascular injury, particularly to the superior and inferior epigastric arteries. The superior epigastric artery (Option A) supplies the upper abdominal wall and is at risk during upper trocar placement. The inferior epigastric artery (Option B) is located lateral to the rectus muscle and is highly vulnerable during mid-to-lower quadrant trocar insertion. Injuries to these vessels can lead to significant abdominal wall hematomas or intraperitoneal bleeding. While the abdominal aorta (Option C) must also be avoided, it is a deep retroperitoneal structure, whereas the epigastric arteries are frequently encountered in the anterior wall during entry. To minimize risk, secondary trocars should be inserted under direct vision, ideally lateral to the rectus sheath or using transillumination for guidance

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In fetal circulation, blood from the umbilical vein bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus. Into which vessel does it continue?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. UV-IVC

The ductus venosus is a fetal vascular shunt that allows oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the liver and enter the inferior vena cava (IVC). This ensures that highly oxygenated blood reaches the heart and brain with minimal loss of oxygen.

Normal pathway of oxygenated fetal blood: Placenta → Umbilical vein → Ductus venosus → Inferior vena cava → Right atrium → Foramen ovale → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Aorta → Brain and coronary circulation

Key fetal shunts:

• Ductus venosus: Umbilical vein → Inferior vena cava (bypasses the liver)
• Foramen ovale: Right atrium → Left atrium (bypasses the lungs)
• Ductus arteriosus: Pulmonary artery → Descending aorta (bypasses the lungs)
questions.learning: UV-IVC — The ductus venosus is a fetal vascular shunt that allows oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the liver and enter the inferior vena cava (IVC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The best drug for maintenance therapy of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy in pregnant women with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). It is considered safe throughout pregnancy and should be continued because it reduces disease flares, improves maternal outcomes, and decreases the risk of adverse fetal outcomes.

Discontinuing hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of lupus flares. May reduce the risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro/SSA-positive mothers

Why not the other options?

• B. Sulfasalazine: Used mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, not as maintenance therapy for SLE.
• C. Tacrolimus: May be used in selected cases (e.g., lupus nephritis), but it is not the first-line maintenance drug.
• D. Progestins: Used for contraception or prevention of preterm birth in selected situations, not for treating SLE.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-tubercular drug is not bactericidal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thioacetazone

Thioacetazone is not a bactericidal drug, it is bacteriostatic.

Thioacetazone is never used alone. It is only used as a combination with first-line TB medications, such as isoniazid and rifampicin. It is used primarily to prevent the development of bacteria that are resistant to first-line drugs and to treat patients infected with drug-resistant TB.

It should never be used in HIV patients as it can cause severe and fatal skin reactions. Side-effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, blurring of vision, hemolytic anemia and urticaria.

Isoniazid is a first-line bactericidal drug that is active against both intracellular and extracellular bacilli.

Rifapentin is a rifampin congener having a similar mechanism of action. It is a bactericidal drug having a longer half-life than rifampin.

Kanamycin is bactericidal and is active against bacilli resistant to streptomycin, INH, and cycloserine.
questions.learning: Thioacetazone Thioacetazone is not a bactericidal drug, it is bacteriostatic. It is only used as a combination with first-line TB medications, such as isoniazid and rifampicin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A hypertensive pregnant woman presented with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Abruptio placenta is the partial/total separation of a normally implanted placenta before delivery.

The bleeding may be either

* Revealed - Blood dissects downwards between membranes and uterine wall to escape through the cervix. Or,

* Concealed -Blood accumulates between the detached placenta and uterus. Or,

* Mixed

Risk factors for abruption placenta include prior abruption history, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and pregnancy-associated hypertension. The haemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This compromises fetal circulation leading to fetal distress.

Depending upon the degree of placental abruption and its clinical effects, the cases are graded as follows:

Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3

Vaginal bleeding is slight
Vaginal bleeding mild to moderate
Bleeding is moderate to severe or concealed.

Uterus irritable, minimal tenderness

Uterine tenderness is always present
Uterine tenderness is marked.

Maternal BP and fibrinogen unaffected
Maternal pulse increased, BP maintained
Shock is pronounced

FHS good
Fetal distress present
Fetal death is the rule

Maternal shock absent
Maternal shock absent
Associated coagulation defect or anuria may complicate

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment over or very close to the cervical os. Vaginal bleeding is usually painless in this condition. Fetal condition is generally good until bleeding is severe which occurs in later stages. High-risk factors include multiparty, previous cesarean, or myomectomy scar in the uterus.

In preterm labour, fetal movements are not compromised. Hydramnios does not present with bleeding PV.
questions.learning: Abruptio placenta — The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vagina, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: To perform MTP for a mentally challenged female, consent is obtained from?
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of India, the general rule is that only the consent of the pregnant woman herself is required for the procedure. However, there are specific legal exceptions for minors (under 18 years) and mentally challenged females. In these cases, the law mandates that the written consent of the legal guardian must be obtained before the MTP can be performed. Consent from the husband or partner (Option A) is never a legal requirement for an adult woman of sound mind. The Doctor (Option C) provides the medical opinion but cannot provide the legal consent. A Magistrate (Option D) might be involved in cases of sexual assault or missing guardians, but the primary legal provision is for the guardian. This requirement ensures that the rights of vulnerable individuals are protected while allowing them access to necessary medical services through their designated legal representative
questions.learning: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of India, the general rule is that only the consent of the pregnant woman herself is required for the procedure.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An 18-year-old female patient comes with the following findings. Which of the following is pathognomic of the primary stage of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Comedone

Comedones are pathognomic of the primary stage.

Acne is a polymorphic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit, frequently affecting the face, back, and chest. Comedonal lesions are the earliest lesions of acne. They represent the keratin plugs of the pilosebaceous duct. When the keratin plug is inside the follicle, it is called a closed comedone (Whitehead). When the keratin plug is exposed to the environment, it gets oxidized by the air and turns black which is known as an open comedone (blackhead).

Precipitating factors include:

* Lifestyle and environmental factors, diet, BMI, smoking and alcohol use, menstrual cycle, stress, and sleep deprivation

* Drugs like corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, etc

The severity of acne according to lesion type and extent:

Type of acne
Description

1. Comedonal

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Open comedones/blackheads
- Closed (whiteheads) comedones

2. Mild

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Inflammatory lesions <5 mm

3. Moderate

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Papulopustular lesions

4. Severe

- Deep-seated inflammatory lesions
- Nodules and deep pustules
- Small nodules are >5 mm; large nodules are >1 cm
- Painful lesions with exudative sinus tracts, disfiguring tissue destruction, and scarring
Acne conglabata:

- Multiple-grouped comedones
- Papules, tender inflammatory nodules of varying sizes, suppurative and coalesce to form sinus tract
- Extensive scarring

Assessment of acne includes:

* Leed's photometric grading scale

* Comprehensive acne severity system (CASS)

Management:

* Mild acne -

* Comedonal acne - topical retinoid

* Papular and pustular acne - topical retinoid and topical antibiotics

* Moderate papular or pustular acne and nodular acne - oral antibiotic + topical retinoid ± benzoyl peroxide

* Severe nodular and conglobate acne - oral isotretinoin

* Other therapies -  topical niacinamide, salicylic acid, chemical peels, lasers, and photodynamic therapy

* Novel drugs -

* Drugs that target both retinoic acid receptors -beta and -gamma -

* Adapalene

* Tazarotene

* Tretinoin

* Topical androgen receptor inhibitor - 1% clascoterone cream

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is not true? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) levels are reduced.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and polycystic ovaries. Typical hormonal findings in PCOS:

• Increased LH levels
• Normal or mildly decreased FSH levels
• Increased androgen levels
• Increased estrogen (especially estrone) due to peripheral conversion of androgens

The LH:FSH ratio is often elevated because LH secretion increases disproportionately.

Why option B is NOT true: FSH levels are usually normal or only mildly low, not markedly reduced

Pathophysiology:

• Increased LH stimulates theca cells → excess androgen production
• Hyperinsulinemia further increases androgen synthesis

Failure of normal follicular maturation leads to anovulation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for expectant management in unruptured ectopic gestation?
options: Initial serum beta hCG level < 200 mIU/mL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gestational sac size >4 cm

Gestational sac > 4cm is an indication for surgical management of ectopic pregnancy.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management is where only observation is done hoping for spontaneous resolution.

Indications:

* Asymptomatic

* No evidence of bleeding or rupture on TVS

* Initial serum hCG level <200 mIU/mL

* Gestational sac size less than 4 cm

* No fetal heartbeat on TVS

Medical management with intramuscular methotrexate injection, which can be done in single-dose or multidose protocols. The dose for single-dose therapy is 50 mg/m2.

Indications

* Low initial serum beta-hCG level

* Small gestational sac size- 4cm

* Absent fetal cardiac activity

* Hemodynamically stable

Surgical management of ectopic pregnancy includes laparoscopic salpingostomy/ salpingectomy and microsurgical laparotomy.

Indications

* Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met

* Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

* Gestational sac ≥4cm

* Fetal cardiac activity present

* Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL

* Failure of expectant or medical management

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with fever, chills, and malaise and is diagnosed with malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax. He gives a history of hemolytic anaemia among the male members of his family. Which of the following needs to be checked before starting antimalarial treatment in this patient? G6PD-Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. G6PD levels

In the clinical scenario of a 25-year-old male presenting with fever, chills, and malaise, diagnosed with malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, and having a family history of hemolytic anaemia among males, G6PD levels should be checked before initiating antimalarial therapy to ensure safety.

G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency anaemia is an X-linked genetic disorder that leads to a lack of the G6PD enzyme, which plays a crucial role in protecting red blood cells from oxidative stress. The enzyme deficiency impairs the ability of red blood cells to detoxify reactive oxygen species, making them more susceptible to damage and premature destruction. This results in hemolytic anaemia, especially when exposed to certain triggers such as infections, medications (like sulfa drugs or antimalarials), or fava beans, which can increase oxidative stress in the body.

It is associated with exacerbations after consuming anti-malarial drugs and in periods of oxidative stress. The peripheral smear shows characteristic "bite cells". In G6PD deficiency, uncontrolled oxidative stress causes haemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is largely preventable by avoiding exposure to triggering factors.

The severity of G6PD deficiency varies, with some individuals experiencing mild episodes of hemolysis, while others may suffer from more severe, recurrent crises. Symptoms of hemolytic anaemia include fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, and an increased reticulocyte count. Diagnosis is confirmed through enzyme assays to measure G6PD activity.

The mainstay of management is the avoidance of triggering factors. There is no definitive cure for the enzyme defect.

Other options:

Option A: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that affects red blood cell metabolism, leading to hemolytic anaemia due to impaired ATP production. This results in premature destruction of red blood cells and symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, and splenomegaly.

Option B: Sickling occurs in sickle cell anaemia when abnormal haemoglobin causes red blood cells to assume a crescent shape, leading to blockages and hemolysis. Enzyme deficiencies, like G6PD or pyruvate kinase deficiency, can exacerbate the condition by increasing oxidative stress, leading to further hemolytic episodes.

Option C: Hexokinase deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that impairs the first step of glucose metabolism, leading to reduced ATP production. This condition can result in muscle weakness, hemolytic anaemia, and other metabolic disturbances due to inadequate energy supply.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the term used for a graft transplanted between genetically identical twins?
questions.explanation: In transplantation immunology, grafts are classified based on the genetic relationship between the donor and the recipient. An Isograft (or syngeneic graft) is a transplant between two individuals who are genetically identical, such as monozygotic (identical) twins. Because the MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) antigens are identical, there is no risk of immunological rejection. An Autograft (Option B) is a transplant of tissue from one part of a person's body to another (e.g., a skin graft). An Allograft (Option A) is a transplant between two genetically different members of the same species, such as a kidney from a non-twin sibling or a cadaver. A Xenograft (Option D) is a transplant between members of different species, such as a pig valve used in a human. Isografts represent the ideal transplant scenario because they achieve permanent survival without the need for lifelong immunosuppression
questions.learning: In transplantation immunology, grafts are classified based on the genetic relationship between the donor and the recipient. An Isograft (or syngeneic graft) is a transplant between two individuals who are genetically identical, such as monozygotic…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which cellular component is exclusively present in gram-negative bacteria and not found in gram-positive organisms?
questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria possess a complex cell envelope that includes an outer membrane. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also known as endotoxin, is a major component located exclusively in the outer leaflet of this outer membrane. It is not found in gram-positive bacteria. Capsules (Option A) and Flagella (Option D) are found in both gram-positive and gram-negative species. Peptidoglycan (Option B) is a core component of the cell wall for both types, although gram-positive bacteria have a significantly thicker layer than gram-negative bacteria. LPS is clinically significant because its release into the bloodstream can trigger a massive immune response, leading to endotoxic shock and systemic inflammation. Therefore, lipopolysaccharide is the unique biochemical marker of the gram-negative cell wall
questions.learning: Gram-negative bacteria possess a complex cell envelope that includes an outer membrane. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also known as endotoxin, is a major component located exclusively in the outer leaflet of this outer membrane.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: How should a 40-year-old woman with an asymptomatic gallbladder polyp, detected on ultrasound and without gallstones, be managed?
questions.explanation: Gallbladder polyps are common findings on ultrasound. For a patient who is asymptomatic, has no gallstones, and possesses a small polyp measuring only , the standard of care is regular follow-up via ultrasound (Option A). Most polyps under are benign (cholesterol polyps) and have a very low risk of malignancy. Surgical intervention via Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (Option C) or Open Cholecystectomy (Option D) is generally reserved for polyps , those that are symptomatic, or those that show rapid growth on serial imaging. A simple polypectomy (Option B) is not a standard procedure for gallbladder disease. The frequency of follow-up (2–6 months initially) is designed to monitor for stability. Therefore, because the lesion is small and asymptomatic, conservative monitoring is the definitive and most appropriate management choice to avoid unnecessary surgery. Consequently, Option A represents the standard clinical guideline for this patient
questions.learning: Gallbladder polyps are common findings on ultrasound. For a patient who is asymptomatic, has no gallstones, and possesses a small polyp measuring only , the standard of care is regular follow-up via ultrasound (Option A).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction and difficulty breathing through his nose. Examination reveals an irregular mass extending from the posterior nasal apertures (choanae). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An antro-choanal polyp (ACP) is a benign growth that originates from the maxillary sinus and exits through the natural ostium to extend into the nasopharynx via the posterior choana. Clinically, it presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction that is characteristically worse on expiration (the "ball-valve" effect). On examination, it appears as a smooth, greyish-white mass seen behind the soft palate. Thornwaldt cyst (Option A) is a benign midline bursa in the nasopharynx, not a polypoid mass. Hypertrophic rhinitis (Option C) involves generalized swelling of the turbinates, not a discrete choanal mass. Adenoid hypertrophy (Option D) is a common cause of posterior nasal obstruction in children, but is rare in a 54-year-old man. Diagnosis of ACP is confirmed by CT scan showing the polyp originating in the maxillary sinus. Management is surgical, requiring complete removal of the polyp and its stalk, typically through Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: An antro-choanal polyp (ACP) is a benign growth that originates from the maxillary sinus and exits through the natural ostium to extend into the nasopharynx via the posterior choana.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Kidney responds to shock by _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increasing afferent arteriole resistance

Kidney responds to shock by increasing afferent arteriolar resistance.

During shock, both afferent and efferent arterioles in kidney are constricted, however, the efferent vessels are constricted much more.
The glomerular filtration rate and the plasma renal flow is decreased during shock. As plasma renal flow is decreased to a greater extent, the filtration fraction increases. (Option 1 & 3)
questions.learning: Increasing afferent arteriole resistance Kidney responds to shock by increasing afferent arteriolar resistance. During shock, both afferent and efferent arterioles in kidney are constricted, however, the efferent vessels are constricted much more.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is being evaluated for delayed motor milestones. On examination, the child has poor head control and generalized hypotonia. Birth and immediate neonatal period were uncomplicated. Family history is unremarkable. The pediatric neurologist considers several differential diagnoses that can present with hypotonia in infancy. Which of the following conditions is least likely to present with hypotonia during infancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Periventricular leukomalacia

• Hypotonia (“floppy infant”) in early infancy is commonly seen in genetic, neuromuscular, and endocrine disorders, such as Prader–Willi syndrome, congenital myopathies, and congenital hypothyroidism, due to impaired muscle tone or neuromuscular function.
• In contrast, periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), a form of white matter injury seen in premature infants, typically evolves into spasticity and hypertonia (spastic cerebral palsy) rather than persistent hypotonia. Therefore, PVL is least likely to present with hypotonia in infancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Who comes under category III non-heart-beating donor?
options: A patient who died during transportation to the hospital
A patient who died after failed resuscitation after reaching the hospital
A patient who was brought dead to the hospital
A patient who is awaiting death in the hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patient who is awaiting death in the hospital

Category III donors are patients with non-survivable injuries who have their treatment withdrawn and if such patients wished in life to be organ donors, the transplant team can attend at the time of treatment withdrawal and retrieve organs after cardiac arrest has occurred.

Modified Maastricht classification- Categories of non-heart-beating donors:

Category

Category I
Includes victims of accident and suicide who are found dead at the scene and resuscitation is deemed pointless (e.g. fatal cervical spine fracture).

victims of sudden cardiac or cerebral catastrophe who are brought to emergency departments while being resuscitated by ambulance personnel or who died in the department. Other sources include patients suffering an isolated brain injury, anoxia, and stroke, and victims of major trauma who died soon after hospital admission.

Patients who are dying, often in an intensive care unit. These are the patients awaiting cardiac arrest where the treating clinicians have decided to withdraw treatment and not commence resuscitation for various reasons.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During the autopsy of a 30-year-old man who died due to drowning, the pathologist observes several cut-like marks on the arms. In the context of drowning, these findings raise questions about their origin. What is the most likely explanation for these marks on the victim’s arms?
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple irregular cut-like wounds on the palm and fingers, which are characteristic of defense wounds. These injuries occur when a person actively tries to protect themselves from an assault, typically by raising their hands to block or grab a weapon. As a result, cuts are commonly seen on the palms, fingers, and forearms. In the context of drowning, the presence of such injuries suggests that the victim may have been attacked before or during entry into water, rather than accidental drowning alone. Defense wounds indicate struggle and possible homicidal involvement. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Self-inflicted injury: Usually more superficial, accessible, and patterned (C) Accidental cuts: Random and less localized to defensive areas (D) Washer-women hands: Refers to wrinkling of skin after prolonged immersion, not cuts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the histological image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymph node

The image is that of a lymph node.

Each lymph node is bean-shaped. The concave part consists of the hilum, through which the blood vessels enter and leave the node. Each lymph node is surrounded by a thin capsule. Below the capsule is the clear space, which is called the subcapsular sinus. The lymph node contains the outer cortex and an inner medulla.

Cortex

* The outermost region of the lymph node, located beneath the capsule.

* Primary follicles: Composed primarily of small, resting B lymphocytes (naive B cells). These follicles are unactivated and appear as small, round clusters.

* Secondary follicles: These form when B cells within the primary follicle are activated by antigenic stimulation. They are characterized by a germinal centre (where B cells proliferate and differentiate) and a mantle zone (where small, resting B cells surround the germinal centre).

* Mantle zone: A ring of small, naive B lymphocytes surrounding the germinal centre.

Paracortex (T-cell Zone)

* Situated between the cortex and the medulla, this area is rich in T lymphocytes, which are involved in T-cell mediated immunity.

* The paracortex also contains dendritic cells that present antigens to T cells and is crucial for T-cell dependent immune responses.

* This zone lacks follicles and is more densely populated with T cells.

Medulla

* The innermost part of the lymph node, containing medullary cords and medullary sinuses.

* Medullary cords: These are dense clusters of plasma cells, B cells, T cells, and macrophages that are responsible for producing antibodies and providing immune surveillance.

* Medullary sinuses: Spaces that allow the passage of lymph and contain macrophages that filter out foreign particles and pathogens.

Option A: The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

Option B: The main features that can be used to identify the spleen are:

* Capsule and trabeculae extending from it.

* Arterioles arising from the network of vessels that have branched from the splenic artery in the trabecular spaces.

* White pulp - composed of aggregation of lymphocytes arranged around an arteriole.

* Red pulp - areas between the white pulp and trabecular spaces regions where blood cells flow into.

* Sinusoids -blood from spaces of the red pulp is collected by wide sinusoids that drain into veins in the trabeculae.

Option C: The tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules, which are surrounded by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oropharyngeal surface. The epithelium dips into the substance of the gland and forms tonsillar crypts.
