questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with cervical lymphadenopathy and is found to be retropositive. A fungal culture depicts a velvety growth with red diffusible pigment on the underside, as shown below. Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Talaromyces marneffei

The most likely causative organism based on the history and image given is Talaromyces marneffei (Penicillium marneffei).

T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis). It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. It is diagnosed by blood culture, which shows a mold with a powdery surface and characteristic red pigment that diffuses into the agar. Histopathological examination reveals yeast-like organisms with central septation.

Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.

Mild and moderate infections can be treated with itraconazole. Amphotericin B is recommended for severe infections.

Other options:

Option B - Blastomyces are thermally dimorphic fungi and cause blastomycosis. Primary infection usually affects the lungs, which can later disseminate through the blood to form multiple abscesses at sites such as skin and bone. Culture at 25–30 degrees Celsius promotes hyphal growth. Microscopic examination of stained specimens shows broad-based budding yeast cells.

Option C - Aspergillus colonies have a velvety powdery surface, of which the color varies according to the species. Aspergillus fumigatus is seen as dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black colored. Yellow-green growth is seen in the case of Aspergillus flavus. On microscopy, dichotomous branching at acute angles seen after staining is characteristic. It can cause invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients.

The image below shows Aspergillus niger colonies.

Option D - Pneumocystis jirovecii cannot be cultured. On being stained by methenamine silver, the cyst wall appears black under the microscope. Trophozoites can also be seen after staining. Clinical features include dyspnea, fever, and cough. It can cause lethal pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals. Diffuse bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates can be seen on chest radiograph.
questions.learning: Talaromyces marneffei — The most likely causative organism based on the history and image given is Talaromyces marneffei (Penicillium marneffei). T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used as an anti-smoking agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Varenicline

Varenicline is an α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor partial agonist used in the treatment of nicotine addiction.

The FDA approved medication to aid in smoking cessation include:

• NRT-Nicotine Replacement Therapy
• Bupropion
• Varenicline

Drugs are only adjunctive to behavioral therapy, which is the first line of management.

Behavior therapy is the most widely accepted and well-proven psychological therapy for treating Tobacco use disorder. It consists of several techniques:

• Skill training and relapse prevention.
• Stimulus control.
• Mindfulness approaches.

Bupropion:

• It enhances both noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission by inhibiting reuptake.
• Used for aiding smoking cessation and for the treatment of depression in combination with SSRIs.
• Side effects: seizures, sedation

Varenicline:

• α4β2 Nicotinic ACh receptor partial agonist.
• Used for smoking cessation.
• Side effects: sleep disturbance, may depress mood and increase suicidal tendencies.

Mirtazapine:

• Serotonin receptor antagonist.
• Used for the treatment of depression in combination with SSRIs and for insomnia in depressive patients.
• Side effect: sedation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who shows no improvement on inhaled salmeterol alone, which additional medication can be added to the treatment regimen?
questions.explanation: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is currently taking Salmeterol, which is a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA). The most appropriate and standard "next step" is to add an anticholinergic agent, such as Ipratropium (a short-acting muscarinic antagonist) or Tiotropium (a LAMA) . These drugs provide synergistic bronchodilation by blocking parasympathetic-mediated airway constriction. Theophylline (Option A) is an oral bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic window and more side effects, typically used as a third-line agent. Azithromycin (Option B) is used for its anti-inflammatory properties in patients with frequent exacerbations but is not a primary bronchodilator. Oral glucocorticoids (Option C) are reserved for managing acute exacerbations rather than daily maintenance due to systemic side effects. Therefore, adding an inhaled muscarinic antagonist like Ipratropium to the existing LABA is the definitive and recommended clinical strategy to improve symptoms
questions.learning: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is currently taking Salmeterol, which is a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Blood volume increases during pregnancy above non-pregnant level at 30–34 weeks:
options: Blood volume does not increase at all
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. By 40–50%

During normal pregnancy, maternal blood volume increases by approximately 40–50%, reaching its maximum at around 30–34 weeks of gestation. This physiological hypervolemia helps meet the increased metabolic demands of pregnancy and protects against blood loss during delivery.

Why not the other options?

• A. By 10–20%: Too low.
• B. By 25–30%: Less than the normal physiological increase.
• D. Blood volume does not increase at all: Incorrect.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is suspected to have endometriosis. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopy

For endometriosis, the investigation of choice which can help with both the diagnosis and treatment is laparoscopy. It is used to locate the sites, take a biopsy and surgically remove the deposits.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium at a site outside the uterine cavity. It can be found in ectopic sites such as the ovary, pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, appendix, pelvic lymph nodes, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) scar endometriosis, umbilicus, and lung.

Dysmenorrhea is the most common presenting symptom, associated with abdominal and pelvic pain, menorrhagia, dyspareunia and infertility. Laparoscopy is the gold standard modality for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. Typical characteristics include 'powder-burn' - puckered black spots, red vascular, bluish, blackish cysts, chocolate cysts, and dense adhesions in the pelvis.

For minimal disease, medical management with NSAIDs and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow. For moderate to severe diseases oral progestogens, GnRH agonists or danazol that antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium, causing endometrial atrophy are used.

Surgery is preferred in patients with infertility. Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser, and resection of endometrioma can be done. Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a definitive and most effective therapy for women with endometriosis who do not wish to retain fertility.
questions.learning: Laparoscopy For endometriosis, the investigation of choice which can help with both the diagnosis and treatment is laparoscopy. It is used to locate the sites, take a biopsy and surgically remove the deposits.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What type of MRI image is given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Susceptibility weighted image

The image shown is a susceptibility-weighted image(SWI) as it clearly demonstrates microhemorrhages as hypointense foci.

SWI is a form of MRI sequence that is especially sensitive to substances that distort the local magnetic field. Compounds with diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic properties will interact with the local magnetic field and produce distraction. This would lead to a loss of signal in these areas.

Deoxyhemoglobin, hemosiderin, and ferritin are paramagnetic. Bone minerals and dystrophic calcifications are diamagnetic in nature.

The main clinical use is the identification of microhemorrhages/blood products or calcium that are not detected in other MRI sequences.

Other options:

Proton density image:

It is based on the number of nuclei in the area that is imaged. In PD-weighted image tissues with a higher density of protons produce stronger signals and appear brighter. PD weighted image can be identified by comparing fluid with the fat signal. Fluids in these images appear greyish white similar or the appearance of fat in the body.

Gradient echo sequences(GRE):

It uses gradient fields to generate transverse magnetization. In areas of hemorrhage, the iron that is present in the hemoglobin produces its own local magnetic field and dephases the spinning nuclei. This is useful to identify hemorrhagic contusions in the brain and pigmented villonodular synovitis.

Inversion recovery sequences:

This MRI sequence is used to selectively null certain tissues. It can be:

• Short tau inversion recovery(STIR) where fat is nulled. Fluids appear bright and fat appears dark in these images.
• Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR) or double inversion recovery(DIR where fluid is nulled.- The fluid(CSF) normally appears dark and lesions appear to be brighter on these images.

FLAIR image-

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with long-standing, recurrent watery diarrhea that is refractory to conventional treatment, along with weakness, dehydration, and hypokalemia. Blood tests reveal markedly elevated levels of a specific peptide. Based on these findings, which pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of profuse, chronic, watery diarrhea, dehydration, and hypokalemia is characteristic of "pancreatic cholera," also known as Verner-Morrison syndrome. This syndrome is caused by a VIPoma, a neuroendocrine tumor (usually in the pancreas) that secretes excessive Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP). VIP stimulates intestinal secretion and inhibits gastric acid, resulting in the WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria). Glucagonoma (Option B) presents with necrolytic migratory erythema and mild diabetes. Insulinoma (Option C) causes hypoglycemia. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (Option D) is caused by a gastrinoma, resulting in severe peptic ulcers rather than the painless, watery "cholera-like" diarrhea seen here. Therefore, because the specific biochemical triad of watery diarrhea and low potassium is linked to VIP overproduction, VIPoma is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of profuse, chronic, watery diarrhea, dehydration, and hypokalemia is characteristic of "pancreatic cholera," also known as Verner-Morrison syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 19-year-old otherwise healthy female experiences episodic numbness and tingling of the fingers, precipitated by stress or exposure to cold, with characteristic features shown in the accompanying image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon (Raynaud's disease) is characterized by episodic digital vasospasm, classically triggered by cold temperatures or emotional stress. It typically occurs in young females (late teens to early 20s) who have no underlying connective tissue or systemic disease. The condition involves a symmetric triphasic color change: white (pallor due to ischemia), blue (cyanosis due to deoxygenation), and red (rubor due to reactive hyperemia). The provided image supports this diagnosis by showing the sharp demarcation of pallor in the digits. Secondary Raynaud's phenomenon (Option B) is associated with an underlying autoimmune disorder, such as systemic sclerosis, and usually presents later in life or with systemic symptoms. Cold sores (Option C) are caused by the herpes simplex virus and present with painful vesicles. Scleredema (Option D) involves a distinct thickening of the skin. Therefore, given the demographic and the absence of pre-existing conditions, primary Raynaud's is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon (Raynaud's disease) is characterized by episodic digital vasospasm, classically triggered by cold temperatures or emotional stress.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which staining method is commonly used for identifying Cryptococcus?
questions.explanation: The India ink stain is the classic and most rapid method used for the presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans, particularly in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples. Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast; the ink particles are too large to penetrate the thick polysaccharide capsule, creating a characteristic clear halo around the budding yeast cells against a dark background. Albert's stain (Option A) is used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Auramine-rhodamine (Option D) is a fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Silver staining (Option B) can visualize Cryptococcus in tissue sections but is not the primary rapid diagnostic tool for CSF. Identifying the capsule via India ink is a life-saving diagnostic step in immuno compromised patients (like those with HIV/AIDS) presenting with meningitis. Although more sensitive antigen tests are now available, the India ink prep remains a foundational tool in clinical microbiology for the immediate visualization of this pathogen
questions.learning: The India ink stain is the classic and most rapid method used for the presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans, particularly in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A public witness of the incident is asked to attend the court and record his evidence. Which type of evidence is provided by the witness to the court?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral evidence

The evidence provided by a public witness of the incident to the court is oral evidence.

Oral evidence is given by a person who has personal knowledge of the facts associated with a particular incident. It is the evidence given by an eyewitness. The oral evidence should be direct whenever possible according to Section 60 of the Indian Evidence Act(IEA). It includes all the statements made by the witness in relation to the inquiry which is permitted by the court.

Other options:

Option B: Hearsay evidence is a type of evidence given by a person who has no personal knowledge of the facts in relation to the incident but only repeats what he heard others saying.

Option C: Subpoena is also known as summons. It is an authoritative call to appear in court. It is a document compelling the attendance of a witness in a Court of law under penalty, on a particular day, time, and place, for the purpose of giving evidence. It is issued by the Court. Section 61 to 69 of CrPc deals with the summons.

Option D: Circumstantial evidence is also known as indirect evidence. It is not the direct testimony of an eye witness but has a bearing upon the fact of the other and subsidiary facts which are relied upon as consistent. This type of evidence needs the Court of Law to make reasonable inferences based on the information presented.

IPC section

192

193

Punishment for false evidence

• Judicial proceedings: up to 7 yrs of imprisonment and fine
• Any other case: up to 3 yrs of imprisonment and fine

196

Using evidence known to be false

questions.learning: Oral evidence — The evidence provided by a public witness of the incident to the court is oral evidence. Oral evidence is given by a person who has personal knowledge of the facts associated with a particular incident.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the best imaging modality to diagnose neuroendocrine tumours (NETs)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. PET

Positron emission tomography (PET) is the best modality to diagnose Neuroendocrine tumors(NETs).

The initial imaging investigation is standard cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In patients of suspected NETs, CTs of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis are done for staging, and consideration of an MRI of the liver or pancreas in cases where further definition is required.

PET scans with 111In (indium) labeled pentetreotide somatostatin and 68Ga (gallium) linked somatostatin analogues take advantage of the overexpression of somatostatin receptors commonly seen in NETs. These radiolabeled somatostatin analogues localized with PET scan are the best imaging modality for NETs.
questions.learning: PET Positron emission tomography (PET) is the best modality to diagnose Neuroendocrine tumors(NETs). The initial imaging investigation is standard cross-sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In fetal alcohol syndrome, which of the following is not seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Macrocephaly

Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is associated with microcephaly rather than macrocephaly.

Alcohol exposure during pregnancy results in reduced brain volume in the frontal lobe, striatum, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and cerebellum. It also causes thinning of the corpus callosum and abnormal functioning of the amygdala.

Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASDs) are the leading preventable causes of developmental delay and intellectual disability. FASDs encompass different conditions such as FAS, partial FAS, alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, alcohol-related birth defect, and neurobehavioral disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure.

Diagnostic criteria for FASDs include characteristic facial features, prenatal/postnatal growth deficiency, neurobehavioral impairment, and maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy.

The facial features of FAS include short palpebral fissures, a thin upper lip vermilion border, a smooth philtrum, epicanthic folds, a flattened nasal bridge, lowset and unparallel ears, and retarded midfacial development.

CNS involvement leads to microcephaly, incomplete holoprosencephaly, and agenesis of the corpus callosum and the cerebellar vermis. The neurocognitive features include developmental delays, inattention, impulsivity, social impairments, and behavioral difficulties. Common comorbidities include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), self-regulation problems, and impulse control issues. Cardiac anomalies are also seen, with VSD being more common than ASD and tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.learning: Macrocephaly Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is associated with microcephaly rather than macrocephaly. Alcohol exposure during pregnancy results in reduced brain volume in the frontal lobe, striatum, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and cerebellum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The distance walked in 6 minutes is an indirect measure of which of the following variables of the BODE Index which is used to assess the prognosis in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Exercise capacity

The BODE Index is a multidimensional prognostic scoring system used to predict mortality, hospitalization, and disease severity in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is a better predictor of prognosis than FEV₁ alone.

Components of the BODE Index

| Component | Assessment

| --------- | ----------

| B – Body Mass Index (BMI) | Nutritional status

| O – Airflow Obstruction | Post-bronchodilator FEV₁ (% predicted)

| D – Dyspnoea | Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea scale

| E – Exercise Capacity | 6-minute walk distance (6MWD)

The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) measures the distance a patient can walk in 6 minutes, which is an indirect measure of exercise capacity and functional status.

• Lower 6-minute walk distance is associated with:

• Increased mortality
• More frequent COPD exacerbations
• Poorer quality of life

• A higher BODE score indicates worse prognosis.
questions.learning: Exercise capacity — The BODE Index is a multidimensional prognostic scoring system used to predict mortality, hospitalization, and disease severity in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following is not a criterion to diagnose IUGR?

PI - Pulsatility Index
options: Absent diastolic flow in umbilical artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine artery PI < 95th percentile

Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) < 95th percentile is not a criterion used to diagnose intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).

Fetal growth restriction (FGR)/IUGR is said to be present in those babies whose birth weight is below the 10th centile of the average for the gestational age.

The causes of fetal growth restriction are divided into :

• Maternal - constitutional, nutritional, anemia, hypertension, chronic renal disease, alcohol, smoking
• Fetal - Structural anomaly, chromosomal anomaly, infections, multiple pregnancy
• Placental -placenta previa, abruption, circumvallate placenta
• Unknown

Diagnosis :

Clinical -

• Symphysis fundal height (SFH) measurement in centimeters closely correlates with gestational age after 24 weeks. A lag of 3 cm or more suggests growth restriction.
• Maternal weight gain remains stationary or, at times, falling
• Measurement of the abdominal girth showing stationary or falling values

Ultrasound -

Various criteria and thresholds have been used to define FGR. These have included estimated fetal weights (EFW) below the 3rd, 5th, or 10th percentiles; similar abdominal circumference (AC) percentiles; a specified decline in the EFW percentile or AC percentile over serial assessments; and various abnormal Doppler findings.

Currently, the ACOG (2021) and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (2020) recommend defining FGR as either an EFW <10th percentile for gestational age or an AC <10th percentile for gestational age.

AC is the single most sensitive parameter to detect FGR.

Doppler velocimetry - The umbilical artery Doppler study should be the primary surveillance tool in FGR (RCOG).

• In normal pregnancy, the systolic/diastolic (S/D) ratio, pulsatility index (PI) and resistance index (RI) decrease as the gestational age advances. Values greater than 2SD indicate reduced diastolic velocities and increased placental vascular resistance. These are associated with FGR and intra-uterine fetal hypoxia.
• Reduced or absent or reversed end-diastolic velocity (AREDV) in the umbilical artery indicates fetal jeopardy and poor perinatal outcome.
• Umbilical venous pulsations indicate inefficient cardiac output with a rise in central venous pressure → impending cardiac failure.
• Middle cerebral artery (MCA): Increased diastolic velocity (brain-sparing effect) is observed in FGR. This is due to cerebral vasodilatation in response to hypoxemia. Abnormal MCA PI, suggests fetal compromise.
• Doppler cerebroplacental ratio (CPR): It is calculated by dividing MCA PI by UA PI. In FGR, placental resistance (UA PI) increases and fetal brain vascular resistance (MCA PI) decreases resulting in a decrease in CPR index. CPR is more sensitive compared to UA or MCA Doppler alone.

Management is as outlined below :

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who is on treatment for hyperlipidemia develops gallstones. What is the mechanism of action of the causative drug that was given to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activates PPAR alpha

The antilipidemic drugs likely to cause gallstones are the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) that act by activating PPAR alpha.

PPARs are a superfamily of nuclear receptors involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis and metabolic function. It has three subtypes:

• PPARα - reduces triglyceride level
• PPARγ - causes insulin sensitization
• PPARδ - enhances fatty acids metabolism

Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is a key enzyme in the degradation of VLDL. Fibrates bind to PPAR alpha and cause stimulation of lipoprotein lipase enzyme. Increased LPL synthesis enhances the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Additionally, fibrates also stimulate fatty acid oxidation and reduce the expression of apo C-III (inhibitor of lipolysis). All fibrates increase the lithogenicity of bile, thereby increasing the risk of gall stones

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which is the most common benign tumour of the ovary in the reproductive age group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benign teratoma

A benign teratoma or dermoid cyst is the most common benign tumor of the ovary in the reproductive age group. It is also the:

* Most common benign tumor of ovary diagnosed in pregnancy

* Most common germ cell tumor (overall)

* Most typical tumor to undergo torsion.

* Bilateral in 10-15% cases.

It consists of a Rokitansky’s protuberance, which is a projection covered by skin, sebaceous glands, sweat glands along with teeth & bones can be seen. Sometimes thyroid tissue can be seen on histopathological study – known as Struma Ovarii. The most common tissue elements found are ectodermal derivatives.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is operated when its size is greater than __________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5.5 cm

An asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in an otherwise fit patient should be considered for repair if >5.5 cm  in diameter (measured by ultrasonography). The annual incidence of rupture rises from 1% or less in aneurysms that are <5.5 cm in diameter to a significant level of nearly 25%, in those that are 7 cm  in diameter.

As open elective surgery (transabdominal) carries a 5% mortality rate, the balance is in favor of elective operation once the maximum diameter is >5.5 cm.

6 monthly follow-up ultrasonographic assessment is indicated for asymptomatic aneurysms <5.5cm in diameter.
questions.learning: 5.5 cm An asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in an otherwise fit patient should be considered for repair if >5.5 cm in diameter (measured by ultrasonography).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following are true about subclinical myocarditis?

1. Palpitations
2. Elevated proBNP, Troponins
3. Regional wall motion abnormalities in 2D echo
4. ECG suggestive of myocarditis
5. Low LVEF on 2D echo
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3, 4, 5

A patient is diagnosed with possible subclinical acute myocarditis when there is a typical syndrome but without any cardiac symptoms such as palpitations. Biomarkers of cardiac injury are elevated (statement 2), ECG is abnormal (statement 4), and there is a reduced LV ejection fraction (statement 5) and regional wall motion abnormality on 2D echo (statement 3).

Probable acute myocarditis is diagnosed when the aforementioned criteria are accompanied by cardiac symptoms such as palpitations, shortness of breath, and chest pain. When there are signs of pericarditis along with elevated CK-MB or troponins and regional wall motion abnormalities, the term myopericarditis or perimyocarditis is used.

Definite myocarditis is diagnosed when there is histological evidence of inflammation on endomyocardial biopsy, and does not require any other laboratory or clinical criteria.
questions.learning: 2, 3, 4, 5 A patient is diagnosed with possible subclinical acute myocarditis when there is a typical syndrome but without any cardiac symptoms such as palpitations.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding LNG-20 (Mirena): 1. It is a T-shaped IUD filled with natural hormone progesterone. 2. It is associated with a low pregnancy rate (2 per 1000 women). 3. It is associated with a large number of ectopic pregnancies. 4. It is associated with lower menstrual blood loss as compared to copper IUDs. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 4 only

LNG-20 (Mirena) is a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) that releases 20 µg of levonorgestrel per day. It provides highly effective long-term reversible contraception and has several non-contraceptive therapeutic benefits, particularly in women with heavy menstrual bleeding.

• 1. It is a T-shaped IUD filled with natural hormone progesterone. ✗

• Mirena contains levonorgestrel, a synthetic progestin, not natural progesterone.

• 2. It is associated with a low pregnancy rate (≈2 per 1000 women). ✓

• Mirena has a failure rate of about 0.2% per year (2 per 1000 women), making it one of the most effective reversible contraceptives.

• 3. It is associated with a large number of ectopic pregnancies. ✗

• Mirena reduces the overall risk of ectopic pregnancy because it is highly effective at preventing pregnancy.
• However, if pregnancy occurs with Mirena in situ, the likelihood that it is ectopic is relatively higher, but the absolute risk remains very low.

• 4. It is associated with lower menstrual blood loss as compared to copper IUDs. ✓

• Levonorgestrel causes endometrial atrophy, significantly reducing menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly diabetic patient presented with complaints of blurring of vision. He underwent a cataract surgery 1 month ago. The patient's fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed a flower-petal appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystoid macular edema

The given scenario of a diabetic patient with the blurring of vision and an FFA showing a flower petal pattern (petaloid appearance) is suggestive of cystoid macular edema (CME). It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region.

CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and foveal depression. In advanced cases, a lamellar macular hole may develop.

Treatment includes topical anti-prostaglandins (ketorolac), steroids, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide), and managing the causative factor.

Given below is the FFA image showing the classic flower-petal appearance, followed by an OCT image showing intraretinal cystoid spaces in CME:

Other options:

Option A: Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of the macular region neurosensory retina with/without retinal pigment epithelium detachment. Patients complain of sudden onset painless loss of vision, micropsia, and metamorphopsia. FFA shows two patterns of leakage, ink-blot pattern and smoke-stick pattern. OCT image of central serous retinopathy is seen below which neurosensory retinal detachment and accompanying small detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Option B: Macular hole is a partial or full-thickness hole in the neurosensory retina of the foveal region. Causes include trauma, CME, or idiopathic. There is a decrease in vision, typically around 6/60 for full-thickness holes. FFA shows early foveal hyperfluorescene without a leak.

OCT image of the macular hole is seen below which shows a full-thickness hole in the foveal retina.

Option D: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is bilateral disease affecting people who are above 50 years of age. It can be exudative or non-exudative types. There can be a gradual or sudden loss of vision depending on the type of AMD. Drusens (yellowish-white elevated spots caused by extracellular deposits in the macular region) of various types can be noted. FFA shows punctate hyperfluorescence due to the drusen.

OCT and FFA image of drusens is shown below:
questions.learning: Cystoid macular edema — The given scenario of a diabetic patient with the blurring of vision and an FFA showing a flower petal pattern (petaloid appearance) is suggestive of cystoid macular edema (CME).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A worker in a groundnut factory developed food poisoning after he ate some stale groundnuts which were stored in the factory. What is the most probable cause in this person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aflatoxins

Aflatoxin is the most probable cause in this patient as he had some stale groundnuts in which mycotoxins from Aspergillus fungi can be present.

Aflatoxins:

* These are a type of mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species of fungi, such as A. flavus (secretes B1) and A. parasiticus (secretes B1, B2, G1 and G2)

* Frequently present in moldy foods, like groundnuts, corn, and peas.

* These toxins are highly toxic to animals and birds, as well as to human beings.

* Known to cause hepatomas in lower animals, and carcinogenic effects in humans have also been seen.

Other options:

BOAA (Beta oxalyl amino alanine) is the toxic compound causing Lathyrism.

Sanguinarine is the toxic compound causing epidemic dropsy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding shoulder dystocia? I. It can be predicted during early labour. II. Anencephaly is a risk factor. III. Turtle neck sign is present. IV. Episiotomy should always be given. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency in which, after delivery of the fetal head, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis (or less commonly, the posterior shoulder behind the sacral promontory), preventing delivery of the shoulders. It requires prompt recognition and a series of obstetric maneuvers to prevent fetal hypoxia and birth trauma. The following statements are true:

• II. Anencephaly is a risk factor: Anencephalic fetuses have a small head with relatively normal-sized shoulders, increasing the risk of shoulder dystocia.
• III. Turtle neck sign is present: The turtle sign is the classic clinical sign of shoulder dystocia, in which the delivered fetal head retracts against the maternal perineum after expulsion because the shoulders are impacted.
• IV. Episiotomy should always be given: Although an episiotomy does not relieve the bony obstruction, it is commonly performed to provide additional space for internal maneuvers (e.g., Rubin or Woods screw maneuver). Hence, many traditional examination questions consider it appropriate.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. It can be predicted during early labour: Shoulder dystocia is largely unpredictable. Although several risk factors are recognized, most cases occur without warning, and many women with risk factors deliver without shoulder dystocia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV patient came to the clinic with a history of diarrhea. Stool microscopy showed the oocysts that were 4-8 μm in size. The image is shown below. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryptosporidium

The given clinical scenario and the stool microscopy show oocysts of Cryptosporidium.

Cryptosporidium is a coccidian parasite implicated in causing traveller's diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The two cryptosporidium species responsible are C. hominis and C. parvum.

The infective form is the oocyst excreted in the patient's feces, which can be acquired through drinking water or recreational water activities. The oocysts are immediately infectious (unlike isospora oocysts, which require maturation), and may cause autoinfection.

Because of their small size, they are difficult to see using routine staining and hence, acid-fast staining is done.

Once ingested, the 4 sporozoites are released from each cyst and attach to the small intestinal mucosa. It causes crampy abdominal pain and non-inflammatory watery diarrhea.

Treatment is mainly supportive, though nitazoxanide has been approved for use in cryptosporidium infection.

Other options:

Option A: Oocysts of isospora are 23-36 μm, oval, and contain two sporocysts, each having four sporozoites. They are uniformly acid-fast.

Option B: Sporulated oocysts of cyclospora are 8-12 μm in size, round, and contain 2 sporocysts each having two sporozoites. They are acid-fast.

Option D: Microspora oocysts are 2-4 μm in size, oval to cylindrical in shape with a polar filament. Spores are gram-positive and acid-fast.
questions.learning: Cryptosporidium — The given clinical scenario and the stool microscopy show oocysts of Cryptosporidium. Cryptosporidium is a coccidian parasite implicated in causing traveller's diarrhea in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with high-grade chills and violent shaking (rigors), along with sudden-onset severe pain in the right flank. This clinical picture raises concern for a serious infectious or inflammatory condition involving the abdomen or flank. Based on these symptoms and the expected findings from appropriate diagnostic investigations, including imaging studies, which of the following conditions should be considered in the differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of high-grade fever with rigors and acute right flank pain in a 55-year-old patient points strongly toward a severe renal infection. As established in the previous analysis, Emphysematous Pyelonephritis is the most likely diagnosis that accounts for such intense systemic symptoms and localized flank distress. This condition involves gas-forming bacteria invading the kidney tissue. Cholecystitis (Option A) would typically present with right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder and positive Murphy's sign, rather than primary flank pain and rigors. Small Bowel Obstruction (Option C) and Volvulus (Option D) present with diffuse abdominal distension, vomiting, and constipation rather than localized flank pain and a high febrile response. Diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis is confirmed via CT scan showing gas in the kidney. Immediate management focuses on broad-spectrum antibiotics and stabilization of any underlying diabetes, as this condition carries a high mortality rate without rapid intervention
questions.learning: The clinical combination of high-grade fever with rigors and acute right flank pain in a 55-year-old patient points strongly toward a severe renal infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the incision.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gibson incision

The image above shows a Gibson incision. Gibson incision is used for kidney transplantation or as an extraperitoneal approach to the distal ureter with low morbidity.

The traditional pelvic Gibson incision is an oblique or curvilinear incision that starts 3 cm above and parallel to the inguinal ligament and extends vertically 3 centimeters medial to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) extending down toward the inguinal fold and terminating just lateral to the rectus muscle or continuing to above the symphysis pubis.

The Gibson incision is the traditional approach for renal transplant and transplant nephrectomy. This muscle-splitting incision provides great extraperitoneal access to pelvic vessels, the lower ureter, and the bladder for benign and malignant disease and is also utilized as a part of minimally invasive nephrectomy for specimen extraction or use of a hand port.

Other Options:

Option A: battle incision a lower right paramedian incision but placed more laterally than the standard paramedian incision. It is suitable for dealing with acute appendicitis and pathologies in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen.

Option C: Mayo Robson’s incision is a right upper paramedian incision extended like a hockey stick to the midline. It is indicated in cholecystectomy.

Option D: Lanz incision, a transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis, 2 cm below the umbilicus, centered on the midclavicular–mid-inguinal line. Due to its continuation with Langer’s lines, the Lanz incision produces much more aesthetically pleasing results with reduced scarring.

An image depicting other abdominal incisions is shown below:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are associated with recurrent urinary stone formation except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypercitraturia

• Citrate is protective against stone formation as it binds calcium, preventing precipitation with oxalate or phosphate.
• Hypercitraturia reduces stone risk, while hypocitraturia predisposes to recurrent stones.

So ↑ citrate (hypercitraturia) = ↓ stone risk

Hyperoxaluria : ↑ oxalate → combines with calcium → Forms calcium oxalate stones (most common)

Hyperuricosuria : ↑ uric acid → forms uric acid stones→ Also a nidus for calcium stones.

Hypercalciuria: ↑ calcium in urine → Leads to calcium oxalate / calcium phosphate stones.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intracellular proteins

Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium is mainly due to intracellular proteins.

Donnan and Gibbs showed that "When an ion on one side of a membrane cannot diffuse through the membrane, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affected in a predictable way".

According to this, in the presence of intracellular proteins, which are negatively charged non-diffusable ions, the distribution of other ions to which the membrane is permeable is affected in a predictable way (Donnan Effect) so that at equilibrium their concentration ratios are equal.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the investigation of choice for detecting enteric fever in the first week?
questions.explanation: Enteric fever (Typhoid) is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The diagnostic yield of various tests changes significantly as the disease progresses. During the first week of illness, blood culture is the investigation of choice, with a sensitivity of . As the bacteria move into the lymphoid tissue, stool culture (Option C) becomes more useful in the second and third weeks. Urine culture (Option D) is generally positive in the third week. Antibody detection (Option D), such as the Widal test, only becomes positive after the first week and is notoriously unreliable due to many false positives. A useful mnemonic for the timing of cultures is "BASU": Blood (1st week), Antibody/Widal (2nd week), Stool (3rd week), and Urine (4th week). Bone marrow culture is actually the most sensitive test overall (up to ), even if the patient has already started antibiotics, but it is rarely done due to its invasiveness
questions.learning: Enteric fever (Typhoid) is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The diagnostic yield of various tests changes significantly as the disease progresses.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most effective enzyme in Acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: In the context of the respiratory burst during acute inflammation, Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is considered the most effective bactericidal enzyme within neutrophils. During the inflammatory response, NADPH oxidase (Option A) initiates the burst by converting oxygen into superoxide radicals. MPO then takes the hydrogen peroxide produced from this reaction and, in the presence of chloride ions, converts it into hypochlorous acid (HOCl). HOCl is the active ingredient in household bleach and is a potent oxidant that rapidly destroys bacteria by disrupting their cell membranes and proteins. Defensins (Option B) are antimicrobial peptides that form pores in bacterial membranes but are not enzymes. Catalase (Option C) is an antioxidant enzyme that actually breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, thereby limiting the inflammatory damage. Therefore, while several enzymes participate, MPO is the primary engine for the generation of the most lethal microbicidal substances during acute inflammation
questions.learning: In the context of the respiratory burst during acute inflammation, Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is considered the most effective bactericidal enzyme within neutrophils.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A metal factory worker suffers from noise-induced hearing loss. Which of the following structures will be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Outer hair cells

Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) damages the outer hair cells, starting in the basal turn of the cochlea. Outer hair cells are affected before the inner hair cells.

NIHL occurs after chronic exposure to less intense sounds. The damage caused by noise trauma depends on the frequency of noise (frequency of 2000 to 3000 Hz causes more damage) intensity, duration of the noise, and preexisting ear disease.

The audiogram in noise-induced hearing loss shows a typical notch at 4000Hz both for air and bone conduction known as acoustic dip/boiler's notch. Patients at this stage complain of high-pitched tinnitus and difficulty hearing in noisy surroundings. Pre-employment and annual audiograms for persons working at places where noise is above 85 dB (A) help in the early detection of NIHL.

The human ear can hear frequencies from about 20 to 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz, the vibrations are infra-audible, and above 20,000 Hz, they are ultra-sonic. Pure tone audiometry can detect only up to 8000 Hz.

Extended high-frequency audiometry is recommended for early detection of hearing loss, as it can identify hearing impairments before the frequencies necessary for speech comprehension are affected. Distortion product otoacoustic emissions is a more sensitive tool than conventional audiometry, particularly in children under 5 years old for early detection of hearing loss.

A noise of 90 dB(A) SPL (acceptable noise levels, sound pressure level), 8 hours a day for 5 days per week is the maximum safe limit as recommended by the Ministry of Labour. As per WHO, 85 dB(A) is considered the highest safe exposure level up to a maximum of 8 hours.

The silence zone extends to a distance of 100 meters around the premises of hospitals, nursing homes, educational institutions, and courts.

Other options:

Option A: Crista ampullaris is a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts.

Option B: Macula is the sensory epithelium of the utricle

Option C: Cupula is a gelatinous mass extending from the surface of the crista (peripheral receptor located in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts) to the ceiling of the ampulla, into which project the cilia of sensory hair cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: FAST stands for __________________
options: First assessment with sonography in trauma
Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography in Trauma.

It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It can be performed within 2-4 minutes.

Technique:

• The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

• Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

1. Operator-dependent
2. Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.
3. Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries
4. Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum
5. Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma
6. May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations
questions.learning: Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography in Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Resistance to which of the following anti-tubercular drugs occurs due to mutation in katG?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isoniazid

Mutation in katG results in resistance to Isoniazid (INH).

Isoniazid (INH) is used as chemotherapy for drug-susceptible TB. It is given in combination with pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and rifampin.

Isoniazid is not directly toxic to mycobacteria but gets activated to its toxic form by KatG, which is a catalase-peroxidase. A series of reactions occur which ultimately causes inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis, which leads to bacterial cell death.

The various mechanisms of resistance to INH are:

* Mutation or deletion of KatG genes: this is the most common mechanism seen in clinical isolates and confers a high level of resistance.

* Overexpression of genes for InhA: confers a low level of resistance and cross-resistance with ethionamide.

* Overexpression of genes for ahpC: increases the survival of katG mutants under oxidative stress.

* Efflux pump induction

Pearl PF0763: Key points on the first line drugs used in the treatment of TB

Drugs
Isoniazid
Rifamycins
Pyrazinamide
Ethambutol

Mechanism of action
Blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
Inhibition of RNA polymerase, leading to the inhibition of RNA synthesis.
Inhibition of fatty acid synthase-I, leading to the inhibition of the cell membrane.
Inhibition of arabinosyl transferase, leading to a reduction in arabinogalactan needed for the cell wall.

Unique side effects

Shoulder hand syndrome and CNS side effects.

Orange urine, sweat, and tears. Flu-like symptoms with intermittent dosing.

The most hepatotoxic drug. It also causes hyperuricemia.

Optic neuritis and hence, not preferred in children.
