questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with high- grade fever and a positive Kernig’s sign. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows low glucose levels, elevated protein, and increased leukocyte count, suggesting cryptococcal meningitis. What is the recommended treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis is a major opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS (typically CD4 < 100). The current standard of care for induction therapy, as recommended by the WHO and IDSA, is a combination of Liposomal Amphotericin B and 5-flucytosine for at least two weeks. This combination is highly effective at rapidly clearing the yeast from the CSF. Vancomycin (Option A) is an antibiotic for Gram-positive bacteria and is useless against fungi. High-dose fluconazole (Option B) is used for consolidation and maintenance therapy after the initial induction phase, or as a less-preferred induction alternative if Amphotericin is unavailable. Voriconazole (Option C) is primarily used for invasive aspergillosis but is not the first-line choice for cryptococcosis. Following the induction phase with Liposomal Amphotericin B, patients transition to fluconazole for consolidation (8 weeks) and then long-term maintenance to prevent recurrence. Careful management of increased intracranial pressure through repeated lumbar punctures is also a critical part of treating this condition
questions.learning: Cryptococcal meningitis is a major opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS (typically CD4 < 100). The current standard of care for induction therapy, as recommended by the WHO and IDSA, is a combination of Liposomal Amphotericin B and…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A G5P4 female comes for her routine scan. She is already a mother of 4 girl children and wants a boy this time. She is now interested to know the sex of the current child. According to PCPNDT act, what should you do as a radiologist?

PCPNDT act - Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act
options: Check for congenital anomalies of the fetus but not look for the sex
Check for congenital anomalies, the sex of the child and tell her if it is a female child
Check for congenital anomalies, the sex of the child and do not tell her
Only check routine ANC and do not do USG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Check for congenital anomalies of the fetus but not look for the sex

According to PCPNDT act, the radiologist should check for congenital anomalies of the fetus but not look for the sex.

Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994 is an act of the Parliament of India enacted to stop female foeticides and arrest the declining sex ratio in India.

The few basic requirements of the Act are:

Registration done under Section (18) of the PC-PNDT Act.
Written consent of the pregnant woman and there should be prohibition of communicating the sex of fetus under Section 5 of the Act.
Maintenance of records should be done as provided under Section 29 of the Act.
Creating public awareness at large by placing the board of prohibition on sex determination.

Initiatives Against Sex-Selective Abortions :
Beti Bachao Beti Padhao: Launched by the Government of India in 2015, it aims to address the issue of declining child, sex ratio and empower girls through awareness generation, education, and protection.
The National Plan of Action for Children, 2016 : It identifies the elimination of gender-biased sex selection as one of the key priority areas for children’s rights and well-being.

Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao - “Save the daughter, educate the daughter” is a campaign of the Government of India that aims to generate awareness and improve the efficiency of welfare services intended for girls.

The objectives of BBBP are :

To prevent gender-biased sex-selective elimination
To ensure survival and protection of the girl child
To ensure education and participation of the girl child
questions.learning: Check for congenital anomalies of the fetus but not look for the sex According to PCPNDT act, the radiologist should check for congenital anomalies of the fetus but not look for the sex.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: HEADSSS assessment will be used by an intern for which of the following patient groups?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adolescents

HEADSSS assessment is done in adolescents to determine early symptoms of mental disorders and functional impairment in major life domains such as home and family, school, peers, and community.

These domains are included in the HEADSSS (Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Depression, Safety) Interview Guide. An adolescent’s risk and protective factors are identified during each visit using this assessment. Risk factors increase the likelihood that an adolescent will engage in risky behaviors, whereas protective factors build an adolescent’s resiliency and ability to cope with stress.

Examples of questions in HEADSSS assessment :

Home

• Who lives at home, and where?
• Do you have your own room?
• What are relationships like at home?
• What do parents and relatives do for a living?

Education

• School/grade performance-any recent changes? Any dramatic past changes?
• Any years repeated/classes failed
• Suspension, termination, dropping out?
• Any current or past employment?

Activities

• On own, with peers (what do you do for fun? where? when?)
• Hobbies-other activities?
• History of arrests-acting out-crime?

Drugs

• Use by peers? Use by young person? (include tobacco, alcohol)
• Use by family members?
• Amounts, source, frequency, patterns of use/abuse

Sexuality

• Degree and types of sexual experience and acts? Number of partners?
• Sexually transmitted diseases-knowledge and prevention? Contraception? Frequency of use?
• History of pregnancy/abortion?

Suicide / Depression / Self Image

• Sleep disorders, appetite/eating behavior changes, emotional outbursts and highly impulsive behavior, history of withdrawal/isolation, hopeless/helpless feelings, suicidal ideation
• History of past suicide attempts, depression, psychological counseling

Safety

• Do you ever feel unsafe?
questions.learning: Adolescents HEADSSS assessment is done in adolescents to determine early symptoms of mental disorders and functional impairment in major life domains such as home and family, school, peers, and community.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria, and gait ataxia. MRI of the brain reveals an acute infarct in the right dorsolateral medulla. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as Lateral Medullary Syndrome, results from an infarct in the dorsolateral medulla, typically due to occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery. The clinical presentation includes the "bulbar" triad of dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and dysarthria (speech difficulty) due to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus, as well as gait ataxia from cerebellar tract damage. Dejerine's syndrome (Option A) involves the medial medulla, causing contralateral hemiparesis and tongue deviation. Babinski-Nageotte syndrome (Option C) is a more extensive brainstem lesion combining lateral and medial features. Weber syndrome (Option D) involves the midbrain, presenting with oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia. Because the patient's symptoms perfectly correlate with the specific dorsal and lateral structures of the medulla identified on the MRI, Wallenberg syndrome is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as Lateral Medullary Syndrome, results from an infarct in the dorsolateral medulla, typically due to occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is brought to the pediatrics outpatient department with abdominal distension and jaundice. The mother reports increased appetite in recent months, and examination reveals hepatomegaly. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presentation of hepatomegaly and a distended abdomen in an infant, particularly when associated with "increased appetite" (frequent feedings to compensate for hypoglycemia), is suggestive of von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I). This condition is caused by a deficiency in Glucose-6-phosphatase. This enzyme is critical for the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; its absence prevents the liver from releasing glucose into the blood, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia and massive glycogen accumulation in the liver. Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option B) is McArdle's (muscle) or Hers (liver) disease, which is generally milder than von Gierke's. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency (Option C) is galactosemia, which causes jaundice and hepatomegaly but typically presents with feeding intolerance rather than increased appetite. Glycogen synthase deficiency (Option D) would lead to a small liver and fasting hypoglycemia but not hepatomegaly. Von Gierke's also features doll-like facies and hyperlipidemia
questions.learning: The presentation of hepatomegaly and a distended abdomen in an infant, particularly when associated with "increased appetite" (frequent feedings to compensate for hypoglycemia), is suggestive of von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct about physiological dead space?
options: It is less than anatomical dead space
It can be measured by spirometry
It is because of inadequate perfusion
It is because of inadequate ventilation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is because of inadequate perfusion

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Anatomical dead space | Conducting airways (no alveoli)

| Alveolar dead space | Ventilated alveoli but no perfusion

|  Physiological dead space | Anatomical + alveolar dead space

Physiological dead space includes alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, due to inadequate pulmonary blood flow.

It equals anatomical dead space plus alveolar dead space and therefore is greater than or equal to anatomical dead space.

Spirometry measures volumes, not dead space, and inadequate ventilation cause shunt, not dead space.

| Feature | Dead Space | Shunt

| ------- | ---------- | -----

| Ventilation | ✔️ Present | ❌ Absent

| Perfusion | ❌ Absent | ✔️ Present

| V/Q ratio | ∞ | 0

| Example | PE | Pneumonia
questions.learning: It is because of inadequate perfusion | Type | Definition | ---- | ---------- | Anatomical dead space | Conducting airways (no alveoli) | Alveolar dead space | Ventilated alveoli but no perfusion | Physiological dead space | Anatomical + alveolar dead…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: How is this contraceptive inserted?
questions.explanation: The device shown is an intratubal contraceptive micro-insert (classically known by the brand name Essure). It is a non-incisional form of permanent sterilization. The coils are inserted hysteroscopically (Option A) through the vagina and cervix into the fallopian tubes. Once in place, they induce a localized inflammatory response that leads to the formation of scar tissue (fibrosis), which permanently blocks the tubes. Abdominal (Option B) and Laparoscopic (Option C) methods are used for traditional tubal ligation (e.g., Pomeroy’s technique or applying Falope rings), which involve incisions and general anesthesia. Oral (Option D) refers to birth control pills. The primary advantage of the hysteroscopic coil method is that it can be performed in an office setting without incisions. However, users must use backup contraception for three months until a follow-up test confirms the tubes are completely occluded. Therefore, the visual of the micro-coil coil uniquely identifies the hysteroscopic delivery route
questions.learning: The device shown is an intratubal contraceptive micro-insert (classically known by the brand name Essure). It is a non-incisional form of permanent sterilization.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent surgery for breast carcinoma. She now presents with painless swelling involving the arm as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphedema

The generalized swelling of the left arm of the patient post-surgery for breast carcinoma is suggestive of post-mastectomy lymphedema.

Lymphoedema occurs when interstitial fluid accumulates due to defective lymphatic drainage. It is a common complication of breast cancer treatment, involving axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy. Sentinel lymph node dissection (SLND) reduces the risk of lymphedema significantly.

Clinical signs and symptoms are observed in the ipsilateral arm. A significant increase in limb size due to swelling is seen. Other symptoms are heaviness, tightness, numbness, tingling, limb fatigue, and reduced limb mobility.

Diagnosis is predominantly based on the clinical swelling of the arm. The girth of the affected arm >2 centimetres than the normal limb, a 200-mL or more increase in limb volume, or a 5% or greater limb volume change are other diagnostic criteria.

Management:

1. Limb elevation, elastic arm stockings, and pneumatic compression devices to reduce swelling.
2. Using a low-pH water-based moisturizer to prevent dry skin caused by excess fluid accumulation.
3. Manual lymphatic drainage (MLD) by a therapist followed by simple lymphatic drainage (SLD) by the patient daily aids interstitial fluid evacuation.
4. Surgical options include lymphaticovenular anastomosis, liposuction, and debulking.

Other options:

Option B:   Stewart-Treves syndrome refers to lymphangiosarcoma seen in chronic long-standing lymphedema following mastectomy (more than 10 years). They present as single/multiple bluish-red skin and subcutaneous nodules. They can ulcerate and hemorrhage.

Option C: Axillary venous thrombosis or Paget-Schrotter disease is seen in patients doing rigorous exercise and in weightlifters. The compression of the subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet causes painful swelling of the arm.

Option D: Cellulitis (lymphangitis) is a bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It is characterized by a painful area of erythematous and edematous tissue.
questions.learning: Lymphedema — The generalized swelling of the left arm of the patient post-surgery for breast carcinoma is suggestive of post-mastectomy lymphedema. Lymphoedema occurs when interstitial fluid accumulates due to defective lymphatic drainage.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female went on vacation and fell asleep while sitting on a beach. After some time she woke with sunburn. Later when she went back home, she experienced pain while taking a warm bath (40°C). Which of the following receptors is responsible for the pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Innocuos thermal receptor - allodynia

The receptors responsible for this are innocuous thermal receptors which have perceived ordinarily non-noxious stimulus (i.e., warm bath) as severe pain also known as allodynia.

In this case, the warm bath at 40°C (typically not painful) causes pain due to sunburn, which sensitizes the skin. After sunburn, the skin becomes more sensitive, and thermal receptors that usually detect warmth now trigger pain signals in response to non-painful thermal stimuli, leading to allodynia.

Innocuous thermoreceptors, which detect non-harmful temperature changes(cold and warm), are specialized nerve endings found on the skin. Cold receptors are located on the dendritic endings of Aδ and C fibers, while warm receptors are situated on C fibers. The specific thermosensitive molecular channels mediating innocuous heat stimuli is transient receptor potential (TRP) cation channel TRPV1 and TRPM8 cation channel for innocuous cold stimuli.

Thermal hyperalgesia(increased response to noxious stimulation) is mediated by activation of NMDA receptors.  After tissue or nerve injury, C-fibers discharges release glutamate and neurokinins from primary afferent terminals, leading to the release of peptides (e.g., substance P; calcitonin gene-related peptide, CGRP). As a result, a voltage-dependent magnesium block on NMDA receptors is removed allowing for an influx of calcium that triggers a cascade of intracellular events leading to the development and maintenance of hyperalgesia.(Option D)
questions.learning: Innocuos thermal receptor - allodynia — The receptors responsible for this are innocuous thermal receptors which have perceived ordinarily non-noxious stimulus (i.e., warm bath) as severe pain also known as allodynia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which structures pass between superior and middle constrictor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IX nerve (Glossopharyngeal Nerve)

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles along with the stylopharyngeus muscle.

Key anatomical concept (gaps of constrictors):

1.      Above superior constrictor:

o    Levator veli palatini

o    Auditory (Eustachian) tube

o    Tensor velu palatini

o    Ascending pharyngeal artery

2.      Between superior & middle constrictor:

o    Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

o    Stylopharyngeus muscle

3.      Between middle & inferior constrictor:

o    Internal laryngeal nerve

o    Superior laryngeal vessels

4.      Below inferior constrictor:

o    Recurrent laryngeal nerve

o    Inferior laryngeal vessels
questions.learning: IX nerve (Glossopharyngeal Nerve) — The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles along with the stylopharyngeus muscle.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent bleeding for the past 1 year. Transnasal endoscopic results are shown below. A contrast-enhanced CT revealed a mass extending from the posterior choana to the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The above clinical scenario with recurrent spontaneous bleeding with unilateral nasal obstruction and contrast-enhanced CT showing a growth protruding into the nasopharynx, along with the transnasal endoscopic image, is suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor. It is predominantly seen in adolescent males and is thought to be testosterone-dependent. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity near the sphenopalatine foramen.

The clinical features include epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, and denasal speech. Other symptoms include conductive hearing loss, broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis leading to frog-face deformity, cheek swelling, and involvement of II, III, IV, and VI cranial nerves.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is the investigation of choice that reveals anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (Antral sign/Holman Miller sign), which is pathognomonic of angiofibroma as shown below.

Carotid angiography shows the extent of the tumor with its vascularity. The feeding vessels mostly come from the external carotid artery. In large tumors with intracranial extension, vessels come from the internal carotid system also.

Biopsy of the mass is avoided due to the risk of bleeding.

Surgical approach is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery.

Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.

Other options:

Option B: Antrochoanal polyp (Killian's polyp) arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum. They are usually unilateral and are seen in children and young adults. They present with unilateral nasal obstruction with minimal to no bleeding. X-rays of the paranasal sinuses show opacity of the maxillary sinus.

Option C: Rhinoscleroma is caused by a gram-negative coccobacillus Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It causes this progressive granulomatous infection starting in the nose and extending into the upper respiratory tract. It presents initially with foul-smelling nasal discharge, and then with granulomatous nodules in the nose giving it a woody feeling. The last stage is the cicatricial stage, with stenosis of nares, and adhesions in the nose.

Option D: Concha bullosa is pneumatization of the middle turbinate that leads to an enlarged middle turbinate, which is ballooned out.

The CT image shown below depicts concha bullosa
questions.learning: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — The above clinical scenario with recurrent spontaneous bleeding with unilateral nasal obstruction and contrast-enhanced CT showing a growth protruding into the nasopharynx, along with the transnasal endoscopic image, is…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the type of psoriasis in the given picture.
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple small, drop-like erythematous papules with fine scaling scattered over the skin. This pattern is characteristic of guttate psoriasis. The term “guttate” comes from the Latin word gutta, meaning “drop,” reflecting the raindrop-like lesions. Guttate psoriasis commonly: 1. Affects children and young adults 2. Appears suddenly, often after a streptococcal infection 3. Involves the trunk and proximal limbs 4. Shows numerous small lesions, unlike large plaques Why other options are incorrect: (B) Erythrodermic psoriasis → Diffuse redness involving almost entire body (C) Pustular psoriasis → Presence of pus-filled lesions, not seen here (D) Inverse psoriasis → Occurs in skin folds, smooth and shiny lesions without scaling
questions.learning: The image shows multiple small, drop-like erythematous papules with fine scaling scattered over the skin. This pattern is characteristic of guttate psoriasis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the correct sequence of the auditory pathways: A.Superior Olivary nucleus B. Cochlear Nucleus C. Inferior Colliculi D. Lateral lemniscus E. Medial geniculate ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BADCE

Cochlear nucleus (B), superior olivary nucleus (A), lateral lemniscus (D), inferior colliculi (C), and medial geniculate ganglion (E) represent the correct sequence of the auditory pathway.

The correct sequence of structures involved in the auditory pathway from the periphery to the center is

1. Vestibulocochlear nerve
2. Cochlear Nucleus
3. Superior olivary nucleus
4. Lateral lemniscus
5. Inferior colliculus
6. Medial geniculate body
7. Auditory cortex
questions.learning: BADCE Cochlear nucleus (B), superior olivary nucleus (A), lateral lemniscus (D), inferior colliculi (C), and medial geniculate ganglion (E) represent the correct sequence of the auditory pathway.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is used to clean up blood spills in the operation theater?
questions.explanation: Effective decontamination of blood spills in high-risk areas like operation theaters is critical for preventing the transmission of bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis. Sodium hypochlorite, a chlorine compound, is the globally recommended disinfectant for this purpose. For large spills, a 1% (10,000 ppm) concentration is typically used to ensure complete inactivation of infectious agents. Phenolic compounds (Option B) are less effective against some viruses and are generally used for surface disinfection of walls or floors. Quaternary ammonium compounds (Option C) are low-level disinfectants and are not suitable for blood spills. Alcoholic compounds (Option D), while useful for skin antisepsis, evaporate too quickly to provide the necessary contact time for organic matter like blood. Therefore, due to its potent virucidal properties and ability to neutralize organic biohazards, a chlorine-based compound is the gold standard for managing blood spills in clinical settings
questions.learning: Effective decontamination of blood spills in high-risk areas like operation theaters is critical for preventing the transmission of bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young male presented with cervical lymphadenopathy. The biopsy of the lymph node showed RS cells with vague nodule formation and a background of reactive T-lymphocytes. The cells were positive for CD20, LCA, EMA and negative for CD 15 and CD30. What is the diagnosis?
options: T cell rich B cell lymphoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nodular Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL)

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (NLPHL).

Axial group (cervical) lymphadenopathy and along with the L&H variant of Reed-Sternberg cells is characteristic.

RS cells are neoplastic giant cells. In NLPHL, the cells have vague nodular formation. Immunophenotyping is positive for CD20 (B cell-associated), LCA (CD45), EMA (epithelial marker), and negative for CD15 (monocyte or macrophage-associated) and CD30 (activation marker).

The image given below shows the L&H variant of RS cells seen in NLPHL.
questions.learning: Nodular Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (NLPHL).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Banana sign on USG is associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spina bifida

The banana sign on USG is seen in spina bifida.

Banana sign is an abnormal anterior curvature of the cerebellum along with effacement of the cisterna magna that produces this appearance. It is seen in spina bifida and is also associated with Arnold-Chiari malformation.

Spina bifida is a congenital anomaly occurring due to incomplete development of the neural tube. The most commonly cited signs present in spina bifida are the banana sign and the lemon sign.

The lemon sign occurs due to the overlapping of the frontal bones due to the posterior shift of intracranial contents as shown below.

Other options:

Option B: Omphalocele is a congenital midline anterior abdominal wall defect through which the solid abdominal viscera or bowel herniates. The herniated abdominal contents are covered by a membranous sac as shown below.

The image below shows an ultrasound image of the fetus suggestive of an omphalocele (asterisk).

Option C: Nuchal translucency (NT) is used to antenatally screen Downs syndrome (Trisomy 21) during the first trimester. NT is the maximum thickness of the translucent area between the skin and soft tissue over the fetal spine at the back of the neck. When the NT measurement is increased, it is a marker for fetal aneuploidy and structural anomalies. The ultrasound image below shows increased NT thickness and absent nasal bone of a fetus with Trisomy 21 at 11 weeks gestation.
questions.learning: Spina bifida — The banana sign on USG is seen in spina bifida. Banana sign is an abnormal anterior curvature of the cerebellum along with effacement of the cisterna magna that produces this appearance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a criterion for defining severe acute malnutrition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low Height for age

Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is diagnosed using indicators of acute nutritional deficiency, namely weight-for-height Z score < −3 SD, MUAC <11.5 cm (in children 6–59 months), or bilateral pitting pedal edema.

It reflects severe wasting and acute nutritional deficiency. The diagnostic criteria are defined by the World Health Organization and used in programs like India’s Integrated Child Development Services and POSHAN Abhiyaan.

Low height-for-age indicates stunting, which reflects chronic malnutrition (stunting) rather than acute malnutrition and therefore is not included in SAM criteria.

Types of PEM-
questions.learning: Low Height for age Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is diagnosed using indicators of acute nutritional deficiency, namely weight-for-height Z score < −3 SD, MUAC <11.5 cm (in children 6–59 months), or bilateral pitting pedal edema.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The most common site of obstruction by a nasal polyp from the maxillary sinus is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle meatus

The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus at the lower part of the infundibulum, in its medial wall and thus a nasal polyp will obstruct the middle meatus.

Infundibulum is the space limited medially by the uncinate process and frontal process of the maxilla, and laterally by the lamina papyracea.

Pearl PF1078: Structures opening into meatuses of nose

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus
questions.learning: Middle meatus — The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus at the lower part of the infundibulum, in its medial wall and thus a nasal polyp will obstruct the middle meatus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which segment of the vertebrae is involved in a patient presenting with pain in the back of the thigh and the leg after lifting heavy weight?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. S1

Pain radiating along the back of the thigh and posterior leg corresponds to the S1 dermatome, classically seen in sciatica.

S1 root involvement commonly occurs with L5–S1 disc herniation, affecting the Achilles reflex.

L4 and L5 involve anterior/anterolateral leg regions, while S2 pain is more perineal/posterior thigh only.
questions.learning: S1 Pain radiating along the back of the thigh and posterior leg corresponds to the S1 dermatome, classically seen in sciatica. S1 root involvement commonly occurs with L5–S1 disc herniation, affecting the Achilles reflex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presenting with hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Laboratory evaluation is performed to assess her hormonal status. Which of the following patterns of hormone levels is most consistent with this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FSH ↑, LH ↑, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↓

Menopause is characterized by ovarian follicular depletion, resulting in a marked decline in estrogen and progesterone production. Loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis causes a rise in both FSH and LH, with FSH increasing more than LH because inhibin B levels also decline.

Why not the other options?

• A. FSH ↑, LH ↑, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↑: Progesterone is decreased, not increased, due to cessation of ovulation.
• B. FSH ↓, LH ↓, Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑: This is the opposite of the hormonal changes seen in menopause.
• D. FSH ↑, LH ↓, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↑: LH also increases, though less than FSH, and progesterone is low.
questions.learning: FSH ↑, LH ↑, Estrogen ↓, Progesterone ↓ Menopause is characterized by ovarian follicular depletion, resulting in a marked decline in estrogen and progesterone production.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the ultimate desired state towards which objectives and resources are directed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goal

Goal is the ultimate desired state towards which objectives and resources are directed. It is not constrained by time or resources.

Objective is the planned end point of all activities. It is a precise point. Whereas, target refers to a discrete activity and permits the concept of degree of achievement.

Mission describes the cause of existence of the programme.

Plan is a blueprint for taking action.
questions.learning: Goal Goal is the ultimate desired state towards which objectives and resources are directed. It is not constrained by time or resources.

questions.text: A female patient presents to you with a unilateral headache. It is associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. What is the best drug for acute management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sumatriptan

This presentation is classic migraine with unilateral headache, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with fever of 38.5 °C and fundal spots on eye examination. CBC shows a leukocyte count of 20,000/cu mm. How many minor Duke’s criteria are satisfied in this patient for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis (IE) is based on the Modified Duke Criteria. In this case, the patient fulfills three minor criteria, supporting a diagnosis of possible IE. 1. Predisposition: Intravenous drug use is a well-recognized risk factor for infective endocarditis, particularly right-sided involvement. 2. Fever: Documented body temperature ≥ 38 °C fulfills the fever criterion. 3. Immunologic phenomenon: The retinal findings described are consistent with Roth spots, which are classically associated with infective endocarditis. An elevated total leukocyte count is a nonspecific inflammatory finding and is not included as a Duke criterion. At present, major criteria such as positive blood cultures or echocardiographic evidence of vegetations are not available. According to the Modified Duke Criteria, possible infective endocarditis is diagnosed when either one major and one minor criterion, or three minor criteria are present. Therefore, this patient meets the criteria for possible IE. Given the patient’s high-risk profile, urgent blood cultures from multiple sites and transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography are required to confirm the diagnosis. Early recognition is crucial, as right-sided infective endocarditis, common in intravenous drug users, can result in septic pulmonary emboli, valvular destruction, and serious morbidity
questions.learning: The diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis (IE) is based on the Modified Duke Criteria. In this case, the patient fulfills three minor criteria, supporting a diagnosis of possible IE.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man reports gradual hearing loss over several years. He reports difficulty hearing conversations, particularly in noisy environments, and has difficulty perceiving high-pitched sounds. There is no vertigo, tinnitus, or ear fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presbycusis

This clinical vignette points towards a diagnosis of presbycusis.

It is a type of sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological ageing process in the ear.

The pathogenesis of presbycusis includes:

* Degeneration of the organ of Corti

* Degeneration of the spiral ganglion

* Degeneration of the stria vascularis

* Stiffening of the basilar membrane.

Clinically, it usually manifests in elderly adults over 65 years of age. It is gradually progressive and tends to affect the higher frequencies first. Characteristically, patients with presbycusis have significant difficulty hearing in the presence of background noise. Additionally, patients with presbycusis may also have a paradoxical hypersensitivity to loud sounds. This is due to the recruitment phenomenon. They may also have tinnitus. It significantly affects the quality of life, and patients tend to present with progressive social withdrawal.

On examination, tuning fork tests will show a picture of symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss with

* Positive Rinne's test in both ears, meaning the air conduction is better than bone conduction (AC>BC) in both ears

* Weber's test will show no lateralisation, meaning the sound is heard equally on both sides.

Diagnosis can be confirmed with audiometry. Treatment of presbycusis mainly includes using a hearing aid.

Other options:

Option A: Acoustic neuromas are noncancerous, usually slow-growing tumours that form along the vestibulocochlear nerve. They arise from Schwann cells. Schwannomas can occur on any cranial or peripheral nerve in the body, but in the brain, acoustic neuromas are the most common schwannomas.

Option B: Meniere's disease is usually unilateral. It is characterised by episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of ear fullness. Pure tone audiometry reveals a sensorineural type of hearing loss with lower frequencies affected first.

Option D: Otosclerosis is a disease of the otic capsule that usually presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss. Patients with otosclerosis characteristically hear better in noisy than in quiet surroundings (Paracusis Willisii). Tuning fork tests show negative Rinne's test, i.e., BC > AC. Weber's may be central, as this is typically symmetrical.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve
questions.learning: Presbycusis — This clinical vignette points towards a diagnosis of presbycusis. It is a type of sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological ageing process in the ear.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of blurred vision. On ophthalmic examination, aqueous flare and keratic precipitates are noted. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of blurred vision, aqueous flares (protein in the anterior chamber), and keratic precipitates (KP - inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium) are diagnostic for anterior uveitis, specifically iridocyclitis. Flare and cells are the hallmarks of active inflammation in the anterior segment. Intermediate uveitis (Option A) primarily involves the vitreous (vitritis) and pars plana. Posterior uveitis (Option B) involves the retina or choroid. While Toxoplasma (Option D) is a major cause of posterior uveitis (retinochoroiditis), "iridocyclitis" is the most direct anatomical diagnosis for the anterior chamber findings described. Clinically, these patients also present with eye pain, redness (ciliary congestion), and photophobia. If untreated, active iridocyclitis can lead to complications like posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, and cataracts. Management typically involves topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents to relieve pain and prevent synechiae. A thorough systemic workup is often necessary to identify underlying autoimmune or infectious causes
questions.learning: The clinical findings of blurred vision, aqueous flares (protein in the anterior chamber), and keratic precipitates (KP - inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium) are diagnostic for anterior uveitis, specifically iridocyclitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is the new online software launched under the national tuberculosis elimination program (NTEP) by the government to monitor TB patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NIKSHAY

NIKSHAY is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients. (The word is a combination of two Hindi words NI and KSHAY, meaning eradication of TB).

Nikshay is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients to monitor the Revised National Tuberculosis Programme (RNTCP). This system stores information about the patient, medical history, diagnosis, co-morbidities and lab reports.

The system has been developed jointly by the Central TB Division of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and National Informatics Centre (NIC) and it was launched by the Government of India in June 2012. This is used by health functionaries at various levels across the country in association with Central TB Division (CTD), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

NIKSHAY covers various aspects of controlling TB using technological innovations.

Apart from web-based technology, SMS services have been used effectively for communication with patients and monitoring the program on a day-to-day basis.

Other options:

Option B: Nikusth is the new online software for monitoring leprosy patients.

Option C: Nischay is a pregnancy test kit.

Option D: Axshya is a project that works to improve access to quality TB care and control through a partnership between the government and civil society.
questions.learning: NIKSHAY NIKSHAY is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients. (The word is a combination of two Hindi words NI and KSHAY, meaning eradication of TB).

questions.text: B-cells are induced to produce IgE by which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IL-4

IL-4 stimulates B-cells to differentiate into IgE secreting plasma cells.
questions.learning: IL-4 IL-4 stimulates B-cells to differentiate into IgE secreting plasma cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a palpable lump in the left breast. Mammography suggests malignancy, and tissue diagnosis is required. Which is the preferred biopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Core needle biopsy

• Core needle biopsy (CNB) is the preferred initial biopsy for suspected breast cancer.
• It provides tissue architecture, unlike FNAC which provides only cytology.
• Histology allows assessment of tumor type, grade, ER/PR status, and HER2 expression.
• It guides neoadjuvant therapy and surgical planning.
• FNAC cannot reliably distinguish in situ from invasive carcinoma.
• Excision biopsy is no longer the first-line diagnostic procedure.
• Incisional biopsy is rarely required.
• CNB is usually performed under ultrasound or stereotactic guidance.
• It has high sensitivity and specificity with minimal morbidity.
• Triple assessment = Clinical examination + Imaging + Core needle biopsy.
questions.learning: Core needle biopsy • Core needle biopsy (CNB) is the preferred initial biopsy for suspected breast cancer. • It provides tissue architecture, unlike FNAC which provides only cytology. • Histology allows assessment of tumor type, grade, ER/PR status, and…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the investigation of choice for CML?
questions.explanation: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, caused by a reciprocal translocation t(9;22) that produces the BCR-ABL fusion gene. The investigation of choice today is FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) because it directly detects the BCR-ABL gene rearrangement with high sensitivity and specificity. Unlike conventional karyotyping, FISH: 1. Does not require dividing cells 2. Can detect abnormalities even in a small number of cells 3. Provides faster results Thus, it is widely preferred in modern clinical practice and exam settings. Why other options are incorrect: (A) LAP score : Old test; only supportive, not diagnostic (C) Karyotyping : Detects Philadelphia chromosome but is less sensitive and slower (D) Reciprocal translocation : This is the genetic abnormality itself, not a test
questions.learning: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, caused by a reciprocal translocation t(9;22) that produces the BCR-ABL fusion gene.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can cause granulomatous liver injury? 1. Carbamazepine 2. Allopurinol 3. Diltiazem 4. Acetaminophen Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Granulomatous hepatitis is a rare form of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) characterized by hepatic granuloma formation. Common offending drugs include carbamazepine, allopurinol, diltiazem, sulfonamides, phenytoin, and quinidine.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Carbamazepine ✔️ – Recognized cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 2. Allopurinol ✔️ – Can cause hypersensitivity syndrome with granulomatous liver injury.
• 3. Diltiazem ✔️ – An established cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 4. Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) ❌ – Causes dose-dependent centrilobular (zone 3) hepatic necrosis, not granulomatous hepatitis.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Granulomatous hepatitis is a rare form of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) characterized by hepatic granuloma formation. Common offending drugs include carbamazepine, allopurinol, diltiazem, sulfonamides, phenytoin, and quinidine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text:
A 40-year-old man presents with erythematous painful lesions on the trunk and face, joint pain, and glove and stocking pattern of anesthesia. Which of the following investigations is used for the diagnosis of this condition?

1. Nerve examination
2. Skin biopsy
3. Slit skin smear
4. Mantoux test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy. The diagnosis of this condition requires nerve examination, skin biopsy, and a slit skin smear (option B- 1, 2, 3).

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule. Lesions usually involve the face, extensor aspect of the limbs, trunks, and buttocks. The lesions have impaired nerve function and poor hair growth. The patients may also present with burns or ulcers of the anesthetic limb.

Classification systems of leprosy:

• Ridley-Jopling classification:

• Tuberculoid (TT)
• Borderline tubercular (BT)
• Borderline (BB)
• Borderline lepromatous (BL)
• Lepromatous (LL)

• WHO classification:

• Paucibacillary
• Multibacillary

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

• Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.
• Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.
• Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy. The diagnosis of this condition requires nerve examination, skin biopsy, and a slit skin smear (option B- 1, 2, 3).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In Integrated child development services (ICDS), intersectoral coordination is seen with which organization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NHM

In Integrated child development services (ICDS), intersectoral coordination is seen with NHM(National Health Mission).

The ICDS overlaps with many of the programs of NHM of which the Anemia Mukt Bharat Scheme  is an example, where prophylactic iron and folic acid is given to children, adolescents, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, irrespective of anemia

ICDS:

The blueprint for the scheme was prepared by the Department of Social Welfare in 1975. The Government of India decided to expand the project to cover 100 areas by 1978-79. Two major evaluations were conducted in 1978and 1982. The positive results of these evaluations formed the basis for the government's decision to accelerate the expansion of ICDS in 1982.

Other options:

NACO(National AIDS Control Organization): prevents the transmission of HIV,  decreases the morbidity and mortality associated with it and minimize the socio-economic impact resulting from it.

NLEP(National Leprosy Eradication Programme) : is a centrally sponsored Health Scheme of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Govt. of India.

UNDP (United Nations Development Programme): It is the main source of funds for technical assistance. Its main objective is to help poorer nations develop their human and natural resources to their potential.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A protein is fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin wax. Which of the following methods is the most appropriate means for identification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the preferred technique for detecting and localizing specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. It uses antigen-specific antibodies to identify protein expression while preserving tissue architecture, making it invaluable for tumor diagnosis, classification, and prognostic marker assessment.

• Immunohistochemistry is specifically designed for protein detection in FFPE tissue sections and allows visualization of protein expression within the histological context.

Why not the other options?

• A. Western blot: Detects proteins but requires fresh/frozen tissue lysates and does not preserve tissue architecture.
• C. Flow cytometry: Analyzes proteins on live cells or cell suspensions; not suitable for paraffin-embedded tissue.
• D. In situ hybridization: Detects DNA or RNA (nucleic acids), not proteins.
questions.learning: Immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the preferred technique for detecting and localizing specific proteins (antigens) in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following methods of cold sterilization except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Autoclave

Cold sterilization refers to sterilization methods that do not use high temperatures and are suitable for heat-sensitive materials. Cold methods are used for heat-labile instruments (e.g., endoscopes, plastics).

Cold sterilization methods:

• Plasma sterilization → uses hydrogen peroxide plasma
• Gamma rays → ionizing radiation used for disposable medical equipment
• UV rays → used for surface disinfection (limited penetration)

Not a cold sterilization method:

• Autoclave → uses moist heat under pressure (121°C), hence a heat sterilization method
questions.learning: Autoclave Cold sterilization refers to sterilization methods that do not use high temperatures and are suitable for heat-sensitive materials. Cold methods are used for heat-labile instruments (e.g., endoscopes, plastics).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During the anthropometric evaluation, the height for age of a child is < - 2SD. This is most likely due to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic malnutrition

Low height for the age (height for age < -2SD) in children indicates chronic malnutrition and stunting.

Classification of nutritional status depending on the anthropometry (height/length for age):

Classification
Criteria

Moderately stunted (or) moderate chronic malnutrition

Height/length-for-age

< (–2 SD) and > (–3 SD)

Severely stunted (or) severe chronic malnutrition

Height/length-for-age

< (–3 SD)

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry:

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for the screening of wasting in children. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, MUAC <11.5cm is classified as severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a flowchart illustrating the natural history of a disease, what is the term used for the time interval between points A and B?
questions.explanation: The flowchart shows: Disease Onset → A (First possible point of diagnosis) → B (Final critical point of diagnosis) → C (Usual time of diagnosis) → Outcome The interval between Point A and Point B represents Screening Time. Screening time is defined as the time interval between the first possible point of diagnosis (A) — when disease could earliest be detected through screening methods — and the final critical point of diagnosis (B) — beyond which treatment becomes less effective or irreversible damage occurs. This interval essentially represents the window period during which screening is beneficial and early intervention can meaningfully alter disease outcome. Clinical Significance: Screening time defines the optimal window for screening programs to be effective. A longer screening time means a disease is more suitable for mass screening programs as there is a wider window of opportunity for early detection and intervention. Why other options are wrong: (A) Lead time is incorrect because lead time refers to the interval between Point A and Point C — the difference between earliest possible diagnosis through screening and the usual time of clinical diagnosis. It represents the "head start" gained by screening over conventional diagnosis. (C) Generation time is incorrect because generation time refers to the time between receipt of infection and point of maximum infectivity in communicable disease epidemiology — completely unrelated to diagnostic intervals shown in this flowchart. (D) Lag time is incorrect because lag time refers to the delay between exposure to a risk factor and onset of disease, representing a pre-onset interval — not the interval between two diagnostic points as depicted here
questions.learning: The flowchart shows: Disease Onset → — A (First possible point of diagnosis) → B (Final critical point of diagnosis) → C (Usual time of diagnosis) → Outcome The interval between Point A and Point B represents Screening Time.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, constipation, and fatigue and is subsequently diagnosed with lead poisoning. Which enzyme defect is most likely responsible for the manifestations of lead toxicity in this patient?
questions.explanation: Lead poisoning interferes with several enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway, but its most characteristic and potent effect is the inhibition of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase. This enzyme (also known as porphobilinogen synthase) catalyzes the second step of the pathway, converting two molecules of ALA into one molecule of porphobilinogen. Lead also inhibits ferrochelatase (Heme synthase, Option C), which is responsible for the final step of inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX. Inhibition of ALA dehydratase leads to an accumulation of ALA in the blood and urine, which is thought to contribute to the neurological symptoms and abdominal pain seen in lead toxicity. ALA synthase (Option A) is the rate-limiting enzyme but is not the primary target of lead. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase (Option D) is another pathway enzyme but is less sensitive to lead than ALA dehydratase. Clinically, lead poisoning is often identified by "basophilic stippling" on a blood smear and elevated blood lead levels. Management focuses on removing the source of lead and using chelation therapy in severe cases
questions.learning: Lead poisoning interferes with several enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway, but its most characteristic and potent effect is the inhibition of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the correct anatomies from the CT scan given below:
options: A- Kidney, B- Liver, C- Pancreas
A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen
A- Spleen, B- Kidney, C- Liver
A- Pancreas, B- Liver, C- Spleen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen

The correct identification of structures marked as A, B, and C in the CT image is: A-Liver, B-Pancreas, C-Spleen.

A - Liver: The liver is an organ located in the upper right portion of the abdomen. On a CT scan, the liver has a homogeneous appearance with well-defined borders. The liver's density is higher compared to surrounding organs due to its composition of hepatocytes and blood vessels. Additionally, blood vessels such as the hepatic artery and portal vein can be seen supplying blood to the liver.

B - Pancreas: The pancreas is a glandular organ situated behind the stomach and adjacent to the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). On a CT scan, the pancreas appears as a soft tissue structure with a slightly lower density compared to the liver. It typically has a lobulated appearance and is located in the retroperitoneal space. The pancreatic duct may also be visualized, extending from the pancreas to the duodenum.

C - Spleen: The spleen is an organ located in the upper left portion of the abdomen, beneath the diaphragm and behind the stomach. On a CT scan, the spleen appears as a well-defined structure with a homogeneous density similar to the liver. It typically has a slightly lower density compared to the liver.
questions.learning: A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen — The correct identification of structures marked as A, B, and C in the CT image is: A-Liver, B-Pancreas, C-Spleen. A - Liver: The liver is an organ located in the upper right portion of the abdomen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 65-year-old male, with a known case of coronary artery disease, presented for a general check-up. On examination, vital signs are normal. He has notable long limbs. Blood glucose concentration is 100 mg/dL and homocysteine concentration is 20 μmol/L. Serum lipid levels are normal. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient? Normal homocysteine concentration in blood = 5-15 μmol/L.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystathionine β-synthase

This patient with long limbs, coronary artery disease and elevated homocysteine concentration most likely has homocystinuria, and the enzyme deficiency in this condition is cystathionine β synthase.

Homocystinuria is most commonly caused by a defect in the cystathionine β synthase enzyme leading to the accumulation of homocysteine in urine and blood. They are generally normal at birth and the first sign is subluxation of the lens (ectopia lentis) seen after 3 years of age.

Manifestations of homocystinuria:

* Ectopia lentis.

* Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.

* Thromboembolic episodes.

* Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly.

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic lab findings.

Other Options:

*

Deficiency of homogentisate oxidase is associated with alkaptonuria.

*

Deficiency of Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRTase) is responsible for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

Pearl PF0079: Homocystinuria
questions.learning: Cystathionine β-synthase — This patient with long limbs, coronary artery disease and elevated homocysteine concentration most likely has homocystinuria, and the enzyme deficiency in this condition is cystathionine β synthase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man is admitted with an acute inferior wall myocardial infarction. Shortly after administration of sublingual nitroglycerin, he develops marked bradycardia, hypotension, and lightheadedness. ECG shows no atrioventricular conduction abnormality. On examination, his extremities are warm, and there are no signs of pulmonary congestion. The physician attributes his hemodynamic deterioration to a reflex triggered by reduced left ventricular filling, resulting in enhanced vagal activity. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?
options: Baroreceptor-mediated reflex secondary to elevated arterial pressure
Bainbridge reflex due to increased right atrial filling
Bezold–Jarisch reflex due to ventricular underfilling
Cushing reflex caused by raised intracranial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bezold–Jarisch reflex due to ventricular underfilling

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a cardioinhibitory reflex initiated by stimulation of ventricular mechanoreceptors when the left ventricle is underfilled but contracting vigorously.

It is classically precipitated by:

• Inferior wall myocardial infarction
• Nitrate administration (reduces preload)
• Spinal or epidural anesthesia
• Severe hypovolemia

Physiologic response:

• ↑ Vagal tone → Bradycardia
• Peripheral vasodilation → Hypotension
• Occasionally, transient apnea

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Baroreceptor-mediated reflex secondary to elevated arterial pressure: Activated by increased blood pressure, producing reflex bradycardia; it is not triggered by ventricular underfilling.
• B. Bainbridge reflex due to increased right atrial filling: Caused by increased venous return and right atrial stretch, resulting in tachycardia, not bradycardia.
• D. Cushing reflex caused by raised intracranial pressure: Occurs in raised intracranial pressure and presents with hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
questions.learning: Bezold–Jarisch reflex due to ventricular underfilling The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a cardioinhibitory reflex initiated by stimulation of ventricular mechanoreceptors when the left ventricle is underfilled but contracting vigorously.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following fractures is most prone to non-union?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proximal scaphoid

Among the given fractures, proximal scaphoid fractures are most prone to non-union.

Since the nutrient artery enters the scaphoid near its distal end, proximal fractures are associated with avascular necrosis and non-union. The more proximal the fracture in the scaphoid, the higher the chances of avascular necrosis and non-union.

Certain bones have a relatively limited or watershed blood supply that can potentially get interrupted by fracture. These include:

• Head of the femur: after fracture of the neck or posterior dislocation of the hip.
• Proximal scaphoid: due to fracture through the waist of the scaphoid.
• Lunate: following a dislocation.
• Body of talus: after fracture of its neck.

Fractures in these sites have a higher risk for non-union or development of osteonecrosis.

Other options:

Option B: Inter-trochanteric fractures involve either the greater or lesser trochanters or both, more common in the elderly following a history of a fall. Malunion is the most frequent complication. The vast metaphyseal region has an abundant blood supply, contributing to a higher union rate and fewer chances of avascular necrosis.

Option C: Distal radius fractures occur by fall on an outstretched hand and they include Colles' fracture (most common), Smith's fracture, Barton's fracture, and Chauffer's fracture. The complications include joint stiffness, malunion (more common), carpal tunnel syndrome, subluxation of the inferior radio-ulnar joint, Sudeck's dystrophy, and rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon. Avascular necrosis or non-union is rare.

Option D: Olecranon fracture results from a direct injury as in a fall onto the point of the elbow. Complications include non-union, elbow stiffness, and osteoarthritis.
questions.learning: Proximal scaphoid Among the given fractures, proximal scaphoid fractures are most prone to non-union. Since the nutrient artery enters the scaphoid near its distal end, proximal fractures are associated with avascular necrosis and non-union.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive daytime somnolence, impaired concentration, and poor memory over the past year. She reports loud snoring and unrefreshing sleep. On examination, her BMI is 43 kg/m², and her blood pressure is 170/98 mmHg. An arterial blood gas obtained while she is awake shows: • PaO₂: 70 mmHg • PaCO₂: 53 mmHg • HCO₃⁻: 33 mEq/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

This patient has Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome.

The diagnosis is based on the triad of:

• Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
• Awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg)
• Chronic hypoxemia without another cause of hypoventilation

The elevated HCO₃⁻ (33 mEq/L) indicates renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, confirming long-standing hypoventilation rather than an acute event.

Patients commonly present with:

• Excessive daytime sleepiness
• Cognitive impairment
• Loud snoring
• Systemic hypertension
• Morning headaches
• Signs of chronic hypoventilation

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) – OSA causes recurrent nocturnal airway obstruction but awake ABG is usually normal. Persistent daytime hypercapnia suggests OHS rather than isolated OSA.
• C. Central sleep apnea – Characterized by reduced respiratory drive during sleep and is commonly associated with heart failure, stroke, or opioid use. Severe obesity with chronic daytime hypercapnia favors OHS.
• D. Narcolepsy – Causes excessive daytime sleepiness but does not produce hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or elevated bicarbonate.

High-yield pearl

Differentiate OHS from OSA:

| Feature | OSA | OHS

| ------- | --- | ---

| Obesity | Common | Almost always present

| Daytime PaCO₂ | Usually normal | >45 mmHg ✅

| Serum HCO₃⁻ | Normal | Elevated (chronic compensation)

| Daytime hypoxemia | Uncommon | Common

| Treatment | CPAP | Weight loss + CPAP/BiPAP (BiPAP often required if hypercapnia persists)

Key exam clue:

• An obese patient with daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg) and elevated bicarbonate should be diagnosed with Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome, even if obstructive sleep apnea is also present.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cholera causes diarrhea by binding to specific receptors on intestinal cells. Which factor facilitates the entry of cholera toxin through the intestinal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The cholera toxin, produced by Vibrio cholerae, consists of an A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits are responsible for binding to the host cell. The specific receptor on the intestinal epithelial cell surface that the cholera toxin binds to is the GM1 ganglioside. This binding facilitates the entry of the active A subunit into the cell. GLUT 1 (Option A) is a glucose transporter and is not involved in toxin binding. GM2 ganglioside (Option B) is a related molecule but is not the primary receptor for cholera toxin. Cephalin (Option C, phosphatidylethanolamine) is a common membrane phospholipid but lacks the specific carbohydrate structure required for toxin recognition. Once inside, the A subunit constitutively activates the Gs protein, leading to a massive increase in intracellular cAMP. This causes the hypersecretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen, resulting in the characteristic profuse "rice-water" diarrhea of cholera
questions.learning: The cholera toxin, produced by Vibrio cholerae, consists of an A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits are responsible for binding to the host cell.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the sign given in the image below:
questions.explanation: The image shows the "Double Ring Sign," also known as the "Halo Sign" or "Double Target Sign," which is a bedside test for identifying cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. When blood mixed with CSF is dropped onto filter paper, the CSF, being less viscous than blood, spreads further outward, creating a clear outer ring around a central red blood spot. This is commonly used in cases of CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea following head trauma. Beta-2 transferrin (Option A) is the biochemical gold standard test for CSF but requires laboratory analysis. The "handkerchief sign" (Option C) refers to the fact that CSF does not stiffen a handkerchief when dry, unlike nasal mucus. The "teardrop sign" (Option D) is an imaging finding in orbital floor fractures. Although useful, the halo sign is not 100% specific, as other fluids can also create similar patterns
questions.learning: The image shows the "Double Ring Sign," also known as the "Halo Sign" or "Double Target Sign," which is a bedside test for identifying cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man who was arrested died while he was in police custody. Who will conduct the inquest in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Judicial Magistrate

A magistrate inquest will be carried out for death under police custody.

BNSS 196/Section 176 Cr. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government.

While conducting this inquiry, the Magistrate has all the powers that they would normally have when investigating an offence. This ensures an independent and impartial inquiry into the circumstances of death, disappearance, or rape occurring while a person or woman is in police or judicial custody.

A death is considered custodial when it occurs in any form of detention, including while the person is being arrested, detained, escaping, or attempting to escape from custody.  The Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate conducting the inquiry must, within 24 hours of the death, forward the body to the nearest civil surgeon or other qualified medical professional appointed by the government for postmortem examination.

Indications for Magistrate Inquest:

* Death under police custody

* Death due to police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, borstal schools

* Dowry death

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Exhumation

* Death or disappearance of any person, or rape of a woman who is under the custody of police or any other person authorized by the court.

Other options:

Option A: 194 BNSS or Section 174 CrPC deals with the police inquest. It is done in suicide, homicide, killing by any animal or machinery or accident, and death under circumstances that raise suspicion of another person committing the offence. In all cases where the police normally conduct inquests, the magistrate can hold an additional inquest, or in place of the police inquest.

Option B: Coroner's Inquest is not practised in India. It is done in the U.K. and the U.S.A. The coroner, who is usually a first-class magistrate or attorney, conducts an inquest in all unnatural and suspicious deaths. The doctor is summoned to his Court to give evidence at the inquest.

Option C: The medical examiner's system is not followed in India. It is followed in certain states of the USA and Japan. A medical practitioner known as a 'Medical Examiner' is appointed to perform the functions of a Coroner. He gets first-hand information on the investigation and crime scene, which, when correlated with autopsy findings, carves out a better picture.
Though he is not entitled to any judicial powers, the inquest conducted in the presence of a doctor makes it superior to any other method.
questions.learning: Judicial Magistrate — A magistrate inquest will be carried out for death under police custody. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following structures are not pierced during epidural anesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dura

During epidural anaesthesia, the local anaesthetic is injected into the epidural/extradural space and the dura is not pierced in epidural anaesthesia.

Structures pierced during epidural anaesthesia (in that order):

* Skin

* Subcutaneous tissue

* Supraspinous ligament

* Interspinous ligament

* Ligamentum flavum

* Epidural space

The dura mater is not pierced during epidural anaesthesia. The needle is advanced through the ligamentum flavum and into the epidural space, which is located just outside the dura mater.

Pearl PF1246: High yield points in epidural anaesthesia

* Epidural space lies between dura and ligamentum flavum

* Dura is not penetrated

* The site of action of epidural anesthesia is nerve roots

* Tuohy needle is used for epidural anesthesia

* Methods to identify epidural space:

* Loss of resistance technique

* Hanging drop technique – Gutierrez's sign (sudden sucking of a drop in epidural space)

* Methods to confirm epidural anesthesia

* Test dose with 3cc lidocaine with 15mcg adrenaline (1:2,00,000) - Intrathecal injection will produce spinal anesthesia (lidocaine) that should be rapidly apparent. Intravascular injection will produce significant tachycardia 20% above baseline (adrenaline).

* Durant’s sign – rapid injection of the drug in epidural space causes an increase in rate and depth of respiration

* Westpal sign – absence of knee-jerk after epidural anesthesia

* Anesthetic of choice in epidural anesthesia during labor - Bupivacaine

* Epidural narcotic preferred over epidural local anesthesia because of the absence of motor paralysis

* Drugs used for epidural analgesia- Morphine, Fentanyl

* Epidural opioids act on dorsal horn substantia gelatinosa. It may cause pruritis and respiratory depression

* Drug not given in central neuraxial block or caudal block- Remifentanil

* Walking epidural- Ultra low dose epidural used especially for labor (only sensory blockade)

* Complication of Epidural anesthesia -Total spinal anesthesia

* Not a complication of epidural anesthesia –DIC, Headache

* During epidural anesthesia- sudden hypotension is due to the drug entering subarachnoid space

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A neonate is brought with complaints of photophobia and watering. Clinical examination shows normal tear passages and clear but large cornea. The image of his eye is shown below which reveals Haab's striae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buphthalmos

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of buphthalmos. Haab’s striae are horizontal/circumferential breaks in Descemet’s membrane seen in buphthalmos.

Buphthalmos (Bull-like eyes) is an enlargement of the eyeball seen in true congenital and infantile glaucoma, usually when the disease onset is before 3 years.

The image given below shows Haab's striae and a child having buphthalmos in congenital glaucoma.

Vogt's striae are vertical, fine, whitish lines (folds/tears) in Descemet's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus.

Pearl PF1677: Vogt's striae

The above image shows “Vogt’s Striae” which are characteristically seen in Keratoconus.

* Vogt's striae are vertical (rarely horizontal) fine, whitish lines in the deep/posterior stroma and Descemet's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus.

* It may be asymmetric depending on the degree of keratoconus in each eye.

* It is considered that there is a positive correlation between the orientation of the lines with the steepest axis of the cornea and the mechanism is thought to be related to mechanical stress forces on collagen lamellae radiating from the cone apex.

* The striae can temporarily disappear with external pressure to the globe.
questions.learning: Buphthalmos — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of buphthalmos. Haab’s striae are horizontal/circumferential breaks in Descemet’s membrane seen in buphthalmos.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Increase in glomerular capillary permeability leads to which substance appearing in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein

The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents filtration of large, negatively charged plasma proteins, especially albumin, through its three layers:

• Fenestrated endothelium
• Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (size- and charge-selective)
• Podocyte slit diaphragm

When this barrier becomes more permeable (e.g., glomerular disease), proteins leak into the urine, resulting in proteinuria (albuminuria).

• Protein is normally retained in the circulation. Increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier allows its passage into the urine.

Why not the other options?

• A. Glucose: Freely filtered and normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; glucosuria results from hyperglycemia or tubular dysfunction, not increased glomerular permeability.
• B. Ketone bodies: Freely filtered; ketonuria occurs in starvation or diabetic ketoacidosis.
• D. Uric acid: Freely filtered and undergoes filtration, reabsorption, and secretion; its urinary excretion is unrelated to glomerular barrier permeability.
