questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain four days after undergoing a cholecystectomy. Ultrasonography reveals a significant fluid collection in the right upper quadrant. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: USG-guided aspiration of content In a stable patient presenting with a localized fluid collection post-cholecystectomy, the immediate next step is USG-guided aspiration. This is essential to confirm the nature of the fluid—specifically distinguishing between a bile leak (biloma), an abscess (pus), or a hematoma (blood). Identifying the fluid type directly guides subsequent steps; for example, if bile is found, an MRCP or ERCP (Option C) would then be indicated to locate and treat the leak. Re-exploration (Option A) is overly invasive as an initial step. While antibiotics (Option B) may be started, they cannot replace the diagnostic and therapeutic necessity of drainage. Therefore, aspiration is the most appropriate and conservative first-line diagnostic intervention.
questions.learning: USG-guided aspiration of content — In a stable patient presenting with a localized fluid collection post-cholecystectomy, the immediate next step is USG-guided aspiration.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding Sample Registration System is not correct?
options: It is a dual record system.
It is a continuous enumeration by local enumerators and an independent survey every year by an investigator-supervisor.
It has facilitated more reliable estimates of births and deaths even at State level.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is a continuous enumeration by local enumerators and an independent survey every year by an investigator-supervisor.

The Sample Registration System (SRS) is a dual-record system used in India to provide reliable estimates of birth and death rates.

Its two components are:

1. Continuous enumeration → carried out by a resident/local enumerator.
2. Independent retrospective survey → carried out every 6 months by an investigator/supervisor, not annually.

Therefore, statement B. is incorrect because it says the independent survey is conducted every year.

• A. It is a dual record system: Correct. SRS is a dual-record system.
• B. It is a continuous enumeration by local enumerators and an independent survey every year by an investigator-supervisor: Incorrect. Independent survey is conducted every 6 months.
• C. It covers the entire country: Correct. SRS covers the country through its sample areas.
• D. It has facilitated more reliable estimates of births and deaths even at State level: Correct. It provides reliable estimates of vital rates, including at the State level.
questions.learning: It is a continuous enumeration by local enumerators and an independent survey every year by an investigator-supervisor. The Sample Registration System (SRS) is a dual-record system used in India to provide reliable estimates of birth and death rates.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A histological section is shown, with an arrow indicating a large, flask-shaped cell located in the middle layer. Identify the cell marked by the arrow.
questions.explanation: The histological section shows the cerebellar cortex, which consists of three layers: molecular, Purkinje, and granular. The marked area is a Purkinje cell, identifiable by its large, flask-shaped body arranged in a single row between the other two layers. These cells provide the only output from the cerebellar cortex and have an inhibitory effect on deep nuclei. Stellate and basket cells (Options A and B) are smaller inhibitory interneurons located in the outer molecular layer. Granular cells (Option D) are small, densely packed excitatory neurons found in the innermost granular layer. Purkinje cells are unique for their extensive dendritic branches that extend into the molecular layer. Identifying these cells is fundamental for understanding the architecture and inhibitory coordination of the cerebellum

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is a new drug approved by the FDA for the treatment of Rett syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trofinetide

Trofinetide is the newly FDA-approved drug for the treatment of Rett syndrome.

The mechanism by which trofinetide exerts therapeutic effects in patients with Rett syndrome is unknown. It is a synthetic analog of the amino‐terminal tripeptide of insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) designed to treat the core symptoms of Rett syndrome by potentially reducing neuroinflammation and supporting synaptic function of the protein fragment glypromate (GPE). IGF-1 is produced by both major types of brain cells – neurons and glia; IGF-1 in the brain is critical for both normal development and response to injury and disease. Trofinetide has been shown to inhibit the production of inflammatory cytokines, inhibit overactivation of microglia and astrocytes, and increase the amount of available IGF-1 that can bind to IGF-1 receptors.

It is Indicated for the treatment of Rett syndrome.

Adverse effects include diarrhea, vomiting, fever, seizure, anxiety, decreased appetite, fatigue, nasopharyngitis

Other options:

Option A: Olcegepant is a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonist which was considered for the treatment of migraine, but discontinued.

Option B: Lasmiditan is a nontriptan 5HT1F receptor–selective agonist and is used to treat migraine.

Option D: Erenumab is a CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) blocking antibody used in the treatment migraine.

Note: The spelling of the drug in the options has been corrected from Trofinitide to Trofinetide.
questions.learning: Trofinetide Trofinetide is the newly FDA-approved drug for the treatment of Rett syndrome. The mechanism by which trofinetide exerts therapeutic effects in patients with Rett syndrome is unknown.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a subcentre area with a crude birth rate (CBR) of 20, what would be the expected number of antenatal care (ANC) registrations by the village health nurse (VHN) in a year?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 60

• According to the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) laid down by the Government of India, a subcentre is to serve a population of 5000 in plains.
• In this scenario, the CBR is 20.
• Probable number of pregnancies (Y) = Birth rate x population of the area / 1000 = 20 x 5000/1000 = 100.
• But, we add a correction factor of 10% to adjust for pregnancy wastage in the form of abortions or stillbirths.
• Thus, total number of expected pregnancies= Y + 10% of Y= 110
• As all the pregnancies are not registered, and at any given time an ANM should have atleast half the expected pregnancies registered with her, the number of ANC registrations is taken as 50% of the expected pregnancies.
• Therefore, Total ANC registrations = total number of expected pregnancies/2 = 55
• Hence, the closest answer is 60.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 33 weeks of gestation presents for a routine antenatal visit and reports reduced fetal movements for the past two days. She has a history of gestational diabetes, with an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy. To assess fetal well-being, which antepartum fetal surveillance test should be performed initially?
questions.explanation: In a patient reporting decreased fetal movements, the Non-Stress Test (NST) is the most appropriate initial screening tool for assessing fetal well-being. The NST is a quick, non-invasive method that monitors the fetal heart rate's response to its own movements. A "reactive" NST shows heart rate accelerations, indicating adequate fetal oxygenation and an intact nervous system. The Amniotic Fluid Index (Option A) assesses fluid volume but doesn't track real-time heart rate dynamics. The Biophysical Profile (Option B) is more comprehensive but time-consuming, making it a second-line test if the NST is non-reactive. The Contraction Stress Test (Option C) is more invasive and carries the risk of inducing labor, thus it is not an initial step. Therefore, given the acute concern for movement, the NST provides the fastest reliable assessment of immediate fetal status
questions.learning: In a patient reporting decreased fetal movements, the Non-Stress Test (NST) is the most appropriate initial screening tool for assessing fetal well-being.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents to the surgery out-patient with a left-sided breast lump which she noticed on self breast examination 3weeks ago. She has no other complaints. On palpation, the lump seems to be mobile and firm. Mammogram revealed a benign lesion. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reassurance and follow-up

The most probable diagnosis based on the clinical scenario is fibroadenoma and the best next step in the management of Fibroadenoma is to Reassure the patient and do regular follow-up.

Fibroadenoma is one of the aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI). The most common age group affected is 15-25 years (early reproductive period) with a peak incidence in the second decade.

It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). It is a biphasic tumor consisting of fibroblastic stroma and epithelium-lined gland. Popcorn calcification is seen in mammography.

Option A : Biopsy is not required for Fibroadenoma unless there is a suspicion of Malignancy but based on the clinical and imaging findings the given lesion is benign.

Option C:Excision is not advised unless there is suspicious histology on fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Giant fibroadenomas are >5 cm in size, common in adolescent girls, and require excision by submammary incision.

Option D: Tamoxifen is a SERM-Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator used in the management of ER positive Breast carcinoma.
questions.learning: Reassurance and follow-up — The most probable diagnosis based on the clinical scenario is fibroadenoma and the best next step in the management of Fibroadenoma is to Reassure the patient and do regular follow-up.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man falls into a deep sleep with one arm under his head. He finds he is not able to move this arm when he awakens. However, it tingles and pain sensation in the arm is still intact. What is the reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm?
options: B fibers are more susceptible to pressure than A fibers
A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
Motor nerves are more affected by sleep than sensory nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers

The reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm, A-fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers.

Sleeping for a long period with the arms under the head puts pressure on a nerve. It leads to the loss of conduction in large-diameter motor, touch, and pressure fibers, while pain sensation remains relatively intact. A-fibers (includes the motor fibers) are affected.

The susceptibility of the nerve fibers to pressure is A>B>C.

This is responsible for Saturday night or Sunday morning paralysis.
questions.learning: A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers The reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm, A-fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which is the drug used for refractory intractable rheumatic chorea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sodium valproate

The drug used for refractory intractable rheumatic chorea is sodium valproate, as it doesn't have extrapyramidal side effects.

Sydenham's chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements which mainly affect the head and upper limbs. In the tongue, it is visible as the characteristic darting movements.

Medications used to treat Sydenham chorea are:

• Mild cases - Providing a calm environment.
• Severe cases:

• Dopamine antagonists - haloperidol, pimozide
• Antiepileptic medications - sodium valproate, carbamazepine.

• Severe, refractory cases - Steroids (thought to be immune-mediated)
• IV immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis - limited studies, decreased efficacy (not currently recommended)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In an assaulted patient, you note a wound with irregular, jagged margins. The wound shows obliquely extending tears with characteristic “swallow-tail” appearances, minimal bleeding, and evidence of crushed blood vessels and hair bulbs. How would this wound be classified and recorded in medicolegal documentation?
questions.explanation: The forensic description provided is characteristic of a Lacerated wound. Lacerations are caused by blunt force trauma that shears or tears the skin and soft tissues. Key diagnostic hallmarks mentioned include uneven, jagged edges and the presence of crushed blood vessels and hair bulbs across the base of the wound. The "swallowtail" pattern specifically occurs when the force is applied at an angle, causing a V-shaped tear. In contrast, an Incised wound (Option A) has clean-cut, regular margins and no crushed tissue. A Chopped wound (Option B) is a heavy-force injury with sharp margins but some underlying bone injury. A Stab wound (Option C) is deeper than it is long. Because the clinical features highlight tissue crushing and irregular, jagged tearing rather than clean slicing, laceration is the definitive forensic classification for documentation
questions.learning: The forensic description provided is characteristic of a Lacerated wound. Lacerations are caused by blunt force trauma that shears or tears the skin and soft tissues.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following peritoneal folds are correctly matched with their contents, except:
options: Splenorenal ligament – Splenic vessels and pancreatic tail
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastrocolic ligament – Right gastric artery

Peritoneal ligaments are double layers of peritoneum connecting abdominal organs and usually transmit specific vessels, nerves, or ducts between them. Knowing their contents is important for abdominal surgery and imaging.

Key peritoneal folds and their contents:

• Gastrocolic ligament – Part of the greater omentum connecting the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It mainly contains gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels, not the right gastric artery.
• Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament – Connects the spleen to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.
• Transverse mesocolon – Suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall and contains the middle colic vessels.
• Gastrosplenic ligament – Connects the stomach to the spleen and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels.
questions.learning: Gastrocolic ligament – Right gastric artery Peritoneal ligaments are double layers of peritoneum connecting abdominal organs and usually transmit specific vessels, nerves, or ducts between them.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A female presents with loss of vision in the right halves of both eyes. Where is the lesion located in the optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic tract

Visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

Here, vision is lost in the right half of both eyes, which means:

• in the left eye, the nasal visual field is lost, and
• in the right eye, the temporal visual field is lost.

It means left temporal and right nasal fibers are destroyed, which leads to right homonymous hemianopia. Anatomically, this can be explained by the fact that each optic tract contains fibers from the ipsilateral temporal half of the retina and the contralateral nasal half of the retina.

Optic tract lesions can occur due to pituitary adenomas (most common), craniopharyngioma, tumors of the optic thalamus, large aneurysm of superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries, demyelinating diseases, and infarction.

Other options:

Option B: Optic radiation lesions result in contralateral homonymous hemianopia, which means that the visual loss would occur in the left halves of both eyes rather than the right halves, as described in the question.

Option C: Lesions at the optic chiasma typically cause bitemporal hemianopia, which involves visual loss in the outer (temporal) halves of the visual field in both eyes. This is not consistent with the patient's described symptoms.

Option D: A lesion in the right optic tract would result in left homonymous hemianopia, causing visual loss in the left halves of both eyes. This does not match the patient's presentation of vision loss in the right halves of both eyes.
questions.learning: Left optic tract Visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old child presents to paediatric OPD with hypoglycemia between feeds. ABG analysis revealed evidence of ketosis and lactic acidosis. There is massive hepatomegaly, and the liver is palpable 8 cm below the subcostal margin. Which of the following is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen storage disease

The given clinical vignette points toward a glycogen storage disease.

Von Gierke Disease, or Type 1 Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD), is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiencies in glucose-6-phosphatase or the translocase enzyme responsible for transporting glucose-6-phosphate, affecting glucose production in the liver, kidney, and intestines. There are two subtypes: Type Ia, with defective glucose-6-phosphatase, and Type Ib, with faulty translocase. Both lead to severe fasting hypoglycaemia and symptoms like hepatomegaly, growth retardation, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, and dyslipidaemia. Type Ib also causes recurrent infections and mucosal ulcers due to neutropenia.

Type 2 Glycogen Storage Disorder (Pompe’s Disease) is due to the deficiency of lysosomal acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase), which leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of the liver (hepatomegaly), skeletal muscles in the form of large vacuoles (hypotonia and weakness), and cardiac muscles (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). The child generally dies by the age of 2 years due to cardiac failure. The adult form presents with muscle dystrophies.

Type 3 Glycogen Storage Disorder (Cori's disease) is due to the deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme (amylo-α(1→6)-glucosidase). On liver or muscle biopsy there is an accumulation of branched polysaccharides (limit dextrin). Infants usually present with ketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, and hyperlipidaemia. Muscle weaknesses are mostly seen in the third to the fourth decade of life. Lactic acidosis is a key differentiator between GSD I (von Gierke) and GSD III (Cori disease).

Type 4 GSD (Andersen’s Disease) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by the deficiency of branching enzyme (amylo-α(1→4)→α(1→6)-transglycosylase) activity. These excessively long peripheral glucan chains form polyglucosan bodies, which are positive on periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) and resistant to diastase digestion. Polyglucosan body accumulation is seen in all affected patients but to different degrees and in different tissues. Patients with Type 4 Glycogen Storage Disorder (Andersen’s Disease) present with hepatic cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, myopathy, peripheral neuropathy, motor neuron disease, leukodystrophy, failure to thrive, and death occurs by the age of 5 years due to hepatic failure.

Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease / Type 5 GSD) affects only skeletal muscle, causing exercise-induced cramps and weakness. Muscle glycogen is abnormally high and blood lactate is low after exercise. It does not cause hypoglycaemia or liver enlargement.

Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers disease / Type 6 GSD) results in mild hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly but typically spares muscle and has milder symptoms. Muscle weakness and severe fasting symptoms are uncommon.

Tarui's disease is a type 7 glycogen storage disorder that results from the deficiency of phosphofructokinase. Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. The exercise intolerance worsens after a carbohydrate-rich meal in Tauri's disease, and thus glucose is not metabolised. The ingested glucose prevents lipolysis, thereby depriving muscle of fatty acid and ketone substrates.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following courts has the authority to commute a death sentence?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian legal system, while a Session Court (Option A) or an Additional Session Court (Option B) can pass a death sentence, the sentence cannot be executed until it is confirmed by the High Court. The High Court has the specific authority to confirm, commute, or set aside the death sentence during this mandatory review process. Further appeals can be made to the Supreme Court. Additionally, the President of India and the Governors of States have the constitutional power to grant pardons and commute death sentences. Options A, B, and D in the original list might be incomplete, but the High Court's role in the "confirmation" and potential commutation of capital punishment is a fundamental principle of criminal procedure. This mandatory oversight is a legal safeguard to ensure that the death penalty is reserved for only the "rarest of rare" cases, as mandated by judicial precedent
questions.learning: Under the Indian legal system, while a Session Court (Option A) or an Additional Session Court (Option B) can pass a death sentence, the sentence cannot be executed until it is confirmed by the High Court.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Postmortem hypostasis is best differentiated from a bruise by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cutting the skin

BRUISE (Contusion)

-Blood extravasates (leaks out) into tissues due to trauma during life.

Blunt force → capillary rupture → blood escapes into interstitial tissue.

Classic features :

✔️ Occurs before death

✔️ Shows vital reaction

✔️ Inflammatory cells present

✔️ Hemoglobin breakdown over time (color changes: red → blue → green → yellow)

✔️ Cannot be washed away

ON MICROSCOPY:

• RBCs outside vessels
• Fibrin
• Leukocyte infiltration
• Tissue reaction

LIVIDITY (Livor Mortis)

Passive gravitational pooling of blood inside vessels after death.

No circulation → gravity pulls blood to dependent parts.

Classic features:

✔️ Occurs after death

✔️ Blood remains inside vessels (early stage)

✔️ No inflammatory response

✔️ Blanches in early stage

✔️ Distribution follows gravity

Microscopy (early stage ):

• RBCs inside dilated vessels
• No extravasation
• No inflammation

Late fixed lividity can sometimes look like a bruise because RBCs leak after hemolysis.

But difference:

• No inflammation
• No macrophages
• No tissue repair reaction
questions.learning: Cutting the skin BRUISE (Contusion) -Blood extravasates (leaks out) into tissues due to trauma during life. Blunt force → capillary rupture → blood escapes into interstitial tissue.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old presents with edema and anasarca. A diagnosis of minimal change disease is made. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: Light microscopy shows effacement of podocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Good response to steroids

The true statement about minimal change disease is that it shows a good response to steroids.

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It is more common in males and appears between 2 to 6 years of age.

The causes of MCD are mostly idiopathic. It is usually associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma (due to the increased production of cytokines), respiratory infections, prophylactic immunizations, eczema, and rhinitis.

Clinically, they mostly present with proteinuria. The child presents with a history of edema that is initially noted around the eyes and gradually progresses into generalized edema. Hypertension and hematuria are uncommon.

Levels of the following proteins are increased in nephrotic syndrome:

• Fibrinogen - leads to hypercoagulability.
• Lipoproteins - due to increased synthesis.

Levels of the following proteins are decreased in nephrotic syndrome as a consequence of selective proteinuria:

• Albumin—the protein with the largest proportion of loss in nephrotic syndrome
• Transferrin
• Cholecalciferol-binding protein
• Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)
• Ferritin
• Coagulation factors
• Antithrombin III

Diagnosis can be made by urinalysis showing proteinuria, ranging from 3+ to 4+ protein on urine dipstick and a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio (PCR) >2. The proteinuria principally contains albumin, hence known as selective proteinuria. Serum albumin levels are <2.5 g/dL and there is an increase in serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels.

Biopsy findings include the following:

• Light microscopy- glomeruli appear normal (hence called "minimal change")
• Immunofluorescence studies- no Ig or complement deposits
• Electron microscopy- diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes

The image given below shows biopsy findings seen in minimal change disease on light microscopy.

The illustration given below shows the effacement of foot processes of podocytes as seen in MCD.

The majority of children will respond to corticosteroid (prednisone/prednisolone) treatment and will achieve complete remission (urine PCR<0.2 or <1+ protein on urine dipstick).
questions.learning: Good response to steroids — The true statement about minimal change disease is that it shows a good response to steroids. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 22 year old male presented with progressive left sided facial swelling for 2 weeks. There is history of traumatic injury with wood two months back. CECT nose and paranasal sinuses shows mass in subcutaneous tissue of left cheek. Biopsy of specimen shows foreign body granuloma with positive PAS and GMS stain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phycomycosis

The given clinical scenario is strongly suggestive of Phycomycosis/mucormycosis. A positive fungal stain(Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver stain) narrows down the diagnosis. The cutaneous disease can be highly invasive, penetrating into muscle, fascia, and even bone.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis caused by a number of molds classified in the order ‘Mucorales’. These fungi are ubiquitous thermotolerant saprobes. The leading pathogens among this group are species of the genera Rhizopus, Mucor, and Absidia. Their spores are present in air and dust.

Mucormycosis can occur as isolated cutaneous or subcutaneous infection in immunologically normal individuals after traumatic implantation of soil or vegetation. Angio-invasiveness is one of the characteristics of zygomycosis which makes it fatal. Lungs are usually the primary site of infection. Almost all patients are immunocompromised. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis occurs commonly in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis. It is the most common form; starts as eye and facial pain may progress to cause orbital cellulitis, proptosis, and vision loss. The typical finding is the presence of a black necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity.

Diagnosis:

• Exudate: wet preparation is made in 10% potassium hydroxide. Broad, ribbon-like hyphae are seen.
• Tissue: Hematoxylin & eosin stain shows non-septate, broad hyphae, often invading into blood vessels. Special stains help to identify the fungus in tissue sections.
• Biopsy confirms this diagnosis by revealing non-septate hyphae branching at right-angles, which are characteristic of Mucorales such as Rhizopus delemar. The hyphae are broad (10–15 μm) with uneven thickness, irregular branching, and sparse septations.
• Isolation is by culture on Sabouraud agar with an antibacterial agent but without cycloheximide. The colonies are grey-white with a thick cotton, fluffy surface.

Treatment is primarily with liposomal amphotericin B. Surgical debridement of the affected tissues and control of underlying predisposing cause is equally important.

Other options:

Option D: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibodies (the hallmark of the disease). The pathogenesis of this condition is not understood. This condition leads to fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. The patients may present as Riedel's thyroiditis, autoimmune pancreatitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. But not with ptosis as shown in the image. Diagnosis is established by positive fibrosis and the presence of plasma cells on biopsy. Rituximab is known to be beneficial. Sometimes, as a rare presentation, this can mimic Wegener's granulomatosis.

Option B: Midline lethal granuloma is a rare disease. It is characterized by necrotizing destruction and mutilation of the nose and other structures of respiratory passages. Generally, it is a diagnosis of exclusion. CT may be helpful in picking up the lesions. Negative c-ANCA and fungal stains also aid in the diagnosis.

Option C: NK/T cell lymphoma is a destructive lesion usually starting on one side of nose involving the upper lip, oral cavity, maxilla and sometimes even extending to orbit.Histologically polymorphic lymphoid tissue with angiocentric and angioinvasive features is seen. Immunochemical staining of biopsy material should be done for CD56+ marker for diagnosis. Nearly all cases of T/NK cel lymphomas are associated with EB virus. Localized T/NK-cell lymphoma is treated by radiation while a disseminated disease requires chemotherapy.
questions.learning: Phycomycosis — The given clinical scenario is strongly suggestive of Phycomycosis/mucormycosis. A positive fungal stain(Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver stain) narrows down the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A semen profile showing low sperm count (16 million/ml), reduced motility (40%), and severely abnormal morphology (<1% normal forms) is termed oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OAT).
questions.explanation: According to the latest WHO criteria for semen analysis, the primary abnormality in this case is a severe defect in sperm morphology. Teratospermia is defined as the presence of less than 4% morphologically normal sperm when assessed using Kruger’s strict criteria. In this patient, the morphology is <1%, which represents severe teratospermia. Oligospermia (Option A) refers to a reduced sperm concentration, defined as a count <15 million/mL. Since this patient’s sperm count is 16 million/mL, it lies within the normal reference range. Asthenospermia (Option C) denotes reduced sperm motility (progressive motility <32% or total motility <40%); the patient’s motility is at the lower limit of normal and does not meet criteria for asthenospermia. Normospermia (Option B) indicates normal semen parameters across all domains, which is clearly not the case here. Although abnormalities of count, motility, and morphology may coexist (OAT syndrome), the isolated and most significant defect here is morphology, making teratospermia the correct diagnosis. Severe teratospermia significantly impairs fertilization, and assisted reproductive techniques such as intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) are often required to achieve pregnancy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man is presbyopic. The power of his prescription glasses should be _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. +1.5D

The power of prescription glasses for a 50-year-old woman should be +1.5D.

Presbyopia is the condition of decreasing near vision due to an age-related decrease in the magnitude of accommodation.

Basic principles for correction in presbyopic patients are given below:

• Correct any refractive error for distance present in the patient first.
• Add the presbyopic correction(correction for near vision) of each eye to any distant correction that is present.
• For presbyopic correction, the weakest convex lens(plus lens) with which the patient can see clearly at the near point is prescribed, since over-correction will also result in eye fatigue symptoms.

Presbyopic spectacles may be unifocal, bifocal or Multifocal.

A rough prescription of presbyopic glasses can be made by the age of the patient in an emmetrope as follows:

Age
Power

45 years
+1 to +1.25D

50 years

+1.5 to 1.75D

55 years
+2 to +2.25D

60 years
+2.5 to +3D
questions.learning: +1.5D The power of prescription glasses for a 50-year-old woman should be +1.5D. Presbyopia is the condition of decreasing near vision due to an age-related decrease in the magnitude of accommodation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 49-year-old man presenting with flu-like symptoms, a rash involving the palms and soles, and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy on examination?
questions.explanation: The constellation of flu-like constitutional symptoms, generalized maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, and characteristic epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of Secondary Syphilis. This stage of infection, caused by Treponema pallidum, occurs weeks to months after the resolution of the primary chancre. Epitrochlear lymph node enlargement is highly suggestive of this condition. Primary syphilis (Option A) is characterized by a painless, solitary chancre at the site of inoculation, usually without a systemic rash. Endemic diseases (Option C) refer to localized disease patterns and are not a specific diagnosis for these clinical signs. Steven-Johnson Syndrome (Option D) is a severe hypersensitivity reaction characterized by painful, necrotic skin sloughing and mucosal involvement, usually triggered by drugs, which is inconsistent with this non-painful palm/sole rash. Diagnosis should be confirmed with non-treponemal tests like VDRL or RPR followed by specific treponemal assays. Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G remains the first-line therapeutic intervention
questions.learning: The constellation of flu-like constitutional symptoms, generalized maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, and characteristic epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of Secondary Syphilis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monophasic

The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is monophasic proximal to the level of obstruction.

The normal venous waveform shows a variation (phasicity) secondary to respiration referred to as respirophasic waveform. Loss of this phasic variation results in a monophasic waveform suggestive of venous obstruction proximal to the level of interrogation.

A normal artery has a triphasic signal. The waveform becomes biphasic in mild-moderate stenosis and monophasic in severe stenosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with intense itching of the eyes, photophobia, and a sticky ocular discharge. Ophthalmic examination reveals characteristic findings. Based on these symptoms and examination results, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), or "Spring Catarrh," is a recurrent, bilateral allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva. It typically affects young boys in hot, dry climates. The hallmark symptom is intense itching, often accompanied by photophobia and a characteristic ropy, sticky discharge. Clinical signs include giant papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva ("cobblestone" appearance) or white dots at the limbus (Horner-Trantas dots). Option A (Trachoma) is an infectious scarring disease with follicles. Option C (Phlyctenular conjunctivitis) is a hypersensitivity reaction presenting with localized nodules near the limbus. Option D (Xerophthalmia) is due to Vitamin A deficiency and presents with extreme dryness and Bitot's spots. VKC is a combined Type I and Type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Treatment involves cold compresses, mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines, and occasionally topical steroids. Severe cases can lead to "shield ulcers" on the cornea, which can permanently impair vision
questions.learning: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC), or "Spring Catarrh," is a recurrent, bilateral allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva. It typically affects young boys in hot, dry climates.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which glycosaminoglycan is essential for preserving the transparency of the cornea?
questions.explanation: The transparency of the cornea is vital for vision and depends on the precise, regular arrangement of collagen fibrils within the stroma. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are essential components of the corneal extracellular matrix that help maintain this organization. Keratan sulfate (Option A) is the most abundant GAG in the corneal stroma, accounting for about 60% of the total GAG content. It plays a critical role in regulating collagen fibril diameter and spacing, which prevents the scattering of light. Hyaluronic acid (Option B) is primarily found in the vitreous humor. Chondroitin sulfate (Option C) and Dermatan sulfate (Option D) are also present in the cornea but in much smaller quantities compared to keratan sulfate. Deficiencies or abnormalities in keratan sulfate can lead to corneal opacification, as seen in certain genetic macular corneal dystrophies. Therefore, keratan sulfate is the primary biochemical mediator of corneal clarity

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A teenager has a mass in his nasopharynx that has minimally spread into the sphenoid sinus with no lateral extension. Which stage of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma could this be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage IB

The mass has spread into the sphenoid sinus with no lateral extension, so it's Stage 1B according to the Radkowski classification.

Multiple classification systems exist for the staging of juvenile nasal angiofibroma, of which the most commonly used ones are the Fisch and Radkowski classification systems:

Type

4
A: Intracranial intradural tumor without infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm

B: Intracranial intradural tumor with infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Note: The Fisch system is considered to be the more robust and practical of the two.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Atypical antipsychotic with least metabolic side effects?
questions.explanation: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are generally associated with metabolic side effects like weight gain and diabetes. Among the options, Ziprasidone is known for having the least metabolic side effects, being largely weight-neutral. Haloperidol (Option A) is a first-generation antipsychotic; while it has low metabolic risk, it has very high risks of extrapyramidal side effects. Risperidone (Option B) and Quetiapine (Option D) have moderate-to-high risks of metabolic syndrome and weight gain. Clozapine and Olanzapine (not listed) have the highest risk. While ziprasidone is metabolic-safe, it carries a unique risk of dose-dependent QT interval prolongation, requiring cardiac monitoring in high-risk patients. For a patient already suffering from obesity or diabetes, choosing a "metabolic-friendly" drug like ziprasidone or aripiprazole is a critical part of holistic psychiatric management to ensure physical health along with mental stability
questions.learning: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are generally associated with metabolic side effects like weight gain and diabetes. Among the options, Ziprasidone is known for having the least metabolic side effects, being largely weight-neutral.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following actin myosin cross bridges pair correctly represents the point (B-C) shown on length-tension relationship in the sarcomere curve?
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. [image not included in this edition]

The length-tension relationship describes how muscle force varies with sarcomere length. Point B-C on the graph represents the plateau phase where maximum active tension (100%) is generated. At B–C (Plateau phase):

• Optimal overlap between actin and myosin
• Maximum number of cross-bridges formed
• No interference, no overstretching

Result: Maximum active tension

At this optimal length (2.0-2.2 μm):

• All myosin heads can interact with actin binding sites
• No interference from overlapping actin filaments
• Maximum number of cross-bridges form simultaneously
• This produces peak contractile force

Option B correctly shows this optimal arrangement - complete overlap between actin and myosin without actin-actin interference, allowing maximum cross-bridge formation and force generation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 8‑week pregnant woman is seeking medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). What is the appropriate dose of misoprostol when administered via the mucosal route?
questions.explanation: For medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) in the first trimester (up to 9 weeks or 63 days of gestation), the standard and most effective pharmacological regimen involves a combination of Mifepristone and Misoprostol. Following the oral administration of 200 mg of Mifepristone, the correct dosage of Misoprostol is 800 mcg (Option D) . This dose is typically administered 24–48 hours later via mucosal routes, such as vaginal, buccal, or sublingual, to ensure high efficacy in inducing uterine contractions and complete evacuation. Doses like 200 mcg (Option A) or 400 mcg (Option C) are insufficient for MTP and are used for other indications like cervical ripening or induction of labor at term. A 600 mcg dose (Option B) is standard for the prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. Therefore, 800 mcg remains the definitive standard-of-care dosage for first-trimester medical abortion
questions.learning: For medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) in the first trimester (up to 9 weeks or 63 days of gestation), the standard and most effective pharmacological regimen involves a combination of Mifepristone and Misoprostol.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with cough and hemoptysis and is diagnosed with pulmonary aspergillosis. He was treated with voriconazole. Which of the following is false about voriconazole?
options: It should be taken on an empty stomach
It can be combined with pyrazinamide
A loading dose should be given
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It can be combined with pyrazinamide

Voriconazole should not be combined with pyrazinamide. This is because, both these drugs are hepatotoxic and can cause fulminant liver failure if combined together. Thus, this is false with regards to voriconazole.

Voriconazole is an azole antifungal used in the management of pulmonary aspergillosis. It is also the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis, disseminated infections caused by fluconazole-resistant Candida, Fusarium infections, and febrile neutropenia not responding to antibacterial therapy.

Patients who are started on voriconazole should initially receive a loading dose of 6mg/kg body weight for 24 hours followed by 3-4mg/kg body weight for 12 hours.  After this, patients can be shifted to oral administration of the drug. Voriconazole is metabolized by the cytochrome p450 group of enzymes and thus its blood levels should be monitored. This is especially indicated in patients with liver disease to adequately titrate the drug dosage.(Option B). Patients are advised to take the drug on an empty stomach as fatty meals reduce the absorption of the drug(Option A)

Other adverse effects of voriconazole include rashes, photosensitivity, transient visual or auditory hallucinations and anaphylactoid reactions. Intravenous voriconazole should be used with caution in patients with renal failure.
questions.learning: It can be combined with pyrazinamide Voriconazole should not be combined with pyrazinamide. This is because, both these drugs are hepatotoxic and can cause fulminant liver failure if combined together.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child went to an ophthalmologist and is found to have a power of -1 D spherical and -2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees. What kind of astigmatism does the child have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. With the rule astigmatism

The child with a power of -1 D spherical and -2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees has with the rule astigmatism, as the vertical meridian is greater and more curved than the horizontal meridian.
Step 1 : - 1 D spherical would mean a power of -1 on vertical and horizontal axes.

| (-1)

--------|------- (-1)

Step 2 : - 2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees, would mean a power of -2 D at 90 degrees (perpendicular to 180).

| (-1 - 2 = -3)

--------|------- (-1)

Hence, as the vertical meridian (-3D) is greater than horizontal meridian (-1D), this would be with the rule astigmatism.
Astigmatism refers to the condition where there is different refractory power in both the principal meridians of the eye. Astigmatism is classified into two broad varieties - regular and irregular astigmatism.

• Regular astigmatism: there are two principal meridians.

• With the rule -  principal meridians are vertical and horizontal; both meridians at 90°; and the vertical meridian is more curved than horizontal.
• Against the rule (Option C) -  principal meridians are vertical and horizontal; both meridians at 90°; and the horizontal meridian is more curved than vertical.
• Oblique - the principal meridians are not vertical and horizontal, but they are at 90° to each other; e.g., at 45° and 135°.
• Bi-oblique -  the two principal meridians are not vertical and horizontal, and they are not at 90° each other; e.g., at 40° and 100°.

• Irregular astigmatism: there are multiple meridians.

Clinical presentation of astigmatism include asthenopia (tiredness of eyes relieved by closing the eyes), blurred vision and defective vision, elongation of objects, keeping reading material closer, and half closure of the lid.
Tilted or oval optic disc is seen on ophthalmoscopy. Retinoscopy shows different power on the two meridians. Other investigations include keratometry, astigmatic fan test, and Jackson’s cross-cylinder test.

Prescription in astigmatism: There are 3 components.

1) Power of the spherical component: Convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre sphere (DS)

2) Power of the cylinder: Convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre cylinder (DC)

3) Axis (orientation) of the cylinder

Other options :

Option A : In simple astigmatism, one of the meridia focuses on the retina. The other meridian focuses either in front of the retina (simple myopic) or behind the retina (simple hyperopic). Example, -1.00 DC × 180 degree.

Option D : Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina. Example, -1DS with +2DC at 180 degree.
questions.learning: With the rule astigmatism — The child with a power of -1 D spherical and -2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees has with the rule astigmatism, as the vertical meridian is greater and more curved than the horizontal meridian.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman complains of generalized body aches, fatigue, and difficulty standing. Neurological examination shows impaired vibration sense and proprioception, and laboratory tests reveal a low hemoglobin level. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate treatment to administer?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic triad of Megaloblastic Anemia (Hb 7 g/dL) and Subacute Combined Degeneration of the spinal cord (SCD). The loss of vibration sense and proprioception indicates damage to the posterior columns of the spinal cord, which is pathognomonic for severe Vitamin B12 deficiency. SCD can also involve the lateral corticospinal tracts, causing spasticity. Vitamin B1 deficiency (Option A) causes Wernicke’s encephalopathy (ataxia, confusion) or Beriberi but does not typically cause megaloblastic anemia or isolated posterior column loss. Vitamin C (Option B) deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums). Vitamin D (Option D) deficiency causes osteomalacia (bone pain), which might explain "body pain," but does not account for the specific neurological deficits or anemia. In such cases, Vitamin B12 must be administered parenterally (intramuscularly) to bypass potential malabsorption (like Pernicious Anemia). Clinicians must be careful to exclude B12 deficiency before giving folic acid, as folic acid can correct the anemia while allowing the neurological damage to progress

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A cancer patient undergoing radiotherapy is given a dose of 1.8 to 2 Gy once daily for 5 days per week for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. What is this type of brachytherapy called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient is given a dose of 1.8-2.0 Gy per day for 5 days a week, for 6 to 8 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumor is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximizes the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimizes the damage to the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumor cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells that were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumor cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

Standard Fractionation: Radiotherapy(RT) is given once daily for 5 days/week, not more than 2 Gy/fraction.

Accelerated Fractionation:(Option C) Any fractionation schedule that gives >10 Gy/week. Subtypes include:

* Pure accelerated fractionation (2 Gy/fraction, 6–7 fractions/week)

* Accelerated hypofractionation (>3 Gy/fraction)

* Accelerated hyperfractionation (>1 fraction/day)

Hypofractionation: Increased fraction size, with or without a decreased number of fractions/week.

* Stereotactic Radiation (SRS/SBRT/SABR): RT delivered with stereotactic localization techniques in five fractions or less.

* Fractionated Stereotactic RT (FSRT): RT delivered with stereotactic techniques and more than five fractions.

Hyperfractionation: Decreased fraction size with more than one fraction per day (BID or TID). (Option B)

Concomitant Boost (CB): Two fractions per day with one fraction to a large field and the other to a boost volume.

Simultaneous Integrated Boost (SIB): One fraction per day with a higher dose to a boost volume and a lower dose to the large field.

Note: Brachytherapy(Option D) is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.
questions.learning: Regular Fractionated radiotherapy Since the patient is given a dose of 1.8-2.0 Gy per day for 5 days a week, for 6 to 8 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with the lesion shown in the image. Which of the following will have least priority in calculating the prognosis in this patient? MRND-Modified radical neck dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Duration

The given image dipicts a patient with carcinoma of the lower lip and most likely has a squamous cell carcinoma of the lip. Duration of the lesion will not have any affect on the prognosis.

The factors that affect prognosis are:

* The biological behavior and histological grade (Option A)

* Extent or depth of invasion (Option B)

* Anatomical considerations like the site of the lesion (Option C)

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years old but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Most lip cancers occur in the lower lip followed by the upper lip and commissure. The most common site is the vermilion border of the lower lip. Ulcerative lesion on the vermilion border of the lower lip is the most common clinical manifestation. Mass can extend and fix on the underlying bone. Loss of sensation over the chin indicates mental nerve involvement. The most frequently involved nodes are the submental and submandibular nodes.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How is cerebral perfusion pressure calculated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mean arterial pressure - intracranial pressure

Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated as mean arterial pressure (MAP) - intracranial pressure (ICP).

However, ICP values are not readily available. In this case, CPP may be calculated as MAP - central venous pressure (CVP), and if CVP > ICP.

The brain depends on continuous perfusion for oxygen and glucose delivery, thus its survival. The blood flow to the brain is normally about 55 mL per 100 g of brain tissue. If the cerebral flow reduces to less than 20 mL per minute, the brain undergoes ischemia.

Blood flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP). Normally the CPP is 75-105 mmHg, MAP is 90-110 mmHg and ICP is 5-15 mmHg.

According to Monro Kellie doctrine, the cranium is a rigid box containing a nearly incompressible brain. In cases of head trauma, there is an expansion of cranial content, in the form of hematomas and brain swelling. This increase in cranial pressure is accommodated initially by the exclusion of fluid components, venous blood, and cerebrospinal fluid. Further increase in the cranial pressure leads to an uncontrolled rise in ICP resulting in a compromise in cerebral perfusion and eventually cerebral herniation.

Acute rise in ICP causes Cushing reflex, a triad of widened pulse pressure (increasing systolic, decreasing diastolic) bradycardia, and irregular respirations.

Thus, in cases of head injury with intracranial bleeding, cranial decompression is performed to avoid further complications due to the raised ICP.
questions.learning: Mean arterial pressure - intracranial pressure Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated as mean arterial pressure (MAP) - intracranial pressure (ICP).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the listed arteries is palpable on physical examination in the given image?
questions.explanation: The image shows palpation being performed behind the medial malleolus of the ankle. This is the classical anatomical location where the posterior tibial artery is palpated. The artery runs posterior to the medial malleolus, between it and the Achilles tendon, and is a key site for assessing peripheral circulation in the lower limb. Clinically, palpation of the posterior tibial pulse is important in evaluating peripheral arterial disease, especially in diabetic patients. It is one of the two main pulses checked in the foot, the other being the dorsalis pedis artery. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Anterior tibial artery → Not directly palpable at the ankle; continues as dorsalis pedis (C) Dorsalis pedis artery → Palpated on the dorsum (top) of the foot, not behind medial malleolus (D) Popliteal artery → Palpated in the popliteal fossa (behind knee)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The patient presented with alcoholic gait, and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) after RTA. Which lobe of the cerebellum is likely affected?

RTA - Road Traffic Accident
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flocculonodular Lobe

The flocculonodular lobe is involved in this patient with an alcoholic gait and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) following an RTA.

The cerebellum has three parts based on function.

• Vestibulocerebellum (or flocculonodular lobe): The oldest part of the cerebellum which contains nodulus in the vermis and the flanking flocculus. It has vestibular connections and is concerned with equilibrium and gait.  Loss of it can cause disturbance of equilibrium and postural movements, especially during rapid movements.

• Spinocerebellum: The region that receives proprioceptive input from the body as well as a copy of the “motor plan” from the motor cortex. By comparing the plan with performance, it smooths and coordinates movements that are ongoing. The superior vermis is a part of the spinocerebellum. Loss of it can cause problems with coordination.
• Cerebrocerebellum: They are the newest from a phylogenetic point of view, reaching their greatest development in humans. They interact with the motor cortex in planning and programming movements.

Other options:

Option B: The Dentate nucleus(largest) is one of the 4 deep cerebellar nuclei others being, Emoliform, Globose, and Fastigial nuclei. These receive input from climbing fibers and are the only motor output from the cerebellar cortex.

Option C: Anterior lobe is a part of the Paleo/Spinocerebellum responsible for the coordination of movement and regulation of muscle tone whose lesion results in hypotonia.

Option D: Interposed nuclei / Nucleus interpositus is the term used to describe the cerebellar nuclei, Emboliform, and Globose.
questions.learning: Flocculonodular Lobe — The flocculonodular lobe is involved in this patient with an alcoholic gait and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) following an RTA.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What instrument is required for the following procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystourethroscope

The instrument required for placing the Double J stent (DJ stent), as shown in the radiograph is a cystourethroscope.

Cystourethroscopy allows for the examination and access of the bladder and urethra, which is crucial for guiding the DJ stent from the bladder into the ureter. This procedure involves inserting a flexible or rigid endoscope through the urethra and into the bladder, where the stent can be manoeuvred into the ureter.

While ureteroscopy is typically used to visualize and treat issues directly within the ureter, cystourethroscopy provides the necessary access and visualization to position the DJ stent correctly. This approach is effective for ensuring the stent is placed accurately, particularly in cases where access to the bladder is essential.

Other options:

Option A: A ureteroscope is used to examine and treat the ureters (the tubes connecting the kidneys to the bladder). It is commonly used for removing kidney stones or evaluating issues in the ureter.

Option C: A nephroscope is a type of scope used to examine the kidneys directly. It is often used in procedures like percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) to remove large kidney stones.

Option D: An ultrasound-guided scope refers to an endoscope or medical device used in conjunction with ultrasound imaging to guide procedures. It’s often used in various parts of the body, including the gallbladder, liver, or kidney to help visualize structures during minimally invasive surgeries or biopsies.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a dental health checkup, a 10-year-old child is evaluated for oral development, focusing on the mix of permanent and deciduous (temporary) teeth. At this age, what is the expected number of permanent and temporary teeth?
questions.explanation: At 10 years of age, a child is typically in the late mixed dentition stage, where most permanent teeth have erupted while a few deciduous teeth still remain. By this age, the eruption of permanent teeth includes 8 incisors (4 central and 4 lateral) and 4 first permanent molars (6-year molars). In addition, premolars begin erupting around 10–11 years, and many exam-based standards assume that a majority of these premolars have erupted by age 10. This brings the total number of permanent teeth to approximately 20. At the same time, only a few deciduous teeth remain, usually canines and second molars, totaling about 4 temporary teeth. Although individual variation exists and some children may have fewer erupted permanent teeth, MCQ-based exams like FMGE follow standard eruption charts, which consider this stage as having 20 permanent and 4 deciduous teeth. Therefore, the most appropriate answer is (A) 20 permanent and 4 temporary teeth
questions.learning: At 10 years of age, a child is typically in the late mixed dentition stage, where most permanent teeth have erupted while a few deciduous teeth still remain.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of RCH program?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Women education and empowerment

The Reproductive and child health program(RCH) does not include women's education and empowerment as a component.

RCH program deals with the health status of young women and young children. The main objectives are reducing the total fertility rate, infant mortality rate and maternal mortality rate. It involves the following components:

* Essential and emergency obstetric care

* Control of reproductive tract infections (RTI) and sexually transmitted diseases (STD)

* Safe abortion services

* Full range of family planning services including laparoscopic services

* Essential newborn care and immunization

* Emergency care of sick children including diarrhoeal and acute respiratory disease

* Prevention and control of vitamin A deficiency and anaemia in children.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hereditary tubulo-interstitial kidney diseases has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nephronophthisis

Nephronophthisis (NPHP) is the most common genetic cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in children and adolescents. It is an autosomal recessive tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by mutations in genes encoding nephrocystin proteins (NPHP genes), which are involved in primary cilia function (ciliopathy).

The disease is characterized by progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis, corticomedullary cyst formation, and gradual loss of renal function.

• Polyuria and polydipsia due to impaired urinary concentrating ability
• Progressive CKD leading to ESKD in childhood or adolescence

Why not the other options?

• A. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 1: Autosomal dominant (now classified under Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease [ADTKD]).
• B. Medullary cystic kidney disease type 2: Also autosomal dominant, commonly associated with UMOD gene mutations.
• D. Juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy: Autosomal dominant, characterized by hyperuricemia, gout, and progressive CKD due to UMOD mutations.
questions.learning: Nephronophthisis Nephronophthisis (NPHP) is the most common genetic cause of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in children and adolescents. It is an autosomal recessive tubulointerstitial kidney disease caused by mutations in genes encoding nephrocystin…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following options can be employed for the treatment of Kesari dal toxicity?
questions.explanation: Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) consumption leads to neurolathyrism, a crippling spastic paraplegia caused by the neurotoxin BOAA. Studies and clinical observations have suggested that Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) may offer protective effects or act as an adjunct in management. Vitamin C is thought to help by reducing oxidative stress or potentially influencing the absorption and metabolism of the toxin. Sodium bicarbonate (Option A) is used for metabolic acidosis. Vitamin A (Option B) is used for ocular deficiencies. IV immunoglobulin (Option D) is used for autoimmune neuromuscular disorders like GBS. While the primary prevention is the avoidance of the dal or specialized soaking techniques to leach the toxin, Vitamin C remains the standard "medical" adjunct mentioned in this context. Therefore, Vitamin C is the only correct pharmacological option listed for addressing the toxicity associated with chronic Kesari dal ingestion

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A female presented with burning micturition and symptoms of Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Which of the following fluoroquinolones is least likely to be effective?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Moxifloxacin

Moxifloxacin does not accumulate significantly in urine and is not approved for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin, and Levofloxacin can be used in UTIs caused by susceptible organisms.
questions.learning: Moxifloxacin Moxifloxacin does not accumulate significantly in urine and is not approved for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs). Ciprofloxacin, Ofloxacin, and Levofloxacin can be used in UTIs caused by susceptible organisms.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 75-year-old woman presents with a vaginal mass as shown in the accompanying image. After pre-anesthetic assessment, she is found to be unfit for major surgical intervention. What is the most appropriate management procedure recommended for this patient?
questions.explanation: For an elderly patient (75 years old) with advanced pelvic organ prolapse who is deemed medically unfit for major reconstructive surgery, an obliterative procedure is the safest and most effective option. Le Fort’s colpocleisis involves denuding a portion of the anterior and posterior vaginal walls and suturing them together to obliterate the vaginal canal. This provides excellent support for the prolapsed organs with minimal surgical time and low anesthesia risk. Options A, B, and D are "sling" procedures or suspensions used in younger, sexually active patients to preserve vaginal function while correcting prolapse or nulliparous prolapse. Because the patient is unsuitable for major surgery and likely not prioritizing sexual activity, Le Fort's repair is the definitive gold standard. This procedure essentially "closes" the vagina to keep the pelvic organs in place. It requires the presence of the uterus and must include lateral channels for the drainage of cervical secretions
questions.learning: For an elderly patient (75 years old) with advanced pelvic organ prolapse who is deemed medically unfit for major reconstructive surgery, an obliterative procedure is the safest and most effective option.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The adjoining graph shows the effect of PTH on blood calcium and phosphate in an experimental animal. How does PTH increase plasma calcium?
options: By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. By increasing osteoclastic activity and decreasing renal excretion of calcium

Correct answer is D because PTH raises plasma calcium by stimulating bone resorption (via osteoclast activation indirectly through osteoblast signaling) and by increasing renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.

Bone: Osteoclast Activation

Important nuance: PTH does NOT directly act on osteoclasts

Instead:

1️⃣ PTH binds osteoblasts

2️⃣ ↑ RANKL expression

3️⃣ Activates osteoclasts

4️⃣ Bone resorption → Ca²⁺ released into blood

Kidney: Calcium Reabsorption

PTH acts on distal tubule:

↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption

↓ urinary calcium loss

Also: ↓ phosphate reabsorption

Intestine (Indirect)

PTH stimulates: Calcitriol formation

Which leads to: ↑ intestinal calcium absorption

At the same time, PTH increases phosphate excretion, explaining the fall in plasma phosphate in the graph.

| Organ | Effect

| ----- | ------

| Bone | ↑ Ca release

| Kidney | ↑ Ca reabsorption

| Kidney | ↓ phosphate reabsorption

| Intestine | ↑ Ca absorption (via Vit D)

Thus calcium rises due to combined skeletal release and reduced renal loss.

“PTH = Pulls calcium from bone + Preserves in kidney”
