questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies.

Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa. The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

Other options:

B) Leprosy: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous lesions, without much bacilli. Hence called paucibacillary leprosy. Lepromatous lesions contain large aggregates of lipid-laden macrophages (lepra cells), often filled with masses (globi) of acid-fast bacilli. Because of the presence of abundant bacteria, it is also called as multibacillary.

Given below are the images that depict lepromatous lesion showing foamy macrophages with globi of pink/red acid-fast bacilli and tuberculoid leprosy showing granulomatous lesions, respectively.

C) Mycosis fungoides: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characterized by polymorphic patches and plaques with fine scaling usually present on the limbs, breast, and buttocks. The lesions may be pruritic or even asymptomatic.  Histological hallmarks include: 1. Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/ hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane), 2. Pautrier's microabscesses - tumor cells invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters, forming a collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis and 3. Epidermotropism - pronounced invasion of the tumor cells into the epidermis.

Given below is the image of Sezary-Lutzner cells.

Given below is the arrow pointing at Paurtier's microabcess.

D) Visceral leishmaniasis: In visceral leishmaniasis, parasites invade and activate the macrophages throughout the mononuclear phagocyte system. Hence, these phagocytic cells are enlarged and filled with leishmania species; many plasma cells are also present.

The given slide shows macrophages infested with intracellular Leishmania donovani bodies (arrows) characterized by a kinetoplast and characteristic double dot appearance (Leishman stain).
questions.learning: Pemphigus vulgaris — The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about indications of hysterosalpingography are correct? I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae III. Detection of IUD IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a radiographic procedure in which a water-soluble contrast medium is injected through the cervix to visualize the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy. It is primarily used in the evaluation of infertility, especially to assess tubal patency and abnormalities of the uterine cavity. The following are appropriate uses of HSG:

• I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation: HSG is used to evaluate the success of tubal reconstructive surgery (tuboplasty) by confirming tubal patency.
• II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae: HSG can demonstrate intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) as irregular filling defects or partial obliteration of the uterine cavity.
• III. Detection of IUD: HSG can demonstrate the presence and position of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) within the uterine cavity.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid: Subserosal fibroids lie on the outer surface of the uterus and do not distort the uterine cavity, so they are not detected by HSG. They are better evaluated by ultrasonography or MRI.
questions.learning: I, II and III Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a radiographic procedure in which a water-soluble contrast medium is injected through the cervix to visualize the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A stone impacting on the cystic duct with dilatation of the common hepatic duct, producing CBD obstruction and jaundice is called as ___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mirizzi's syndrome

A stone impacting on the cystic duct with dilatation of the common hepatic duct, producing CBD obstruction and jaundice is called Mirrizi's syndrome.

Pearl PF1152: Mirizzi’s syndrome

Gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct or neck of the gallbladder producing CBD obstruction and jaundice.

* ERCP, PTC, MRCP will usually demonstrate the characteristic extrinsic compression of the CBD.

* Surgery consists of removing the cystic duct, diseased gallbladder, and the impacted stone.
questions.learning: Mirizzi's syndrome — A stone impacting on the cystic duct with dilatation of the common hepatic duct, producing CBD obstruction and jaundice is called Mirrizi's syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following combinations of seizure types and their corresponding medications is not accurate? 1. Generalized onset tonic-clonic: Lamotrigine 2. Focal seizures: Levetiracetam 3. Typical absence seizures: Topiramate 4. Myoclonic: Valproic acid
questions.explanation: The combination of "typical absence seizures with Topiramate" is "not accurate". Typical absence seizures (formerly petit mal) are standardly treated with "Ethosuximide" (the first-line agent) or Valproate. While Topiramate is broad-spectrum, it is not a primary or indicated treatment for absence seizures and can occasionally worsen them. Combination 1 is accurate: Lamotrigine is an effective first-line agent for "generalized onset tonic-clonic" seizures. Combination 2 is accurate: Levetiracetam is a first-line treatment for "focal (partial) seizures" due to its favorable side-effect profile (Option B). Combination 4 is accurate: Valproic acid remains the most effective "broad-spectrum" anticonvulsant and is the drug of choice for "myoclonic seizures" (Option D). Understanding the correct medication for each seizure type is critical, as giving the wrong drug (e.g., Carbamazepine for absence or myoclonic seizures) can lead to paradoxical exacerbation of the patient's epilepsy
questions.learning: The combination of "typical absence seizures with Topiramate" is "not accurate". Typical absence seizures (formerly petit mal) are standardly treated with "Ethosuximide" (the first-line agent) or Valproate.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
A 70 kg patient who presented to the emergency with acute pancreatitis was shifted to the ICU and intubated. His ventilatory settings are: FiO2 90%, PEEP 12 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, and tidal volume 420 ml. The results of the ABG analysis are given below. Which of the following would be the next step in the management of this patient?

pH: 7.33

PaO2: 110 mmHg

PaCO2: 58 mmHg

SpO2: 100%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reduce FiO2

In a patient with a history of acute pancreatitis who needed to be intubated, the diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most likely. In this patient, the PaO2 is 110 mmHg and the SpO2 is 100%, which are significantly higher than the target recommended in patients with ARDS. The next step in the management of this patient would be to reduce the FiO2 to prevent any further lung injury and worsening of ARDS due to oxygen toxicity. In the initial phase of the management, the FiO2 of the patient should be kept ≤ 60% and SpO2 should be maintained between 88-95%.

The main treatment strategy which has been shown to reduce mortality in patients is low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg of predicted body weight). Increasing the tidal volume (option B) in this patient will lead to barotrauma to the alveoli because air is pushed through the alveoli which are already collapsed.

Although a high PEEP keeps the alveoli opened up, there is no rationale for increasing the PEEP further (option A) in this patient because the oxygenation is adequate. Furthermore, PEEP must be adjusted to minimize FiO2 and provide adequate PaO2 at the same time.

Hypercapnia is expected in a patient on low tidal volume ventilation. It can be managed by increasing the respiratory rate. However, respiratory acidosis is tolerated by the patient up to a blood pH of 7.2. This is known as permissive hypercapnia. Reducing the respiratory rate (option C) in this patient will increase the PaCO2 further and cause a worsening of respiratory acidosis.

Apart from these, prone position, early neuromuscular blockade (to prevent the patient from fighting the ventilator), and use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) have also been shown to improve mortality in patients with ARDS. Management strategies that have not been shown to improve the outcome in ARDS patients include glucocorticoids, surfactant replacement, anti-inflammatory therapies like NSAIDs, and inhaled vasodilators.
questions.learning: Reduce FiO2 — In a patient with a history of acute pancreatitis who needed to be intubated, the diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most likely.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the following instrument?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Unipolar cautery

The given instrument is a unipolar cautery/monopolar cautery.

Other options:

Option B: The bipolar cautery contains two tips, unlike unipolar cautery which has only one tip. The current flows between these two tips and hence it does not need a return electrode, unlike the unipolar cautery.

Option C: The harmonic scalpel (shown below) is a surgical instrument used to simultaneously cut and cauterize tissue. Ultrasonic energy is used in Harmonic scalpel where ultrasonic energy is converted to mechanical energy at the active blade.

Option D: LigaSure vessel sealing system (shown below) is a bipolar apparatus for sealing vascular tissue. It applies a high coaptive pressure during the generation of tissue temperature under 1000°C, hydrogen cross-links are first ruptured and then renatured, resulting in a vascular seal that has high tensile strength.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with bitemporal hemianopia, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, and features suggestive of acromegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a complex endocrine profile: amenorrhea and lactation (indicating excess prolactin) combined with acromegaly-like features (indicating excess growth hormone). This dual secretion is characteristic of a mammosomatotroph adenoma (Option C). The presence of bitemporal hemianopia confirms a large pituitary tumor (macroadenoma) compressing the optic chiasma. Corticotroph adenomas (Option A) cause Cushing's disease. Gonadotroph adenomas (Option B) are usually clinically non-functioning. Gliomas (Option D) are tumors of the brain parenchyma rather than the pituitary gland and would not typically cause this specific hormonal triad. Mammosomatotroph cells are a single cell type that can produce both GH and prolactin. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring serum GH, IGF-1, and prolactin, along with an MRI of the sella turcica. Therefore, the combined hormonal symptoms and the visual field defect identify the specific pituitary tumor subtype
questions.learning: The patient presents with a complex endocrine profile: amenorrhea and lactation (indicating excess prolactin) combined with acromegaly-like features (indicating excess growth hormone).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort study

Cohort study is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect.

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect) because it eliminates many of the problems of the case-control study.

Relative risk (RR) calculated using cohort study demonstrates the relationship between cause and effect. It is a direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect. The larger the RR, the greater the strength of the association between the suspected factor and disease.

The advantages of cohort study are the following:

• The incidence can be calculated.
• Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied simultaneously.
• Provides a direct estimate of relative risk.
• Dose-response ratios can be calculated.
• Bias like misclassification can be minimized.

Other options:

Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins from the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.

Option C: A cross-sectional study is a prevalence study which is more useful for the study of chronic diseases. It is more appropriate for the study of the distribution of a disease in a population than studying its etiology.

Option D: Clinical trials are research studies performed on people that are aimed at evaluating new tests and treatments and their effects on human health outcomes.
questions.learning: Cohort study Cohort study is the best study design to demonstrate the relationship between cause and effect. A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the nerve action potential curve is correct?
options: At point E, the nerve is more excitable
Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels
Point B to D is refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point B to D is refractory period

Segment B to D spans depolarization and early repolarization when voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated. During this interval, a second action potential cannot be generated, defining the absolute refractory period.

Excitability only begins to return after further repolarization. Hence B to D represents the refractory period.
questions.learning: Point B to D is refractory period Segment B to D spans depolarization and early repolarization when voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated. During this interval, a second action potential cannot be generated, defining the absolute refractory period.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The rupture of penile urethra does not cause extravasation of blood into which of the following spaces?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ischiorectal fossa

Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial perineal pouch is a compartment of the perineum enclosed by the membranous layer of the perineal fascia that surrounds the scrotum or labia and penis or clitoris.

Anteriorly, the membranous layer of perineal fascia is continuous over the pubic symphysis and pubic bones. It is later continuous with the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall.  Thus, the fluid that accumulates in the perineal pouch extends to the lower anterior abdomen.

In the lower lateral abdominal wall, the abdominal fascia is attached to the deep fascia of the thigh, inferior to the inguinal ligament. Thus, on trauma at the penile urethra, urine does not extravasate into the anterior thigh.

The superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly by attaching the membranous layer of superficial fascia to the posterior margin of the urogenital diaphragm. Thus, commonly there is no extravasation into the deep perineal pouch and the ischiorectal fossa.

Also, the membranous layer of superficial fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami and forms the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle. Thus, the urine does not extravasate to the thigh.

But, the ischiorectal fossa would be a better answer because of the following reasons:

1. Bulbourethral glands that lie in the deep perineal space open their ducts into the spongy urethra, which is related to the superficial perineal space. Also, the muscles surrounding these glands were recently found to be a continuation of the deep transverse perinei and tail of the external urethral sphincter, both of which are components of the deep perineal space. Injury to the penile urethra can damage bulbourethral glands' ducts, which can lead to damage to the above-mentioned structures and may cause extravasation of urine into the deep perineal space.
2. Previously, the perineal membrane was thought to be a triangular membrane. However, recent studies show that it is contiguous anteriorly with the structures that support the urethra. Posteriorly, it is related to the support of the perineal body and lateral vaginal wall. So damage to the urethra might damage the anterior part of the perineal membrane which can make way for extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space.
3. Deep perineal pouch: It was believed initially that the urogenital diaphragm was formed by 3 layers: An inferior fascia (also called the perineal membrane), deep perineal space, and a superior fascia. The superior fascia formed the inferior border of the ischioanal fossa. The Colles fascia also separates the perineal membrane from the ischioanal fossa. So, extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space is possible but extravasation into the ischioanal fossa due to penile urethral injury is highly unlikely. Recent studies have shown that this might be a slightly more complex structure.
questions.learning: Ischiorectal fossa Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of chest pain at rest for 6 hours and ECG suggestive of Myocardial Ischemia. Which among the following is used for diagnosis? LDH - Lactate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LDH1

Measurement of LDH1 is suggestive of MI as it is seen predominantly in the heart.

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)

* Normally, serum levels of LDH2 are greater than those of LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1 is more than LDH2. This is called flipping of the LDH ratio.

*

LDH: A tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (Heart) and M isoform (Muscle)

* LDH-1: Heart.

* LDH-2: Blood.

* LDH-3: Brain, kidney, lungs, spleen, pancreas.

* LDH-4: Liver and skeletal muscle.

* LDH-5: Liver and skeletal muscle.

* MI diagnosis: LDH no longer recommended.

The other cardiac biomarkers are:

Troponin T and Troponin I

* These are the proteins that mediate calcium-mediated contraction of the cardiac and skeletal muscles.

* They are highly specific for MI.

* Troponin I is more important than troponin T.

* Troponins will remain elevated longer than creatine kinase (CK), for up to 14 days.

* This makes troponins a superior marker for diagnosing MI in the recent past (late diagnosis).

* Reinfarction: It is now clear that cardiac troponin (cTn) increases rapidly, even if it is from an abnormal baseline in patients with reinfarction.

* If the cTn concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction, the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement

Creatine kinase (CK).

* It is less sensitive and specific than troponins.

* For initial diagnosis of acute MI, cTn is preferred over CK

Myoglobin

* It is the earliest enzyme to increase after MI.

* Myoglobin is a protein found in the skeletal and cardiac muscles, which binds oxygen.

* It is a very sensitive indicator of muscle injury.

* However, it is not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle.

* The rise in myoglobin can help to determine the size of infarction.
questions.learning: LDH1 Measurement of LDH1 is suggestive of MI as it is seen predominantly in the heart. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) * Normally, serum levels of LDH2 are greater than those of LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1 is more than LDH2.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the Miami criteria for intraoperative parathyroid hormone (PTH) measurement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Half fall in 10 min

A drop in the level of PTH to less than half the maximum value (corresponding to the preoperative levels)  at 10 min postresection is the Miami criteria.

It is used to determine the extent of resection of the parathyroid gland which is done in a case of primary hyperparathyroidism due to adenoma.

Intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring is a commonly used adjunct, which guides the surgeon on when to stop parathyroid exploration and helps in confirming there is no residual hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue. The PTH levels are expected to drop after the gland is excised due to its short half-life (3-5 minutes). Blood is drawn at various time points and the hormone levels are assessed.

Based on the Miami Criteria, a more than 50% decline in PTH at 10 minutes following parathyroid gland removal compared to the highest baseline level, either the pre-incision or pre-excision, suggests a cure, and the procedure can be terminated.

Indications for parathyroidectomy:

All symptomatic patients with hyperparathyroidism should be offered surgery. Indications for surgery in asymptomatic patients include:

Serum calcium levels
0.25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit serum calcium of normal

Skeletal

• BMD by DEXA: T score –2.5 at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third of radius
• Vertebral fracture

Renal

• Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
• 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day)
• Increased risk of stone formation by risk analysis

Age
<50 years

*BMD - bone mineral density
questions.learning: Half fall in 10 min — A drop in the level of PTH to less than half the maximum value (corresponding to the preoperative levels) at 10 min postresection is the Miami criteria.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Oral contraceptives act by all of the following mechanisms except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase GnRH release

Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) do not cause an increase in GnRH, they inhibit the release of GnRH.

OCPs act via the following mechanisms:

• Inhibiting ovulation - Both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH). Seen in combined oral pills.
• Preventing implantation - Under the effect of OCPs, endometrial stroma undergoes hypoplasia, with atrophy of glands. This makes it unfavorable for implantation of the embryo. Seen primarily with mifepristone, but is a secondary mechanism of action with progesterone-only pills as well.
• Cervical mucus becomes thick and scanty under the effect of progesterone. This makes it difficult for sperm to enter. Seen in progesterone-only pills.
questions.learning: Increase GnRH release Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) do not cause an increase in GnRH, they inhibit the release of GnRH. OCPs act via the following mechanisms: • Inhibiting ovulation - Both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the examination of a patient, a professor asks the patient to invert his foot and points to a prominent tendon located behind the medial malleolus. Which tendon is being highlighted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tibialis posterior

The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior.

It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion. The tendon of this muscle becomes prominent in this area during foot inversion. Dysfunction of this tendon can lead to flatfoot deformity.

The given image shows the tarsal tunnel and position of the tendon of tibialis posterior:

Other options:

Option A: Tibialis anterior lies anterior to the medial malleolus and aids in dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot but is not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option B: Extensor digitorum is involved in extending the toes and runs anteriorly to the foot, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: Extensor hallucis longus extends the big toe and runs along the anterior portion of the foot, also not behind the medial malleolus.
questions.learning: Tibialis posterior — The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior. It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the Michaelis-Menten graph?
options: Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration
Km is directly proportional to enzyme concentration
Km is indirectly proportional to substrate concentration
Km has no relation to substrate concentration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration

The Michaelis-Menten equation/graph represents the enzymatic rate (Km) at different substrate concentrations i.e Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration

For a typical enzyme, as the substrate concentration increases, initial velocity (Vi) increases until it reaches a maximum value Vmax. With further increase in the substrate concentration, the enzyme is said to be “saturated” with the substrate and the velocity remains the same. Hence, the shape of the curve that relates to the velocity of the reaction to substrate concentration is hyperbolic.

The Michaelis-Menten equation illustrates mathematically the relationship between Vi and [S] i.e,

Vi = Vmax ×[S]/Km+[S]

The Michaelis constant (Km) is the substrate concentration at which Vi is half the maximal velocity (Vmax/2).

The plot of initial reaction velocity against substrate concentration is hyperbolic.
questions.learning: Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration The Michaelis-Menten equation/graph represents the enzymatic rate (Km) at different substrate concentrations i.e Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration For a typical enzyme, as the…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a bluish, translucent swelling under her tongue. She describes it as cystic, with visible veins on the surface. On examination, the swelling transilluminates, indicating a fluid-filled structure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a bluish, translucent, cystic swelling located specifically under the tongue on the floor of the mouth is highly characteristic of a ranula. A ranula is a type of mucocele that arises from the sublingual salivary gland due to ductal obstruction or trauma, leading to mucus extravasation into the surrounding tissues. Its characteristic "frog-belly" appearance and positive transillumination confirm its fluid-filled nature. In contrast, a dermoid cyst (Option B) typically presents as a midline swelling that is doughy on palpation and does not transilluminate. A thyroglossal cyst (Option C) is a midline neck mass that moves with tongue protrusion and is not located sublingually. A sublingual tumor (Option D) would typically be firm, non-translucent, and solid rather than cystic. Therefore, the anatomical location and classic physical signs documented in this 28-year-old patient definitively point toward a ranula as the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a bluish, translucent, cystic swelling located specifically under the tongue on the floor of the mouth is highly characteristic of a ranula.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the growth rate if the crude birth rate is 19 and the crude death rate is 7?
questions.explanation: The annual population growth rate (also known as the rate of natural increase) is determined by the difference between birth and death rates. The formula is: . 1. Calculate the Natural Increase: per 1,000 people. 2. Convert to Percentage: . Option B (0.7%) is merely the death rate expressed as a percentage. Options C (1.1%) and D (1.5%) are mathematically incorrect for this data set. This calculation assumes a "closed population" with zero net migration; in actual demographic studies, migration would also be factored in. A growth rate of 1.2% reflects a population in the middle stages of demographic transition, where mortality has dropped significantly, but fertility is still in the process of declining. This metric is vital for government planning regarding future needs for schools, housing, and healthcare

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is it called when a tour guide leads a group of tourists as they follow him through various attractions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herd

When a tourist guide directs a group of people who closely follow him at different tourist sites, it is referred to as herd behaviour.

A herd is a group of animals or people moving together, often following a leader or collective behaviour. In tourism, herd behaviour refers to a group of tourists following a guide, making collective decisions rather than acting independently.

Temporary social groups

* Crowd: It is a temporary group motivated by a common interest or curiosity. It lacks an internal organization and has no leader.

* Mob: The mob is a crowd with a leader, and is more emotional than a crowd. It is unstable and has no internal organization.

* Herd: This social group has a leader and the members have to follow his/her orders without question.

* A band is a permanent spatial group that constitutes a few families living together.

* Other permanent spatial groups are villages, cities towns and the state.
questions.learning: Herd When a tourist guide directs a group of people who closely follow him at different tourist sites, it is referred to as herd behaviour. A herd is a group of animals or people moving together, often following a leader or collective behaviour.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old morbidly obese patient develops respiratory distress on the third day after major surgery. What is the most likely initial differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A morbidly obese patient who develops sudden respiratory distress on postoperative day 3 is at extremely high risk for Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Obesity and major surgery are potent risk factors for DVT and subsequent PE (as established in Question 161). The timing is also characteristic, as PE most commonly occurs between days 3 and 7 post-op. Atelectasis (Option C) is the most common cause of fever and mild distress in the first 24-48 hours, but day 3 with "respiratory distress" strongly favors PE. Air embolism (Option B) occurs during the procedure or line insertion. Pneumothorax (Option D) usually presents immediately after trauma or a procedure. Clinicians must immediately order a CTPA or V/Q scan and start anticoagulation if clinical suspicion is high. This case highlights the critical importance of post-operative mobilization and prophylactic anticoagulation in high-risk patients to prevent this common and potentially fatal surgical complication
questions.learning: A morbidly obese patient who develops sudden respiratory distress on postoperative day 3 is at extremely high risk for Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Obesity and major surgery are potent risk factors for DVT and subsequent PE (as established in Question 161).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine examination, a neonate is noted to have poor weight gain and features suggestive of malnutrition, prompting the need for oral glucose supplementation. The pediatrician explains that intestinal absorption of glucose occurs via specific transport mechanisms in enterocytes, involving transporters on the basolateral membrane. Which cotransporter is primarily responsible for mediating glucose absorption in this context?
questions.explanation: The absorption of glucose from the intestinal lumen into the bloodstream involves two distinct steps. First, glucose is transported across the apical (brush border) membrane by the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT 1 (Option A). Once inside the enterocyte, glucose must pass across the basolateral membrane to enter the circulation; this second step is mediated by GLUT2. GLUT2 is a facilitative glucose transporter that moves glucose down its concentration gradient into the interstitial fluid. GLUT5 (Option C) is responsible specifically for fructose absorption. SGLT2 (Option D) is found in the kidneys, where it is responsible for glucose reabsorption from the renal tubules, not the intestine. Therefore, for the specific anatomical location of the basolateral membrane mentioned in the question, GLUT2 is the correct physiological transporter. Malfunction in these transporters can lead to malabsorption syndromes and failure to thrive in neonates
questions.learning: The absorption of glucose from the intestinal lumen into the bloodstream involves two distinct steps. First, glucose is transported across the apical (brush border) membrane by the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT 1 (Option A).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The best way to plot trends in the incidence of diarrheal disease in a given area is by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Line graph

Line graphs or line diagrams are the best way to plot trends in the incidence of a disease in a given area.

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.
questions.learning: Line graph Line graphs or line diagrams are the best way to plot trends in the incidence of a disease in a given area. Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data 1.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child is brought to the casualty with a history of dyspnea. His mother gives a history of foreign body aspiration. What is the first investigation to be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xray

The first investigation in a child with suspicion of foreign body aspiration is Xray.

Food items (nuts, seeds hard candy, gum, bones raw fruits, and vegetables) account for the majority of choking cases in children. The most common site of foreign body lodging is the bronchus. Foreign body aspiration into the airway has three stages: immediate symptoms of coughing and choking, an asymptomatic interval, and later complications such as fever, atelectasis, and pneumonia.

When a child presents with a history of choking, detailed history taking and physical examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx, neck, and lungs are necessary.

The next step for suspected foreign body aspiration is to obtain a chest X-ray, including the abdomen, despite most foreign bodies being radiolucent. Secondary findings on the X-ray can indicate foreign body involvement, such as air trapping, atelectasis, obstructive emphysema, asymmetric hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or consolidation. While a CT scan has high accuracy, it is not typically performed due to radiation risks.

The treatment of choice for a foreign body in the airway is its endoscopic removal with a rigid instrument, usually a bronchoscope, by a specialist otolaryngologist or pulmonologist. Bronchoscopy must be performed even if there is a high suspicion of an airway foreign body in spite of negative or inconclusive imaging.
questions.learning: Xray — The first investigation in a child with suspicion of foreign body aspiration is Xray. Food items (nuts, seeds hard candy, gum, bones raw fruits, and vegetables) account for the majority of choking cases in children.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presented with acute epigastric pain and nausea. Lab reports showed an increase in serum lipase levels. He received 2L of fluids during admission, and three days after stabilization, he developed sudden breathlessness. Chest X-ray is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

Non-Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema. It occurs due to: Increased permeability of pulmonary capillaries

Unlike cardiogenic edema:

• The problem is not heart failure
• It is due to inflammation and capillary leakage

Acute pancreatitis can trigger a systemic inflammatory response, increasing capillary permeability.

This leads to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, especially after aggressive fluid resuscitation.

Chest X-ray typically shows bilateral infiltrates with normal cardiac size.

PCWP is normal, distinguishing it from cardiogenic edema, and timing favors ARDS over embolism or aspiration.

| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic

| ------- | ----------- | ---------------

| Cause | Heart failure | Lung injury

| PCWP | Increased (>18 mmHg) | Normal (<18 mmHg)

| Heart size | Enlarged | Usually, normal

| Mechanism | Hydrostatic pressure | Capillary leak

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male with a history of chronic smoking is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip stage. Further investigations revealed that the lymph nodes are not involved. What is the treatment of choice in this patient?
options: Wide local excision with negative margins
Wide local excision with frozen borders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wide local excision with negative margins

This pateint has an early stage squamous cell carcinoma. Wide local excision with negative margins is the preferred treatment for this type of cancer.

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.
questions.learning: Wide local excision with negative margins — This pateint has an early stage squamous cell carcinoma. Wide local excision with negative margins is the preferred treatment for this type of cancer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following may be used to find the normalcy of data except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mantel-Haenszel test

Mantel-Haenszel method is used to calculate adjusted odds ratio during stratified analysis. It is not a test to detect normalcy of data.

A plot histogram and a box whisker plot are visual methods to assess if a given set of data is distributed normally. A normal distribution curve is an example of a plot histogram.

Sometimes just the visual representation of the data might not be enough to tell whether the data is normally distributed. This is where Shapiro-Wilk test comes in. It examines how closely a given set of data fits a normal distribution. The sample data is first ordered and standardized. An assessment is then made how the sample quantiles fit the standard normal quantiles. Shapiro-Wilk test is commonly used on small samples.

Stratified analysis of the data is done to reduce confounding. In such a scenario, multiple odds ratios are obtained — one for each stratum of the data. These have to be combined to give an adjusted odds ratio. This represents the effect of the exposure adjusted for the confounding factor. Mantel-Haenszel method is used for this purpose.
questions.learning: Mantel-Haenszel test Mantel-Haenszel method is used to calculate adjusted odds ratio during stratified analysis. It is not a test to detect normalcy of data.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Physiological dead space :
options: Is lesser than anatomical dead space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Represents inadequately perfused alveoli

Physiological dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli.

Physiological dead space is the part of the respiratory system where no gas exchange occurs. It includes:

1. Anatomic dead space: Air in the conducting airways (nose, trachea, bronchi) that doesn't reach the alveoli.
2. Alveolar dead space: Air in alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused by blood.

Together, it represents the total volume of air that doesn't participate in oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.(Option B)

Anatomical dead space refers to the volume of all the space of the respiratory system other than the alveoli that do not participate in gas exchange. The anatomical dead space is not altered with a change in ventilation.

In healthy individuals:

• Anatomical dead space = 150 mL.
• Alveolar dead space is usually zero (increased in diseased conditions).

Alveolar Dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli (wasted ventilation). (Option C)

In normal individuals, physiological dead space remains unaltered and is equal to the anatomical dead space (volume of all the space of the respiratory system other than the alveoli that do not participate in gas exchange).

Dead space cannot be measured using spirometry. (Option A)
questions.learning: Represents inadequately perfused alveoli Physiological dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli. Physiological dead space is the part of the respiratory system where no gas exchange occurs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 28-year-old male presents with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination throughout the day, as well as having to wake up several times at night to urinate. When questioned further, he admits to having sustained a head injury one month prior. His fasting blood glucose is within normal limits. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Desmopressin

The clinical vignette suggests the probable diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus, which is treated with desmopressin.

Diabetes insipidus of central or nephrogenic origin is characterised by low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a syndrome characterised by the excretion of abnormally large volumes of dilute urine. The 24-hour urine volume exceeds 40 mL/kg body weight, and the 24-hour urine osmolarity is <280 mOsm/L. There will be a slight increase in plasma osmolarity/sodium that stimulates thirst (polydipsia). Hence, clinical symptoms and signs of dehydration are uncommon unless thirst and/or water intake are also impaired.

Desmopressin is the drug of choice for neurogenic diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin is a selective vasopressin V2 receptor agonist. V2 receptors are present throughout the collecting ducts. The V2 receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor, which, when activated, results in a signaling cascade of adenyl cyclase, prompting an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) in the renal tubule cells, ultimately resulting in increased water permeability. This activity leads to a decrease in urine volume and an increase in urine osmolality. Extrarenal V2-like receptors are involved in the release of coagulation factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, which increases platelet aggregation. Desmopressin is used for the management of nocturnal polyuria, hemophilia A, central diabetes insipidus, and von Willebrand disease. Desmopressin can be administered orally at high doses and is contraindicated in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Its major adverse effect is water intoxication. It can also give rise to flushing and transient headaches.

In post-traumatic DI, patients lose their ability to concentrate urine due to the failure of anti-diuretic hormone secretion in acceleration-deceleration injury, leading to ischaemia and discontinuity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This leads to hypotonic polyuria with low osmolality. When this is associated with altered mentation and damage to the central osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus, thirst regulation is also impaired, preventing adequate fluid intake to compensate for the losses, leading to severe hypernatremia.

DI can be central or nephrogenic.

* Central DI occurs due to damage to the neurohypophysis in the posterior pituitary. It is characterised by decreased ADH. It can be treated with desmopressin, an ADH analogue.

* In nephrogenic DI, ADH levels may be normal or increased because the kidney has become resistant to its effects. Nephrogenic DI requires treatment with a thiazide diuretic, amiloride, a low-sodium diet, and indomethacin.

Other options:

Option A: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits the NaCl symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride. It may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Option B: The drug of choice for chronic SIADH is the oral administration of a vaptan (e.g., tolvaptan). They are selective V2 receptor antagonists that act by increasing urinary water excretion by blocking the antidiuretic effect of AVP.

Option C: Insulin is used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Wasting in a child is assessed by which of the following measures?
questions.explanation: Anthropometric indices are essential for identifying different forms of malnutrition in children. Wasting is defined as low weight-for-height and is a sensitive indicator of "acute" malnutrition. It reflects a recent and severe process of weight loss, often caused by acute starvation or a severe infectious disease episode. Height-for-age (Option D) is used to identify stunting, which represents chronic or long-term malnutrition resulting in a failure to reach linear growth potential. Weight-for-age (Option B) identifies a child as underweight; this is a composite indicator that can reflect both acute and chronic malnutrition but does not distinguish between them. Height-for-weight (Option C) is not a standard index used in pediatrics. Wasting is critical to detect because it carries a significantly high risk of mortality if the child does not receive immediate therapeutic feeding. The WHO growth standards use Z-scores for weight-for-height to diagnose moderate or severe acute malnutrition in community settings
questions.learning: Anthropometric indices are essential for identifying different forms of malnutrition in children. Wasting is defined as low weight-for-height and is a sensitive indicator of "acute" malnutrition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Fetal anaemia is primarily determined by Doppler assessment of which artery?
questions.explanation: Fetal anemia is best assessed using Doppler to measure the peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). In anemic fetuses, decreased blood viscosity and increased cardiac output lead to a measurable increase in blood flow speed. An MCA-PSV > 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) is a strong indicator of moderate-to-severe anemia. The umbilical artery (Option B) primarily assesses placental resistance and is used to monitor IUGR. The ductus venosus (Option C) evaluates fetal cardiac function and late-stage compromise. The uterine artery (Option D) measures maternal blood flow to the placenta to screen for preeclampsia risk. Because the MCA Doppler specifically reflects the fetal hemodynamic compensation for low hemoglobin, it is the primary diagnostic tool for fetal anemia
questions.learning: Fetal anemia is best assessed using Doppler to measure the peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). In anemic fetuses, decreased blood viscosity and increased cardiac output lead to a measurable increase in blood flow speed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, group A received placebo while group B received a new drug. In group A, 36 deaths were reported out of a sample of 120. In group B, 26 deaths were reported out of a sample size of 130. How many patients should be treated to avert 1 death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 10

10 patients need to be treated with the new drug to avert 1 death.

The number needed to treat (NNT) is defined as the number of individuals to be treated with the new drug to prevent 1 death (or to save 1 life).

NNT = 100/ARR

Where, ARR is the absolute risk reduction, which is the difference in the absolute risk rates between the placebo group and drug group. The absolute risk is usually expressed in percentage.

ARR = (No. of deaths/Sample population) x 100

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculation of absolute risk rate

The absolute risk rate in group A (placebo)

= (36/120)x100

= 30%

The absolute risk rate in group B (new drug)

= (26/130)x100

= 20%

Step 2: Calculation of absolute risk reduction (ARR)

ARR = Absolute risk rate in group A - Absolute risk rate in group B

= 30 - 20

= 10%

Step 3: Calculation of number needed to treat

NNT = 100/ARR

= 100/10

= 10

Therefore, 10 individuals need to be treated with the new drug to save 1 life.
questions.learning: 10 10 patients need to be treated with the new drug to avert 1 death. The number needed to treat (NNT) is defined as the number of individuals to be treated with the new drug to prevent 1 death (or to save 1 life).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following about Minimal Access Surgery are correct? I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss II. Improved visualization III. Increased chances of herniation IV. Improved mobility Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

Minimal Access Surgery (MAS), also known as laparoscopic surgery, is performed through small incisions using a camera and specialized instruments. Compared with open surgery, MAS is associated with reduced surgical trauma, faster recovery, less postoperative pain, and shorter hospital stay.

The following statements are true:

• I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss: Smaller incisions and reduced exposure of abdominal viscera result in less evaporative heat loss, thereby reducing intraoperative hypothermia.
• II. Improved visualization: The laparoscope provides magnified, high-definition visualization, allowing better identification of anatomical structures and meticulous dissection.
• IV. Improved mobility: Patients experience less postoperative pain, allowing earlier ambulation, reduced pulmonary complications, and faster recovery.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Increased chances of herniation: Laparoscopic surgery is associated with a lower incidence of incisional hernias because of the small port-site incisions. Although port-site hernias can occur, they are uncommon and mainly seen with ports ≥10 mm if fascial closure is inadequate.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Minimal Access Surgery (MAS), also known as laparoscopic surgery, is performed through small incisions using a camera and specialized instruments.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The given condition is caused by which drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleomycin

The given image shows flagellate dermatitis. It is caused by bleomycin.

Flagellate dermatitis starts as bands of pruritic, flagellate, erythema over the trunk, and extremities within few hours to 6 months after administration. The rash heals with persistent flagellate hyperpigmentation.

No treatment is necessary since the lesions usually disappear when bleomycin is discontinued. If the patient is itchy, managing pruritus with an antihistamine may limit trauma to the skin, and thus avoid further hyperpigmentation.

Another side effect that one needs to watch out for with the use of bleomycin is the development of pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.learning: Bleomycin — The given image shows flagellate dermatitis. Flagellate dermatitis starts as bands of pruritic, flagellate, erythema over the trunk, and extremities within few hours to 6 months after administration.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient came to the gynecology OPD with complaints of foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge and intense itching. On examination, the cervix appeared strawberry-like. Which of the following statements is false regarding the causative organism?
options: It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM or PEM
The treatment of choice is metronidazole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It exists in cyst and trophozoite form

The given clinical picture is suggestive of Trichomonas vaginalis infection.

Trichomonas vaginalis is the only protozoa with one stage in its life cycle ie., trophozoite form (No cyst stage is seen).

It is an obligate parasite and cannot live without close association with vaginal, urethral, or prostatic tissues. Sexual transmission is the main route of infection.

Trichomonas vaginalis has a jerky or twitching type of mobility on the wet saline mount.

The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM (cystine-peptone-liver infusion-maltose) or PEM.

The treatment of choice  is the oral dose of metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days.

questions.text: Which of the following organs can differentiate between the action of epinephrine and nor-epinephrine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bronchus

The bronchus can differentiate between epinephrine and norepinephrine because bronchial smooth muscle expresses predominantly β₂**-adrenergic receptors**. Epinephrine has strong β₂ agonist activity and causes bronchodilation, whereas norepinephrine has minimal β₂ action and therefore produces little to no bronchodilation. This functional difference allows clear distinction between their effects in the bronchial tree.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Atrioventricular node: Both act via β₁ receptors, increasing conduction similarly.

B. Iris of the eye: Both cause mydriasis via α₁ receptors.

D. Renal JGA: Both stimulate β₁ receptors, increasing renin release similarly
questions.learning: Bronchus — The bronchus can differentiate between epinephrine and norepinephrine because bronchial smooth muscle expresses predominantly β₂**-adrenergic receptors**.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the OPD due to acute-onset right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient had an extensive small bowel resection due to bowel ischemia a year ago and has been receiving total parenteral nutrition since then. Abdominal ultrasonography is shown below. Which of the following is most likely factor responsible?
options: Decreased cholecystokinin release due to lack of enteral stimulation
Decreased cholesterol conversion to bile acids due to liver dysfunction
High cholesterol content of the nutritional fluids
Inadequate supplementation of essential fatty acids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased cholecystokinin release due to lack of enteral stimulation

Patients receiving prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN) are at risk of developing gallbladder stasis and gallstones due to reduced enteral stimulation.

• Normally, fat and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin (CCK).
• CCK causes gallbladder contraction and bile release into the intestine.
• In patients on TPN, nutrients bypass the gastrointestinal tract, so CCK secretion decreases.

Consequences:

• Reduced gallbladder contraction
• Bile stasis within the gallbladder
• Formation of biliary sludge and gallstones
• Increased risk of acute cholecystitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has presented with multiple episodes of hematemesis. On admission his vitals are stable and splenomegaly is noted. The mother tells that at birth the boy had developed jaundice and an exchange transfusion procedure had been performed through the umbilicus after birth. The most likely cause of hematemesis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Portal vein thrombosis

The most likely cause of hemetemesis in this patient is Portal vein thrombosis.

Hemetemesis along with splenomegaly is suggestive of portal hypertension.

The mother says that he has gone an exchange transfusion via umbilical catheterization and after birth. As catheter acts as a foreign body it might have caused thrombosis of the portal vein leading to portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein drains into portal vein with around 50% of the blood entering  the hepatic circulation while the other 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava.

The fetal circulation :

Other options:

B) Sinusoidal fibrosis refers to the deposition of fibrous tissue within the liver sinusoids. While this condition can contribute to liver dysfunction, it is less likely to be the primary cause of hematemesis in this case.

C) Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (previously known as veno-occlusive disease) is a condition characterized by the blockage of small hepatic veins, resulting in congestion within the liver. It can cause liver dysfunction but is not typically associated with hematemesis.

D) Budd-Chiari syndrome is a condition characterized by the obstruction of the hepatic veins, leading to impaired blood flow out of the liver. It can cause liver dysfunction and portal hypertension, but it is less likely to present with splenomegaly and hematemesis in a young child.

Pearl PF1530: Classification of Portal Hypertension

* Prehepatic

* Portal vein thrombosis

* Splenic vein thrombosis

* Massive splenomegaly (Banti's syndrome)

* Hepatic

* Presinusoidal

* Schistosomiasis

* Congenital hepatic fibrosis

* Sinusoidal

* Cirrhosis of Liver (Most Common)

* Alcoholic hepatitis

* Postsinusoidal

* Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction (venoocclusive syndrome)

* Posthepatic

* Budd-Chiari syndrome

* Inferior vena caval webs

* Cardiac causes

* Restrictive cardiomyopathy

* Constrictive pericarditis

* Severe congestive heart failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with heartburn and chest pain described as a burning sensation, worsened after meals and when lying down, along with occasional regurgitation of acidic fluid into the throat. What is the most common condition causing these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of "burning" retrosternal pain, "heartburn," and "acidic regurgitation" that worsen after meals and with recumbency are pathognomonic for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD). The most prevalent underlying clinical condition or complication resulting from chronic acid reflux that actually causes this perceived pain and heartburn is esophagitis (Option D). Esophagitis is the inflammation of the esophageal lining due to gastric acid exposure. While myocardial infarction (Option C) is a critical life-threatening differential for chest pain, it would not typically be triggered by lying down after a meal. Pneumonia (Option B) involves fever and productive cough. Barrett's esophagus (Option A) is a premalignant metaplastic change resulting from chronic reflux, but the acute burning sensation itself is directly caused by the inflammatory state of esophagitis. Therefore, esophagitis is the definitive condition responsible for the patient's acute symptoms. Treatment involves lifestyle changes and proton pump inhibitors
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of "burning" retrosternal pain, "heartburn," and "acidic regurgitation" that worsen after meals and with recumbency are pathognomonic for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How can lead time in disease screening programs be minimized?
options: By implementing periodic screening of the target population
By delaying diagnostic confirmation until symptoms appear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. By implementing periodic screening of the target population

Lead time is the interval between detection of disease by screening and usual clinical diagnosis. Excessive lead time can distort survival statistics (lead time bias).

How to minimize lead time in screening programs:

• Periodic (regular) screening ensures cases are detected closer to the time they would become clinically apparent, rather than too early.
• This reduces artificial inflation of survival time without truly improving prognosis.
questions.learning: By implementing periodic screening of the target population Lead time is the interval between detection of disease by screening and usual clinical diagnosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the cause of the constriction encountered at the oesophageal junction, approximately 25 cm from the incisors, during endoscopic examination?
questions.explanation: The esophagus has four physiological constrictions where foreign bodies are most likely to lodge and which are important landmarks during endoscopy. These are measured from the upper incisor teeth: 1. At the pharyngoesophageal junction (15 cm), caused by the cricopharyngeus muscle. 2. Where it is crossed by the arch of the aorta (25 cm) (Option B). 3. Where it is crossed by the left main bronchus (not the right, Option C) (28 cm). 4. Where it passes through the diaphragmatic opening (40 cm) (Option D). The inferior vena cava (Option A) does not cross or constrict the esophagus. Therefore, a constriction felt specifically at the 25 cm mark during an endoscopic procedure is anatomically localized to the site where the aortic arch indentates the esophageal wall. Accurate knowledge of these distances is essential for endoscopists to accurately describe the location of lesions or obstructions

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with supraspinatus tendinitis. At what degree of shoulder abduction is pain most likely to occur in this condition?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus tendinitis is a common cause of shoulder pain. The hallmark clinical finding is the "Painful Arc" sign. A patient with this condition typically experiences maximal pain during mid-range shoulder abduction, specifically between 60 and 120 degrees (Option B) . This occurs because the inflamed supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa are compressed against the acromion as the humerus rotates upward through this specific range. Pain from 0-60 degrees (Option A) is less common and may suggest other pathologies. Pain after 120 degrees (Option C) often diminishes as the greater tuberosity cleared the acromion, or it may indicate an AC joint issue. Because the subacromial space is most narrow during the middle of the abduction arc, the 60-120 degree range is the definitive clinical hallmark for subacromial impingement and supraspinatus tendinitis. This is a fundamental concept in orthopedic physical examination of the shoulder
questions.learning: Supraspinatus tendinitis is a common cause of shoulder pain. The hallmark clinical finding is the "Painful Arc" sign.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man with a chronic history of IV drug use presented with a progressively increasing swelling in the groin on the right side. It is is non fluctuant but pulsatile on examination. He has diminished pulses on the same side distal to the swelling. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
options: CT angiography followed by surgical intervention
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT angiography followed by surgical intervention

The patient most likely has a pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery, caused by repeated penetrating injuries during intravenous drug administration. The recommended approach includes conducting a CT angiography for diagnosis, followed by surgical intervention.

In pseudoaneurysm, the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only compared to a true aneurysm where all three layers are involved. It usually occurs secondary to trauma- arterial samples, arterial catheterization and IV drug users. It is usually pulsatile and systolic bruit can be heard on auscultation.

Doppler ultrasound reveals a bidirectional, 'to-and-fro' flow of blood which is known as the yin-yang sign. Management includes the delineation of anatomy using CT-Angiography. Treatment options include open or endovascular surgery.

Other options

Option B: Antibiotics are used when the local wound appears infected with pus discharge or systemic symptoms of malaise and fever. However, imaging and surgical intervention will be needed.

Option C: Compression stockings are used in the management of chronic venous insufficiency.

Option D: Incision and drainage are required for the management of abscesses.  It should be avoided in the case of a pseudoaneurysm.
questions.learning: CT angiography followed by surgical intervention — The patient most likely has a pseudoaneurysm of the femoral artery, caused by repeated penetrating injuries during intravenous drug administration.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an idiosyncratic reaction of carbamazepine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blurred vision

Blurred vision is not an idiosyncratic reaction of carbamazepine.

Idiosyncratic blood dyscrasias with carbamazepine, include fatal cases of aplastic anaemia and agranulocytosis. The most common idiosyncratic reaction is an erythematous skin rash. It can rarely cause Steven Johnson Syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At which vertebral level is the abdominal plane marked as 2?
questions.explanation: In the anatomical division of the abdomen into nine regions, specific horizontal planes are used as landmarks. The plane marked as '2' in the provided diagram is the subcostal plane. This plane is defined by a line connecting the lowest points of the costal margins (the 10th costal cartilage). Anatomically, the subcostal plane corresponds to the level of the upper border of the L3 vertebra. The transpyloric plane, which is often labeled above it, is located at the lower border of the L1 vertebra (Option A) or the upper border of L1 (Option B) depending on the anatomical reference used for the pylorus. The supracristal plane, used to mark the highest points of the iliac crests, typically corresponds to the lower border of L4 (Option D). Therefore, based on standard anatomical conventions for the subcostal plane, the correct vertebral level is L3
questions.learning: In the anatomical division of the abdomen into nine regions, specific horizontal planes are used as landmarks. The plane marked as '2' in the provided diagram is the subcostal plane.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding acute radiation syndrome?
options: GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression
Bone marrow suppression appear at doses greater than 1 Gy
Bone marrow suppression occurs earlier than neurovascular effects
GI manifestations occur at a lower radiation dose than neurovascular effects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression

GI manifestations do not occur at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression.

Stages of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)

The prodromal phase manifests with non-specific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia. Early and persistent symptoms predict severity.

Latent phase: The patient looks and feels generally healthy for a few hours or even up to a few weeks. In severe cases, this phase may be absent.

Manifest illness phase: Symptoms are seen as per the radiation dose. Tissues with greater rates of cellular division are most radiosensitive, and hence the hematopoietic and gastrointestinal systems are the most affected.

Recovery phase or Death: The recovery phase will be seen after the manifest stage when the patient recovers from the acute exposure. The time taken for recovery will depend on the severity of the injury and the organ system affected.

Radiation dose
Sub-syndrome
Features

~1-2 Gy
Hematopoietic

Bone marrow suppression

~6-10 Gy
Gastrointestinal
Nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, malabsorption,

~20Gy
Neurovascular

irritability, altered mental status, seizures, coma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive mother with a viral load of 1200 copies/mL delivers a newborn baby. What is the most appropriate antiretroviral prophylaxis for the newborn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nevirapine + Zidovudine for 12 weeks

In infants born to HIV-positive mothers, the choice and duration of antiretroviral prophylaxis depend on the risk of transmission, primarily determined by maternal viral load.

• High-risk exposure (maternal viral load >1000 copies/mL or unknown) requires combination prophylaxis
• Recommended regimen: dual therapy with Nevirapine + Zidovudine for extended duration (e.g., 12 weeks)
• Low-risk exposure (viral load <1000 copies/mL, good ART adherence) may receive single-drug prophylaxis

Clinical importance:

• Early initiation (within hours of birth) significantly reduces vertical transmission
• Adherence to prophylaxis and follow-up testing is essential

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure and a history of chronic atrial fibrillation, currently on digoxin therapy, presents with episodes of palpitations and light-headedness. Based on this presentation, which drug should be administered for effective management of her ventricular arrhythmias?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of palpitations and light-headedness while on digoxin suggest Digoxin Toxicity, which can cause a variety of arrhythmias. For ventricular arrhythmias specifically caused by digoxin toxicity, "Lignocaine" (lidocaine) is the drug of choice. Lignocaine is a Class IB antiarrhythmic that effectively suppresses ventricular irritability without significantly worsening the AV conduction delay often associated with digitalis. Procainamide (Option A), a Class IA agent, is generally avoided as it can increase digoxin levels and prolong the QT interval. Atropine (Option C) is used for symptomatic bradycardia but not for ventricular arrhythmias. Propranolol (Option D), a beta-blocker, can worsen the heart block caused by digoxin. Definitive management for severe toxicity includes the administration of Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab) and correction of electrolyte imbalances, particularly hypokalemia, which potentates digoxin's effects
